## 2026-10-17 — Settings pane: layout direction, Voice pickers, dark mode

### The section list rendered as a strip across the top, content underneath it [FIXED]

- Attempted: answer "why content is not on the right side and is on the bottom?" about
  Settings.
- Symptom: the pane is `class="main-pane settings-layout"`. `.settings-layout` declares
  `display: flex; min-height: 100%` but no `flex-direction`, while `.main-pane` declares
  `flex-direction: column`. Both are single-class rules on the same element, and only one
  of them sets the property, so the pane kept `column`. Measured live:
  `flexDirection: "column"`, `nav { x: 64, y: 0, w: 200, h: 535 }`,
  `body { x: 64, y: 535, w: 982, h: 281 }` — a 200px-wide section list across the top with
  the section's content under it, and a `border-right` on the nav with nothing to its
  right.
- Resolution: FIXED — `flex-direction: row` on `.settings-layout`, plus `flex: none` on
  `.settings-nav` (mirroring `.rail { flex-shrink: 0 }`) so a wide body cannot squeeze the
  list below its labels. Measured after: `flexDirection: "row"`,
  `nav { x: 64, w: 200, h: 816 }`, `body { x: 264, w: 782, h: 816 }`.
- Re-checked the previous slice's scroll fix under the new layout: the About pane
  (scrollHeight 519, clientHeight 480) scrolled to 39, "Check for updates" clicked, and
  `scrollTop` was still 39 with the outcome note up.
- Lesson: a modifier class that sets `display: flex` but not `flex-direction`, stacked on a
  base class that does, is invisible in the CSS file and only shows up as geometry. The
  nav's `border-right` was the tell that the intended direction was row. Introduced with
  the settings pane itself (`5faea5e`), so it predates every slice in this log.

### Device pickers stacked one pair per selection [FIXED]

- Attempted: fix the reported "when u choose something it creates another and another and
  another drop downs".
- Symptom: `renderVoiceSettings` built its device pickers inside `fill()`, and `pick()`
  appended the label and the `<select>` to `wrap` — the outer section container, which is
  never cleared. `fill()` runs again from the `.then()` of every `voiceSelectDevices`
  call, so each selection appended another Microphone/Speaker pair. Confirmed live before
  the fix path was written: two selections produced four dropdowns.
- Resolution: FIXED. The pickers are now created once, held in a `pickers` map keyed by
  side, and re-synced in place (options rebuilt only when the device list actually
  changed, value re-set from `selected`). Verified live: after two selections the pane
  still holds exactly two `<select>`s (`["pipewire","pulse"]`, 4 and 16 options), and the
  picker the user just used keeps focus instead of being destroyed under it.

### Voice section had no colour scheme, so native controls stayed light [FIXED]

- Attempted: explain "it doesnt' appear good in dark mode".
- Symptom: nothing in the stylesheets declared `color-scheme`. The theme is
  `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, which recolours the app's own CSS variables but says
  nothing to the platform, so a `<select>`'s option list (and scrollbars, and the date
  picker) render light while the app is dark — the classic white-menu-with-light-text
  result, since `base.css` sets `select { color: inherit }`.
- Resolution: FIXED at the root, not on the one picker: `color-scheme: light` on `:root`
  and `color-scheme: dark` on `:root[data-theme="dark"]` in `tokens.css`. Verified live in
  dark mode: `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).colorScheme === "dark"`, and the
  picker computes `background rgb(27,27,36)` / `color rgb(242,242,247)`.
- Not verified: the open popup itself could not be captured — it is a platform menu, not
  page DOM, so `browser_select_option` sets the value without opening it. The claim rests
  on `color-scheme` being what the platform reads, not on a screenshot of the menu.

### Pickers spanned the whole settings pane [FIXED]

- Symptom: "its wide af". `.input-field` is `width: 100%`, and the Voice section had no
  cap, so on a 1000px window the selects were 967px wide (the full `.settings-body`)
  while the meter beside them was capped at 420px.
- Resolution: FIXED with `.voice-settings { max-width: 480px }`, matching the meter's
  column. Measured live after the change: pane 480px, both selects 480px, against a
  967px settings body.

### The session's starting git status was stale [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: read `git diff` on `app.ts` to review only my own edits.
- Symptom: the session context's `git_status` snapshot listed four modified files and did
  not include `app.ts`, but `git diff` showed a large uncommitted voice/conclave-unread
  feature in that same file. The snapshot is documented as taken at conversation start
  and not updated; it was also simply incomplete, which briefly made another session's
  work look like mine.
- Resolution: worked around by re-running `git status` before attributing any hunk.
  No repo change; the other session's work is untouched.
- Lesson: treat the injected `git_status` as a hint, never as the working tree.

### A `/status` probe returned empty and read as "daemon down" [FIXED]

- Attempted: check whether a daemon was listening and whether its vault was locked.
- Symptom: `curl http://127.0.0.1:9899/status` printed nothing, which looked like a dead
  daemon (the process was alive and listening). The route is `/api/status`; the 404 body
  is empty, so a wrong path and a dead server are indistinguishable by output alone.
- Resolution: FIXED by probing `/api/status`. Worth remembering that this daemon answers
  an unknown path with an empty body and no status line.

### CSS edit collapsed a rule onto one line [FIXED]

- Attempted: insert a new rule above `.voice-meter` in `app.css`.
- Symptom: the `old_string` ended with `.voice-meter {\n` and the `new_string` with
  `.voice-meter {`, which joined the selector to the next declaration —
  `.voice-meter {  width: 100%;`. Still valid CSS, but mangled formatting.
- Resolution: FIXED with a follow-up edit that restored the line and added the new rule.

  or drops a trailing newline. Check the boundary characters, not just the anchor text.

## 2026-10-17 — App smoothness slice (render coalescing)

### Rail search fields drop the caret after one character [FIXED]

- Attempted: while auditing every `this.render()` call site for the swap to a coalesced
  `scheduleRender()`, classify which sites depend on the render completing synchronously.
- Symptom: `render()` wipes `this.root.innerHTML = ""` and restores focus afterwards only
  for composer textareas (keyed by `data-composer-key`). Search inputs that re-render in
  their own `oninput` — Chats (`this.search`), Mail (`this.mailSearch`), Drops
  (`this.dropInboxSearch`), torrents library (`this.torrentsLibrarySearch`) — are destroyed
  mid-typing, so focus falls to `body` and the second keystroke goes nowhere. The atproto
  explore search documents the identical mechanism in-repo and fixes it by re-querying the
  new tree and re-focusing ("without this the field drops the caret after one character");
  the four rail search fields have no such fix. Not reproduced in the running app —
  inferred from the code plus that comment.
- Resolution (2026-10-18): the four fields no longer render at all. Each list now draws
  every row and a keystroke hides the ones that do not match, which is the Trusts and
  Conclaves pattern the entry named, extracted into `lib/rowFilter.ts` and used by all six
  filters. A keystroke touches only rows, so the field it came from is still in the
  document and still has the caret. See the 2026-10-18 section above for what the change
  cost and what it could not cover.
- Status: FIXED in code; not verified in a running app (see the 2026-10-18 section).
  Pre-existing, not introduced by the render-coalescing slice.

### hush-daemon PSS unreadable: /proc smaps_rollup permission denied [WORKED AROUND]

## 2026-10-17 — Paper save feedback and the announce() sweep

### announce() is sighted-invisible, so most error feedback never showed [FIXED]

- Attempted: add "saved" feedback to the paper's Save-as-note button after the user
  reported none. The success toast was already there; the real gap was elsewhere.
- Symptom: `App.announce` writes to an `sr-only` aria-live region — deliberate per the
  toast.ts header — so every error path that only called `announce()` (paper save/start,
  chat sends, conclave create/invite/kick/leave/end/delete, presence, zines, mail delete,
  drop keys, backups, clipboard failures — 52 sites) was invisible to sighted users. A
  failed save looked exactly like a dead button. The paper-save button also disabled
  with no label change, so a slow daemon (1–33 s, see the peer-A entry below) read as
  "nothing happened".
- Resolution: FIXED in two steps. (1) The paper pane's Save-as-note button now shows
  "Saving…" → "Saved ✓" in place (safe because `paperHost` DOM is stable across
  re-renders), and its failure paths toast. (2) User approved a sweep: all
  announce-only error/refusal paths now `showToast(..., { kind: "error" })` (toasts
  carry `role="status"`, so SR support is kept, no double-announce). 51 announce() sites
  remain, all success confirmations, ambient arrivals, or already paired with a visible
  inline error. `tsc --noEmit` clean, node tests 83/83, no lint errors.
- Lesson: an a11y channel is not user feedback. Success-path announce()-only sites
  ("Invite sent", "Mail sent", copy confirmations) remain invisible to sighted users —
  a deliberate scope cut for this pass; they are the natural next sweep if the
  pattern proves itself.

## 2026-10-17 — Voice device settings (Settings → Voice)

### The device thread never wrote the input rates it opened [FIXED]

- Attempted: build the device health panel on the existing `DeviceAudio.in_rate` /
  `in_channels` fields.
- Symptom: the comment claimed "the real rates are written by the device thread" but no
  write existed — the fields kept their 48 kHz mono construction defaults forever. A mic
  opened at 44.1 kHz (HDA analog's common default) or in stereo was resampled as if it
  ran 48 kHz mono: wrong speed and doubled samples, i.e. garbled voice.
- Resolution: FIXED — fields are atomics written from the config actually opened; the
  device-tap test now asserts the opened rate is the device's real one.
- Lesson: a comment that promises a write is not a write; the health panel exists
  precisely because this class of silent wrongness had nowhere to surface.

### Malformed JSON rejects before the lock check on POST routes [FIXED]

- Attempted: assert every `/api/voice/*` route answers 401 while locked, including the
  new device routes.
- Symptom: `POST /api/voice/devices` with a malformed body returned 422 (and a bodyless
  `POST` to a `Json<T>` route returned 415) instead of 401 — axum's extractor rejects the
  request before the handler's lock check runs.
- Resolution: FIXED for the test (valid JSON bodies); the pre-auth rejection itself is
  API-wide, pre-existing behavior, and leaks nothing (a body shape error says nothing
  about rooms). Left as-is, logged so it is not re-diagnosed.
- Lesson: extractor rejections happen before handler auth; a 401-sweep must use bodies
  the extractor accepts.

### First open of the selected "pipewire" input takes seconds [OPEN]

- Attempted: select the `pipewire` input by name through `POST /api/voice/devices` and
  watch the probe's meter go live.
- Symptom: `input_live` stayed false for ~3–11 s, then came up with real levels. The
  slow part is pipewire's ALSA plugin negotiating its first open; the API answered 200s
  in ~2 ms the whole time (the open lives on the device thread, as designed).
- Resolution: OPEN, environment (ALSA/pipewire on this box), not a repo bug. The health
  panel renders the wait honestly ("not opening" then "live"); if it bothers someone,
  the fix is a pre-open warmup or a native pipewire host, not this panel.
- Lesson: "selected device not yet live" and "daemon hung" must be distinguishable from
  the outside — the meter's `input_live` plus the responsive API is that distinction.

### A `&`-backgrounded `&&` chain loses its variables [FIXED]

- Attempted: scratch-daemon curl check as one compound line ending in `... init ... && ... daemon ... &`.
- Symptom: `&` backgrounds the whole chain, so `T=$(mktemp -d)` existed only inside it —
  every following command saw an empty `$T` and curl hit nothing.
- Resolution: FIXED by backgrounding only the daemon (`... daemon ... & DPID=$!`) with the
  setup chain in the foreground.
- Lesson: `&` binds to the entire preceding `&&`/`;` list, not the last command.

## 2026-10-17 — AppImage version forensics

### Reading the running version off the AppImage filename is wrong [FIXED]

- Attempted: report which version the prod AppImage instance runs, judged from the
  filename `/home/sam/Applications/Hush_0.2.0_amd64.AppImage` — told the user they were
  on 0.2.0 while the relay serves 0.3.1.
- Symptom: user corrected it — the running instance reports 0.3.1. The updater rewrites
  the AppImage **in place** (the documented RELEASING.md behavior via the `APPIMAGE` env
  var) and never renames the file, so the filename is the first-install version, not the
  running one. File mtime (2026-10-17 18:18) is the last update, not the install.
- Resolution: diagnosis corrected with evidence. The live tree (hush-tauri pid 2584826,
  daemon 2584908) executes from `/tmp/.mount_Hush_0PLCcGP`, whose binaries are stamped
  23:10 UTC — the v0.3.1 workflow build (tag created 22:48 UTC, published 23:15 UTC);
  instance started 23:18 UTC. The on-disk file carries the same v0.3.1 content. The
  daemon API cannot answer this: `/api/status` has no version field.
- Lesson: version questions are answered by `/proc/<pid>/exe` + the mount's binary
  mtimes mapped against `gh release view` build times — never by the AppImage filename.

### The updater leaves a childless husk process after an in-place update [OPEN]

- Attempted: reconcile two `Hush_0.2.0_amd64.AppImage` PIDs (15:51 and 18:18) with the
  user's "both instances are 0.3.1".
- Symptom: pid 2334948 (15:51) has exe `/home/sam/Applications/tauri_current_appLY2QUj/
  current_app.AppImage (deleted)` — the updater's staging copy from the afternoon's
  v0.3.0 relaunch — with no children (no hush-tauri, no daemon), 2 threads, and no mount
  of its own. It looks like a second running instance in `ps` but runs nothing.
- Resolution: OPEN (cosmetic). Harmless; can be killed. The exact relaunch choreography
  that strands it was not investigated — updater internals, not an app bug.
- Lesson: count Hush instances by `hush-tauri` + daemon processes, not AppImage PIDs.

## 2026-10-17 — Conclave invite button investigation

### Prod "fresh meeting" invite can never arrive: mahmood is on the old relay [OPEN]

- Attempted: explain why the conclave invite to `mahmood` sat in state `invited` with the
  contact permanently `online: false`.
- Symptom: sam's vault queues the invite on `hushrelay.space`, but mahmood's vault still
  points at the old relay and is offline, so mahmood never drains sam's writes. Regrants do
  not bridge this: the regrant announcement itself rides the old queue.
- Resolution: diagnosed, not fixed — nothing to fix in the repo. The user confirmed mahmood
  is on the old relay and offline. When mahmood returns they must repoint their vault to
  `https://hushrelay.space` (`hush-cli relay set`) before any queued invite/message can
  arrive, and whether the queued invite is still there depends on the relay's retention TTL.
  Evidence is the user's own report, not a wire capture.
- Lesson: `invited` forever + never-online is a relay-mismatch signature; check both vaults'
  `client-config.json` before suspecting the invite path.

### Peer A's dev daemon answers in 1–33 s per request; peer B answers in 1 ms [OPEN]

- Attempted: open peer A's vite pane (`:5173/?api=http://127.0.0.1:9876`) to exercise the
  conclave Invite button in the real UI.
- Symptom: `#app` stayed empty for minutes. Resource timing inside the page shows the app's
  own requests crawling: `/api/ui-prefs` 28 s, `/api/status` 22.5 s and 18 s, `/api/contacts`
  32.8 s — while the same `/api/status` answers curl in 0.2–4.2 s on A and 1 ms on B, from the
  same machine, with A's process at 0.8% CPU. A raw in-page fetch also hung past an 8 s abort
  on one try after succeeding in ~4 s earlier, so latency is wildly variable per request. The
  boot chain awaits five endpoints serially (`refreshStatus`: status → contacts → messages →
  mailbox → conclaves), so first paint takes minutes and the pane reads as dead.
- Resolution: none yet. A's state differs from B's in one visible way: A's contact view of bob
  has `inbound_ready: false` (B's view of alice is `true`), and `POST /api/outbox/retry` did
  not flip it, so A runs a stuck reach handshake that retries every outbox tick (30 s) over the
  remote relay on the single worker actor — every API call queues behind it. That fits the
  bursts but not the continuously high per-request latency; root cause not found. Daemon stdout
  could not be read (sandbox denies `/proc/<pid>/fd`). Restarting A's daemon is the obvious
  next experiment, and serializing the boot chain or adding a timeout to `request()` would
  keep the pane usable while a daemon is slow.
- Lesson: a "blank pane" was two problems stacked — a slow daemon and a boot chain that paints
  nothing until every serial fetch lands. Measure inside the page (`performance` resource
  entries) before concluding the frontend hung.

### Inbound conclave delivery never advances on a headless daemon — only a UI poll pulls [OPEN]

- Attempted: create a conclave as peer A inviting bob (`POST /api/conclaves`, the exact call
  behind the create dialog), then watch peer B's `/api/conclaves/invites` arrive on its own.
- Symptom: after 25 s B still had no invite; it appeared only after forcing
  `POST /api/recv` on B. The daemon's `outbox_loop` retries the send side every 30 s, but
  nothing on the daemon drains inbound on a schedule — `pollRecv()` in the UI (4 s) is the
  only `POST /api/recv` caller. Delivery latency is therefore "next time the recipient opens
  the app", which is by design for store-and-forward but surprising when testing: a daemon
  left running with no pane never receives the invite.
- Resolution: worked as designed once a drain ran; no code change. Logged because the
  invite-never-arrives symptom will be misread as a broken button whenever the recipient's
  pane is closed.
- Lesson: the relay holds, the sender retries, but the pull is UI-driven — test invite flows
  with both panes open or drain via the API.

### The Invite button is enabled for mail-only candidates the modal will not offer [FIXED]

- Attempted: read the convener header button against the invite modal it opens
  (`apps/hush-tauri/src/app.ts` ~4090 vs ~5250).
- Symptom: the button computed `candidatesToInvite(conclave, all contact nicks)` — it ignored
  reach — so a vault whose only contacts are mail-only (or whose full-reach contacts are all
  trustees) rendered an enabled button; the modal then filtered to `reach === "full"` and the
  picker was empty ("Everyone you know is already here, or is mail only."). The create dialog
  handled the same case with distinct empty messages; the header button's disabled state
  contradicted the modal's.
- Resolution: FIXED on `fix/conclave-invite-ux`. Both now derive from one helper,
  `invitableCandidates(conclave, contacts)` in `conclaveStore.ts` (reach-full filter +
  existing-trustee exclusion in one place). Evidence: 5 new node-test cases in
  `conclaveStore.test.ts` (mail-only excluded, left/kicked excluded, newcomer kept), full
  suite 83/83 green, `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Lesson: when a button gates a dialog, derive both from one candidate list.

### A trustee who left can never be re-invited — terminal by protocol, surfaced in the UI [OPEN]

- Attempted: explain why the Invite button is permanently disabled in the prod vault's
  "secret meeting" where the only other member (`mahmood`) is in state `left`.
- Symptom: `invite_conclave_trustee` refuses anyone already in the trustees list
  (`Error::AlreadyConclaveTrustee`) regardless of state, and `upsert_trustee` merges
  monotonically — `left`/`kicked` are never revived (`docs/PROTOCOL.md`: "a terminal state is
  never revived"). So a left member is locked out of the conclave forever. The UI used to
  show only a disabled Invite button whose tooltip ("Everyone you know is already in this
  conclave") misstated the situation.
- Resolution: split. The UI half is FIXED on `fix/conclave-invite-ux`: the disabled button's
  tooltip now names the departed member and the terminal state ("mahmood left this conclave
  and can't be re-invited" / "was removed and can't be re-invited"). The design half stays
  OPEN: whether a convener should ever be able to re-invite a `left` member is undecided. If
  yes, the core needs a revive transition and the monotonic merge needs a carve-out for it;
  if no, the tooltip is the whole answer.
- Lesson: terminal-state semantics need a surfaced explanation, or users read the disabled
  button as a bug.

### Release workflow leaves the GitHub release as a draft, so the relay mirror never runs [FIXED]

- Attempted: tag `v0.3.1`, wait for the Release workflow to finish, expect `publish-updates.yml`
  (`on: release: types: [published]`) to mirror `latest.json` to `hushrelay.space` — the
  sequence that worked for v0.3.0.
- Symptom: the Release run completed and uploaded every asset, but the relay kept serving
  0.3.0 and no `Publish updates` run appeared. `gh release view v0.3.1` showed `draft=true`
  with `publishedAt: null` — the Release workflow creates the release as a draft, and events
  generated by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger other workflows.
- Resolution: `gh release edit v0.3.1 --draft=false` as the user. The publish event then
  fired, `Publish updates` ran (45 s), and the relay served `latest.json` at 0.3.1 with every
  asset answering 200. Lesson: after a release build goes green, check the draft flag — the
  mirror depends on a publish event the build itself cannot emit. Candidate follow-up: have
  the Release workflow create the release non-draft, or gate publish-updates on workflow
  completion instead of the release event.

## 2026-10-17 — Composer focus fix and dev-rig wiring

### Dev peers had no chats, so the "fixed" composer was invisible [FIXED]

- Attempted: after implementing the focus fix, tell the user to test it in the dev pane.
- Symptom: the user saw "i dont see nothing" — the peer A pane showed the empty state ("No
  chats yet", "Quiet in here") because the dev vaults at `/home/sam/hush-dev-peer-*` had
  contacts created but no chat thread, and peer B's plaintext `client-config.json` was
  missing entirely. A composer fix cannot be seen where no composer renders.
- Resolution: rebuilt both dev vaults (`hush-cli init` with known passphrases, relay
  `https://hushrelay.space`), exchanged invites for mutual trust, restarted the daemons, and
  seeded a message. Lesson: before asking someone to verify a UI fix, confirm the surface it
  lives on actually exists on screen.

### `HUSH_PASSPHRASE` does not unlock the daemon — it must be POSTed [FIXED]

- Attempted: pass the passphrase via env when starting `hush-daemon`, expect heartbeats.
- Symptom: `/api/status` on both dev daemons reported `"locked": true`, chat sends failed
  with `Error: ContactOffline` even 90 s after start (no heartbeat → relay presence stale).
  The env var works for `hush-cli` but the daemon ignores it.
- Resolution: `curl -X POST /api/unlock -d '{"passphrase":"..."}'` on each daemon (204),
  first heartbeat fires ~30 s later, sends succeed. Lesson: the daemon owns the session and
  only unlocks via its API; env vars are a CLI-only convenience.

### CLI send/recv while the daemon is unlocked corrupts the daemon's session view [FIXED]

- Attempted: drain queues with `hush-cli recv` to seed chat history while both daemons were
  unlocked and heartbeating.
- Symptom: subsequent drains printed "Could not decrypt a queued message — unknown sender or
  session not ready." and the daemon's `/api/messages` returned `[]` even though the same
  vault's CLI recv had just printed filed messages. Root cause: two processes (CLI and
  daemon) held independent in-memory copies of the same encrypted vault; the CLI's ratchet
  advances were invisible to the daemon's stale in-memory account, so its decrypts failed.
- Resolution: restarted both daemons so they reloaded the vault with the CLI-filed sessions;
  the undecryptable blob then decrypted (the drain path leaves Session-error blobs on the
  relay unconsumed, so nothing was lost). Lesson: never mix `hush-cli` sends/recvs with a
  running unlocked daemon on the same vault — stop the daemon or use its API instead.
- Status: FIXED for this session by restart; the vault lock file does not prevent the CLI
  from opening a daemon-held vault, which is the underlying papercut.

### Dev vaults auto-lock after 15 minutes, silently dropping presence [FIXED]

- Attempted: leave both dev daemons running for the user to test the composer fix later.
- Symptom: the composer in the pane flipped to disabled ("Waiting for them to come online…",
  banner "bob is offline") about 15 minutes after setup. B's daemon had self-locked via
  `auto_lock_loop` — `ui-prefs.json` defaults to `auto_lock_minutes: 15` when the file is
  absent, and a locked daemon stops heartbeating, so presence goes stale within 90 s.
- Resolution: wrote `auto_lock_minutes: 0` (off) into `ui-prefs.json` in both dev dirs and
  re-unlocked B via the API. Lesson: a dev rig meant to sit idle between human tests must
  disable auto-lock, or the first test after a gap starts from a locked daemon.

## 2026-10-17 — Relay redesign: the bottleneck measured end to end

### The drain peek loop re-read the same page forever — `recv()` spun at 100% CPU for 24 minutes [FIXED]

- Attempted: page through a deep queue by repeating the non-consuming peek
  (`POST /q/{id}/drain?limit=N`) inside `Account::fetch_queue` until an empty page came
  back, with acks deferred to the filing phase.
- Symptom: the flood suite's first test never finished — the test binary sat at 100% CPU for
  24 minutes with three temp dirs and no progress (`ps` showed 140996 ticks of CPU on one
  core). The peek is a pure `SELECT ... ORDER BY created_at LIMIT ?`: with nothing acked yet,
  page 2 is page 1, so the fetch loop can never reach an empty page. Every queue looped
  forever, so the run wedged on the very first test.
- Resolution: restructured to progress-gated rounds in `recv()` (`crates/hush-core/src/account.rs`).
  Each round: peek one page per queue concurrently -> file serially -> one ack per queue
  (awaited) -> re-peek only queues whose ack was non-empty. The ack is what moves the peek
  forward; a queue that files nothing (all blobs held) stops until the next poll. Whole flood
  suite after the fix: 4/4 passed in 104.79 s release.
- Lesson: a non-consuming read cannot be paged by repetition — pagination needs a cursor or
  an interleaved consume. Also: a `loop` over a page endpoint belongs behind the same
  progress guarantee as the data it reads; and an unattended `cargo test` needs `timeout` and
  output capture so a wedge is visible in minutes, not half an hour.

### Release-only test failures: config precedence tests and the drops page-url test were debug-hermetic only [FIXED]

- Attempted: run all three suites under `cargo test --release` (the load-restricted box
  pushed every run into release after the concurrent debug runs crashed it).
- Symptom: `hush-core` config tests panicked with `insecure relay URL: use HTTPS except for
  localhost` — they use `http://10.0.0.5` LAN addresses, and `HttpPolicy::current()` is
  `Allow` in debug but `LoopbackOnly` in release. `hush-daemon`'s drops test failed with
  `page_url follows the vault's relay: http://qvo7….onion/drop`: release builds bake in
  `DEFAULT_RELAY_ONION_URL`, and `apply_relay_prefs` staged it into every unlocked vault,
  so `drop_page_url` preferred the production onion even for a test vault created against a
  localhost relay. Both suites had only ever been run in debug.
- Resolution: config tests now use loopback URLs, which pass both policies (they exercise
  precedence, not URL validation). The real bug got a product fix, not a test tweak: the
  worker's `RelayApply` handler (`crates/hush-daemon/src/account_worker.rs`) now refuses the
  baked-in default onion unless the vault's relay is the baked-in default relay — a
  self-hoster's drop page no longer silently points at the production relay. Added
  `config::is_baked_default_onion` to recognize it. All suites green in release:
  relay 31, core 149 lib + 12 + 5 integration, daemon 219.
- Lesson: `cfg!(debug_assertions)` in production defaults makes every test that depends on
  the default profile-hermetic in debug only. Any default that varies by build profile needs
  a test pinned in both, or the release CI run lies.

### The production VPS still runs the pre-WAL binary — the Oct 17 store fix never reached it [FIXED]

- Attempted: verify which relay binary `hushrelay.space` runs, after finding the fsync/WAL fix
  sitting uncommitted in the working tree (`git diff crates/hush-relay/src/store.rs`).
- Symptom: the deployed binary is dated Oct 16 16:53 (the cross-build in terminal 358792), one
  day before the WAL fix existed. `ssh hush-relay-prod 'grep -c "journal_mode = WAL"
  /usr/local/bin/hush-relay'` returns **0** — the pragma block is not in the binary — and
  `/var/lib/hush-relay/relay/` holds a bare `relay.db` with no `-wal`/`-shm` beside it. So prod
  still runs rollback-journal with `synchronous=FULL`, and every PUT/DELETE still pays the
  multi-fsync autocommit plus the reader/writer serialization the fix removes.
- Resolution: deployed 2026-10-17. Cross-built hush-relay aarch64 from the working tree in the
  disposable container (the doc's command), verified the artifact locally (aarch64 ELF,
  `journal_mode = WAL` present, drain route strings present), backed up the old binary to
  `/usr/local/bin/hush-relay.bak-20261016`, installed and restarted. Evidence after restart:
  unit `active`; `https://hushrelay.space/health` → 200; tokenless probe of
  `POST /q/x/drain` → 401 (route registered); legacy route still 401 (old clients fine);
  onion `/health` → 200; `relay.db-wal`/`-shm` exist beside the DB.
- Lesson: a performance fix that never ships fixes nothing. Check what the deployed artifact
  contains (`strings`/`grep` the binary) before crediting the working tree.

### A chat send pays two fresh TLS handshakes because `relay_client()` builds a new `reqwest::Client` per call [OPEN]

- Attempted: explain why the real relay feels slow when the relay's per-op latency is
  sub-millisecond with WAL, by counting network round trips in the client paths.
- Symptom, measured against `https://hushrelay.space` (Hetzner `37.27.150.250`): ping RTT
  **164 ms**; a request on a reused connection costs **~165 ms**; a request on a fresh
  connection costs **0.55–0.65 s** (DNS 40 ms + TCP 205 ms + TLS 390–450 ms + request).
  `Account::relay_client()` (`crates/hush-core/src/account.rs:1019`) constructs a brand-new
  `RelayClient` — and therefore a new `reqwest::Client` with an empty connection pool — on
  **every call**, and there are 13 call sites. A live chat send calls it twice
  (`contact_is_online`, then `deliver_to`), so one chat line costs ~1.1–1.3 s of handshakes
  before any queueing; `recv()` builds one client per poll, so only the drain's first request
  pays and the per-blob `get`/`delete` reuse that connection.
- Resolution needed: construct the `RelayClient` once (at unlock/create, or lazily cached on
  the account) and reuse the pool. No protocol change; purely client lifetime.
- Lesson: `Client::new` per operation silently discards keep-alive. On a 164 ms link each
  discarded pool costs half a second, which dwarfs everything the server does per request.

### Round-trip arithmetic on the real link: a message costs 2 RTT to send, 3 RTT to receive, plus a 4 s poll [OPEN]

- Attempted: account for every round trip in the send and drain paths at the measured 164 ms.
- Symptom: a chat send is a presence `GET` + the payload `PUT` (2 RTT ≈ 330 ms, or ~1.3 s with
  the fresh-client bug above). Receiving is `list` + per message `get` + `delete`, all
  sequential: 3 RTT ≈ 0.5 s per message, and a poll walks the inbox plus one queue per contact
  serially (a list per queue per 4 s `RECV_POLL_MS` tick). A ten-trustee conclave fan-out is
  one PUT per trustee, sequential, each subject to that queue's 60/60 s rate limit. The UI
  polls every 4 s, so inbound latency floor is 4 s + queue-walk + drain.
- Resolution needed (redesign, ranked): batch the drain (one authenticated call returning and
  consuming a page of blobs collapses 2N+1 RTT to 1); long-poll or notify on queue depth
  instead of fixed 4 s polling; drop the presence round trip from the send path (cache presence
  from the poll, or let the PUT answer it); honor `Retry-After` on 429 (the new binary sends
  it). Server-side, WAL + a small read pool behind `spawn_blocking` is the next ceiling after
  that, at ~5k ops/s for one connection today — not the current bottleneck.
- Caveat: `hush.space` (the name used in conversation) is not the relay — it resolves elsewhere
  (28 ms ping, `/health` fails). The production relay is `hushrelay.space` per
  `docs/ops/relay-prod-vps.md`. The 164 ms RTT is to that box.
- Lesson: on a far relay the bottleneck is RTT × round trips, not bytes or bandwidth. Count
  round trips per message before redesigning storage: the store's fsync fix mattered 22 ms per
  write; the network costs 165 ms per *request*, and the client issues three per message.

## 2026-10-17 — `pkill -f` / `pgrep -f` matched their own shell wrapper

### "Tests are still running" was wrong, twice, and one command killed its own session [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: check whether the background test run had finished, and separately stop a benchmark
  relay, using `pgrep -f 'cargo test -p hush'` and `pkill -f 'target/debug/hush-relay'`.
- Symptom: both patterns match the `bash -c` wrapper that is *executing* them, because the pattern
  text appears in that wrapper's own command line. Two consequences:
  - `pgrep -f 'cargo test -p hush'` kept reporting a match after the run had genuinely finished, so
    the user was told the suite was still running when it was done (466 passed, 0 failed, 23
    binaries). Caught only by cross-checking `pgrep -x cargo` and `/proc/loadavg`, both of which
    showed idle.
  - `pkill -f 'target/debug/hush-relay'` killed the shell running it. The command returned exit 0
    with no output at all, which reads as success.
- Resolution: use exact-name matching — `pgrep -x cargo`, `pkill -x hush-relay` — or verify with a
  second, independent signal (process count by exact name, or load average) before reporting
  anything as running or stopped.
- Lesson: a `-f` pattern is matched against the invoker's own command line, so a check can report on
  itself. Exit 0 from `pkill` proves nothing; it reports "signalled", not "found and killed". Any
  claim of the form "X is still running" needs a signal that cannot be satisfied by the checking
  command itself. This is tooling, not a repo problem.

## 2026-10-17 — Relay write path is fsync-bound and single-threaded

### An 8-byte write costs 22 ms, and no two writes can overlap [OPEN]

- Attempted: answer "why is the relay slow when we send so little data?" by reading the store and
  then measuring the built relay rather than reasoning about it.
- Symptom: it is not bandwidth. Timed against the real `target/debug/hush-relay` over one
  keep-alive connection, 300 samples each, median:

  | request | DB on ext4 | DB on tmpfs |
  |---|---|---|
  | `GET /health` (no SQL) | 0.57 ms | 0.56 ms |
  | `GET /q/{id}` (read) | 1.13 ms | 1.08 ms |
  | `PUT /q/{id}` (8-byte blob) | 22.33 ms | 1.15 ms |
  | `GET /q/{id}/{blob}` (read) | 1.21 ms | 1.04 ms |
  | `DELETE /q/{id}/{blob}` (write) | 29.82 ms | 0.95 ms |

  Reads are identical on both; writes fall ~25x when the disk is taken out of the path. The cost
  is the durability syscall, not the payload. Cause: `Connection::open` in `store.rs` is followed
  by the schema batch and **no PRAGMA at all** — no `journal_mode`, no `synchronous`, no
  `busy_timeout` — so SQLite runs at defaults, rollback journal with `synchronous=FULL`, and
  every autocommitted `INSERT`/`DELETE` pays journal-create, two fsyncs and an unlink.
- Second symptom: writes cannot overlap at all. `Store` holds one `Mutex<Connection>`, `Store::open`
  runs once in `router()`, and the whole relay shares it through `Arc<AppState>` — so reads block
  writes too. Twenty concurrent clients writing to twenty *distinct* queues took as long as
  twenty sequential ones:

  ```
  20 writes sequential :  523.8 ms  (26.2 ms/write)
  20 writes concurrent :  613.8 ms  (30.7 ms/write)
  speedup from concurrency: 0.85x
  ```

  That puts the relay's ceiling at roughly 38 writes/sec for the whole process, and one client's
  burst stalls every other client's reads.
- Contributing, not yet measured at depth: `purge_expired()` runs on every `list` and every `get`
  and issues three unbounded `DELETE`s. `DELETE FROM blobs WHERE created_at < ?` has no supporting
  index — the only index on `blobs` is `idx_blobs_queue` — and neither does
  `bulletin.inserted_at` (`drops` does, via `idx_drops_created`). Cheap today only because nothing
  is expired yet, so no page is dirtied and no fsync happens; it becomes a write cost on every
  read once rows start expiring, and the scan is linear in table size.
- Client-side amplification, DB-independent: `recv()` walks the inbox plus one queue per contact
  and does a separate `get` and `delete` per message, sequentially. Draining 41 messages is 1 list
  + 41 gets + 41 deletes = 83 round trips, 41 of them ~30 ms fsyncs, about 1.2 s of pure disk sync
  before any network latency.
- Resolution needed: none was applied — recorded by choice. The measured fix is
  `journal_mode=WAL` plus `synchronous=NORMAL` plus `busy_timeout`, which targets exactly the
  22 ms; then batching the drain and wrapping `purge_expired` plus the read in one transaction.
  WAL also lets readers proceed alongside the single writer. Postgres was considered and is the
  correct answer to the *concurrency* half (it removes the single-writer cap and group-commits
  concurrent fsyncs) but not to the per-write latency half, since it also syncs on commit by
  default — and it would trade a single binary plus one file plus one systemd unit for a service
  to run, back up and secure.
- Caveat on the numbers: measured on this machine's disk (ext4 on `/dev/sda2`). On slower storage
  the fsync cost is worse, so the PRAGMA change is worth more, not less.
- Lesson: "we send almost no data" and "it is slow" are compatible whenever the cost is per
  transaction rather than per byte. Measure the same binary against tmpfs before theorising about
  bandwidth — it separates the syscall from everything else in one run.

## 2026-10-17 — Relay flood (what a burst does to each surface)

### A chat line the relay rate-limits is dropped, while mail, conclave messages and paper deltas queue [OPEN]

- Attempted: flood one peer with chats, conclave messages, paper deltas and mail and see which
  surfaces queue rather than fail.
- Symptom: with one write per two seconds allowed on a queue, six sends per surface measured one
  surface at a time: chat accepted 3/6 and **lost the other 3**, while conclave messages 6/6,
  paper deltas 6/6 and mail 6/6 all arrived after the window rolled. `send_payload_inner` returns
  `Err` on the refusal and nothing queues a chat line; mail goes to the chat log's queued state,
  and conclave payloads go to `pending_conclave`, so those two survive by construction. Chat is
  live-only by design, so a refusal is reported to the caller — but the default window is 60 s,
  and the retry below cannot outlast it, so a burst over 60 lines a minute to one peer loses
  everything past the limit with only an error string to show for it.
- Resolution needed: a product decision, not a code fix. Either chat lines get a durable queue
  (they stop being live-only), or the refusal is surfaced to the user as "not sent, retry" and
  the UI stops pretending otherwise. Recorded rather than chosen.
- Evidence: `a_refusal_that_outlasts_the_retry_is_lost_for_chat_and_queued_for_the_rest` and
  `a_refusal_costs_each_surface_the_same` in `crates/hush-core/tests/relay_flood.rs`.

### The delivery retry is shaped for a dropped packet and applied to HTTP 429 [OPEN]

- Attempted: measure what a refused send costs the caller, per surface.
- Symptom: `send_payload_inner` retries three times with 400 ms and 800 ms sleeps before giving
  up. Against a rate limit that is both useless and expensive: the relay's window is a minute by
  default, so all three attempts land inside the window that refused the first, and every
  surface pays ~1 s of blocking retry per refused send regardless of whether it queues
  afterwards. Measured per surface (1 write / 2 s, 6 sends): chat 1 s avg, conclave message
  940 ms, paper delta 978 ms, mail 965 ms. For a conclave fan-out the cost is per trustee, so a
  ten-trustee conclave refused once blocks the send call for ~10 s.
- Resolution needed: distinguish a 429 from a transport blip. The relay now sends `Retry-After`
  (below), so the delivery path can either wait it out for a live-only send or hand straight to
  the durable queue for a store-and-forward one. Both are behaviour changes; neither was made.
- Evidence: the per-surface table in `a_refusal_costs_each_surface_the_same`.

### The relay could not say whether a write ever arrived [FIXED]

- Attempted: work out from the client side whether a flood was being refused or dropped.
- Symptom: nothing. `put` collapsed every non-2xx into `Error::Relay("put failed: 429 Too Many
  Requests")` with no `Retry-After`, and the relay had no counters, no request log and a `/health`
  that returned a bare 200. A sender that queues a refusal cannot tell "the relay took it" from
  "the relay refused it and my outbox will retry" — the two look identical to the caller.
- Resolution: the relay counts responses by outcome (`puts`, `gets`, `deletes`, `rate_limited`,
  `unauthorized`, `rejected`, `other_errors`) through one middleware and reports them on
  `/health`; a 429 now carries `Retry-After` with the seconds left in the window; and the client
  carries that into its error text. `/health` still answers 200, so every script and
  `RelayClient::ping` that only checks for success is unaffected.
- Evidence: the flood tests read the counters and assert `rate_limited > 0`, which is what makes
  "the burst actually crossed the limit" checkable at all.

### Two wrong readings of the burst, both from measuring four surfaces at once [FIXED]

- Attempted: read the per-surface cost out of one mixed burst of chats, conclave messages, paper
  deltas and mail.
- Symptom: the first burst reported conclave messages at 66 ms and mail at 78 ms while chat and
  paper deltas took ~900 ms, which reads as "conclave and mail queue cheaply, chat and paper
  retry expensively". It is an ordering artefact: `send_payload_inner` blocks ~1 s retrying a
  refused write, which rolls the one-second window, so whichever surface runs next inherits a
  fresh budget and looks instant. The four surfaces share one delivery path; the difference was
  only their position in the loop. The second run of the same test showed the opposite
  assignment, which is what exposed it. Separately, an earlier assertion counted
  `inbox.messages` to prove a conclave invite had arrived, but an invite is a control payload and
  never appears there, so the check failed against working code.
- Resolution: `a_refusal_costs_each_surface_the_same` measures one surface at a time, on its own
  pair of vaults, and that is the measurement to trust. The invite check reads
  `pending_invites()`.
- Lesson: a shared resource plus a sequential loop means position in the loop is a hidden
  variable. When every subject rides the same path, measure them one at a time or the numbers
  describe the loop, not the subject.

## 2026-10-16 — Conclave delivery hardening (stale per-contact queue)

### A re-grant sweep for a restored vault was a false fix [FIXED]

- Attempted: treat a fresh device identity (a restore that carried the shared vault but not
  `device.enc`) the same as a queue rotation, and re-grant every contact its new per-contact
  queue on the outbox timer.
- Symptom: the sweep reported success and cleared its own flag, while the peer kept delivering
  into the abandoned queue. The relay accepted the blob, so nothing on the sender's side failed.
  On the receiver, `apply_queue_grant` verifies the grant signature against `contact.identity_key`
  — the key pinned from the *invite* — and a fresh device signs with a **new** identity key, so
  every re-grant was refused with a bare `Ok(false)` and discarded silently. Both ends saw
  success.
- Resolution: split the two cases instead of pretending they are one. `queue_rotated` (a v1 file,
  or a migration off the legacy layout) keeps the identity key and every session, so peers verify
  the re-grant against the key they already pinned and the sweep genuinely converges. A fresh
  device is recorded as `identity_restored` and reported through `/api/queues` and one stderr
  warning at open, because the relationship needs a re-add. Accepting a changed identity key
  automatically is exactly the substitution the pin exists to stop, so it is not repaired.
- Evidence: `a_restored_vault_reports_the_identity_its_contacts_pinned` asserts the restore is
  reported, is *not* queued as a re-grant, and that the peer keeps the dead queue after a sweep;
  `a_regrant_from_the_same_identity_replaces_the_stored_queue` and
  `a_grant_signed_by_an_unpinned_identity_is_refused` pin the accept/refuse split; the existing
  `a_v1_device_file_rotates_its_queue_once_and_keeps_its_identity` now also asserts the open
  queues a re-grant and does not claim an identity restore.
- Lesson: `Ok(false)` on a security check is invisible to the sender. A repair built on the
  assumption that the far side accepted the payload cannot be validated from the sender's side
  alone; the check that refuses it has to be read first.

### `grant_queues_to` swallowed delivery failures [FIXED]

- Attempted: build a retry that clears its flag once every contact has been re-granted.
- Symptom: `grant_queues_to` logged a failed delivery with `eprintln!` and returned `Ok(())`, so
  every caller saw success. A retry built on it would clear its flag on a grant that never left
  the process.
- Resolution: it now returns whether the grant reached the relay (`Result<bool, Error>`); a
  revoked contact reports `true` because nothing is owed, so a sweep does not retry it forever.
  `add_contact` still ignores the value, but now warns that the peer will keep delivering to the
  shared inbox.
- Evidence: `a_regrant_sweep_keeps_its_flag_while_the_relay_is_unreachable` asserts the flag
  survives an unreachable relay.

### The rotation sweep's relay-level convergence is not covered end to end [OPEN]

- Attempted: reach the queue-rotation path from an integration test in
  `crates/hush-core/tests/two_party_relay.rs`.
- Symptom: a rotation needs either a v1 `device.enc` or a legacy `signal.enc`, and both are
  written with `crypto::encrypt` under the vault master key. `encrypt` is private, and the only
  public route to the master key (`Vault::master_key`) does not include a way to re-encrypt a
  device file, so no test outside the crate can build one. `DeviceKeys::from_store` and
  `DeviceKeys::load` are the only producers of a rotated queue and both are out of reach.
- Resolution needed: either a `#[doc(hidden)]` test hook that rotates a device queue without
  touching the identity (it must keep the identity, or it stops testing the case that works), or a
  feature-gated fixture. The pieces are covered individually — rotation detection and the queued
  re-grant, the accept/replace of a second grant, and the sweep's failure handling — but nothing
  asserts the full loop of rotate, re-grant, drain, converge against a live relay.
- Note: a v1 rotation test already existed in `account.rs` (`a_v1_device_file_rotates_its_queue_
  once_and_keeps_its_identity`), so the rotation trigger was covered before this slice; the first
  draft of this slice added a second, near-identical test in `device.rs` and it was removed. The
  duplicated test was written before reading the surrounding test module.
- Lesson: an in-crate integration path that needs the master key cannot be tested from `tests/`.
  When a helper is only reachable through private crypto, plan the test seam before writing the
  test.

## 2026-10-16 — macOS vault lock (`flock` was Linux-only)

### The vault lock was a no-op on macOS, so the two-daemon bug was never fixed there [FIXED]

- Attempted: work out why a MacBook (macOS 27.0.1, build 26A434) showed relay-dependent UI
  actions lagging, dropping, and sometimes not completing, while the same build behaved on Linux.
- Symptom: `acquire_vault_lock` — the fix logged further down as "Two daemons ran against one
  vault — FIXED" — was gated `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`, with a stub returning `Ok(None)`
  everywhere else under the comment "No-op on platforms without `flock`". macOS is not such a
  platform: Darwin has `flock(2)`, and `libc::flock` is declared for it. So on macOS the lock was
  never taken, `libc` was not even a dependency of `hush-daemon` (it sat under
  `[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]`), and the only guard left was the socket
  liveness probe that the earlier entry had already ruled out as insufficient. A force-quit on
  macOS leaves `hush-daemon` running (the shell stops it only on a clean `RunEvent::Exit`) and the
  next launch cannot see it, so two daemons run against one vault: whole-file `account.enc`
  overwrites, duplicated queue drains, clobbered Signal sessions, invites that never arrive.
- Resolution: widened the gate to `#[cfg(unix)]`, with `#[cfg(not(unix))]` for the Windows stub;
  moved `libc` to `[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]` (`zbus` stayed Linux-only — logind is a
  Linux API); corrected the stub's comment, which named a limitation that does not exist. Three
  tests in `vault_lock_tests` assert the lock is a held file, that a second daemon on one vault is
  refused by name, and that a daemon that exits leaves no stale lock.
- Evidence: the daemon builds and the three tests pass. Two real daemons on one temp vault with
  *different* sockets give `Error: "another hush-daemon is already running on /tmp/hush-lock-e2e
  (Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)); stop it before starting a new one"`, exit 1,
  and never create their socket. `SIGKILL`ing the holder leaves the lock file on disk and the next
  daemon still starts. `cargo check` for `aarch64-apple-darwin` is blocked here by `ring`'s build
  script (it wants a macOS SDK), so the darwin side was checked by compiling the verbatim
  `acquire_vault_lock` block from `main.rs` as a standalone crate for that target: it compiles,
  `cfg!(unix)` is true, `libc::flock` resolves, and a `compile_error!` under `cfg(not(unix))` does
  not fire.
- Not verified: the macOS runtime path itself. No Mac was available, so "the lock is taken on
  Darwin" rests on the target compiling the unix branch, not on having run it there.
- Lesson: a platform gate written `target_os = "linux"` around a POSIX API makes a fix a
  Linux-only fix while the log entry still reads `FIXED`. `flock`, `AsRawFd` and the unix socket
  types are `unix`, not `linux` — gate on the API, not on the OS the bug was first seen on.

## 2026-10-16 — relay drop diagnosis (chat/mail on prod)

### `sqlite3` is not installed on the production relay host [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: read aggregate state out of `/var/lib/hush-relay/relay/relay.db` directly on
  `hush-relay-prod` to see queue/blob/burn counts and blob ages.
- Symptom: every query returned `sudo: sqlite3: command not found`. The relay ships the SQLite
  library statically via `rusqlite`, but no `sqlite3` CLI is present on the box, and the deploy
  user has passwordless sudo so the workaround was not blocked, only unexpected.
- Resolution: copied the DB off-box (`sudo cp` to `/tmp`, `scp` to `/tmp/hush-relay-inspect/`)
  and queried it locally, where `sqlite3` exists. The DB is 139 KB, so the copy is trivial.
- Lesson: the ops runbooks describe reading the relay DB but never say what reads it. Either
  install `sqlite3` on the box or keep the copy-local step in the runbook. Tooling gap, not a
  repo bug.

### A relay queue id cannot be mapped back to a vault or contact with the tools on hand [OPEN]

- Attempted: decide whether the two queues accumulating blobs on the prod relay belonged to the
  local vault (a local drain bug) or to the remote peer (a consumer-side stall), to attribute a
  "messages never arrive" report.
- Symptom: nothing maps a queue id to a vault. `hush-cli` has no queue-id command, `/api/status`
  returns `protocol_name` but no queue ids, and the ids are HMACs over the vault read token, which
  lives only in the encrypted `device.enc`. Attribution had to be inferred indirectly: the two
  queues have `presence_at = 0` (presence is inbox-only, so these are per-contact queues), and the
  local vault's own `/api/recv` is clean, which rules the local vault out as their reader.
- Resolution needed: a local diagnostic that prints this vault's own queue ids (inbox plus one per
  contact) turns this into a one-line check. It does not exist.
- Lesson: derived-only, never-stored identifiers are the right call for privacy and the wrong call
  for operations. An opt-in local "which queues are mine" view costs nothing and would have
  replaced the inference above with a fact.

### The production relay logs no per-request detail, so a drop could not be attributed [OPEN]

- Attempted: pin down why chat/mail messages were reported as dropped by reading the relay's
  request log for `429` (rate limit), `401` (auth), `403` (burned) or `500` responses.
- Symptom: there is nothing to read. `hush-relay` logs only its startup line
  (`hush-relay listening on ...`), and the Caddy front end is configured with `log { output
  discard }`, so no access log is kept either. The relay DB shows the residue (23 blobs, one
  queue holding 17 undrained blobs, all under ~3 h old) but not the cause.
- Resolution needed: the drop mechanism is inferred from the code paths, not observed on the
  wire. To close this, add request-level logging to the relay (or stop discarding Caddy's access
  log) and reproduce. Until then, the "17 blobs stuck on one queue" is a lead, not a diagnosis.
- Lesson: a store-and-forward service with no request log cannot be debugged from its own host.
  The absence of observability is itself the defect to fix first.

## 2026-10-16 — macOS ad-hoc code signing

### v0.2.0 shipped an unsigned macOS bundle, so Gatekeeper called it damaged [FIXED]

- Attempted: downloaded the published `Hush_0.2.0_aarch64.dmg` the way a user would (through
  a browser) and launched it. macOS refused with "Hush is damaged and can't be opened. You
  should move it to the Trash." — a dialog with only *Move to Trash* and *Cancel*, no Open
  button, so no bypass was offered.
- Symptom: the published `Hush_aarch64.app.tar.gz` contains no
  `Hush.app/Contents/_CodeSignature/CodeResources`. Parsing the Mach-O load commands of
  `Contents/MacOS/hush-tauri` and `Contents/MacOS/hush-daemon` showed a single
  `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE` superblob each, holding one blob of type `0x0` (CodeDirectory) and
  nothing else — the signature `ld` writes automatically on arm64, never a `codesign`
  invocation. The root cause is that `apps/hush-tauri/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` had no
  `bundle.macOS` section at all, and the release workflow passes no `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`,
  so `tauri build` had no identity and skipped signing entirely. The browser's
  `com.apple.quarantine` flag then made Gatekeeper assess the bundle, find no signature, and
  report it as damaged. The app itself was never broken. A second contributor, from the CLI's
  own `--no-binary-patching` help text: `tauri build` patches the main executable in place to
  record the bundle type, which invalidates whatever signature the linker wrote, and Tauri
  re-signs after patching only when it has an identity — so the linker's automatic signature
  cannot stand in for a real one.
- Resolution: added `"macOS": { "signingIdentity": "-" }` to `bundle` in
  `apps/hush-tauri/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, per Tauri's "Ad-Hoc Signing" documentation. This
  is the no-Apple-account option: it does not remove the Gatekeeper warning, but it downgrades
  it from "damaged and can't be opened" (unbypassable) to "cannot be checked for malicious
  software" (clearable from Finder or Privacy & Security). RELEASING.md's macOS platform note
  and its first-install section were rewritten to match.
- Lesson: an unsigned macOS bundle and an ad-hoc-signed one produce two different Gatekeeper
  dialogs, and only one of them is survivable by the user. "Unsigned" was documented here as a
  known state, but nobody had checked what the dialog actually said — the documented Finder
  bypass was written for the ad-hoc case and never applied to what shipped.

### RELEASING.md documented a Finder bypass that this dialog does not offer [FIXED]

- Attempted: followed the repo's own "Installing an unsigned macOS build" section on the
  refusal above.
- Symptom: the section offered, as an alternative to `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine`, "in
  Finder, right-click the app → Open → Open in the dialog, which is offered only the first
  time." The dialog in the screenshot has no Open button and no way to reach one — that route
  is offered for "developer cannot be verified", not for "is damaged and can't be opened". The
  instruction sent the reader to a dead end at the exact moment they were stuck.
- Resolution: the section is now titled "Installing an ad-hoc-signed macOS build", states
  plainly that the Finder route exists only for the ad-hoc case, and no longer presents it as a
  fallback for a build with no signature.
- Lesson: a documented bypass is a claim about UI the document cannot see. It should say which
  error it applies to, not just that it works.

### The ad-hoc signature could not be verified on this host [FIXED]

- Attempted: to confirm that `signingIdentity: "-"` produces a signed bundle, by building the
  macOS bundle and running `codesign -dv --verbose=4` against it.
- Symptom: this is a Linux workstation. `codesign`, `xattr`, `spctl` and Gatekeeper do not
  exist here, and the macOS leg of the release workflow is the only macOS in reach. Everything
  in the entry above is read from the published artifact's bytes, not from a signing run. The
  config change was therefore unverified: it matched Tauri's documentation and the schema, and
  nothing more.
- Resolution: closed by the new `verify the macOS bundle is signed` step, which runs on the
  macOS runners. In release run 38976342470 (aarch64 leg) it printed
  `Hush.app: valid on disk`, `Hush.app: satisfies its Designated Requirement`, and
  `CodeDirectory v=20500 size=34417 flags=0x10002(adhoc,runtime) hashes=1069+3 location=embedded`,
  with the nested `Contents/MacOS/hush-daemon` reported as `--prepared`/`--validated`. That was
  then confirmed independently, off the runner: the rebuilt `Hush_aarch64.app.tar.gz` contains
  `Contents/_CodeSignature/CodeResources`, which the v0.2.0 artifact did not, and the copy on
  the relay is byte-identical (`sha256 7e0716b887dc9bf45f480dcf9bd807e1ad7d2f853042ce455503919e9042b2a5`).
  `scripts/verify-update-signature.py --manifest https://hushrelay.space/updates/latest.json --all`
  reports OK for all seven platform entries.
- Lesson: "the artifact has no signature" is provable from anywhere; "the build now signs" is
  not. Do not let the first, which was measured, stand in for the second, which was not. A CI
  step is what converts the second into something measurable.

### A published release cannot be rebuilt by re-running the tag [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: to rebuild v0.2.0 with the signing fix and no version bump, by re-running
  `release.yml` for the existing tag.
- Symptom: two traps, both silent until they bite.
  (1) `release.yml` is `on: push: tags: v*` and `actions/checkout` takes the *tag's* commit, so
  re-running the workflow without moving the tag builds the old, unfixed code.
  (2) tauri-action's `getOrCreateRelease` looks for a **draft** when `releaseDraft: true`; on
  finding a published release with that tag it logs "Found release with tag v0.2.0 but it's NOT
  a draft!" and then throws `release not found` — after the whole build has already run. A
  re-run against a published release therefore burns a full multi-leg build and fails at the
  upload.
- Resolution: unpublish the release first (`gh release edit v0.2.0 --draft=true`, which keeps
  the release and its assets and does not touch the relay's copy), then move the tag to the
  merged fix (`git push --force-with-lease`), which triggers the build; tauri-action then finds
  the draft and replaces the same-named assets. Publishing the draft again fires
  `publish-updates.yml`, which re-mirrors. The relay keeps serving the old manifest throughout,
  so there is no window where downloads break. Written up in RELEASING.md, "Re-releasing an
  existing tag".
- Lesson: `release.yml` has no `workflow_dispatch`, and adding one would not have helped — the
  build reads the tag's commit, so the tag has to move either way. Rebuilding a release is a
  tag rewrite, and the release has to be a draft when the build starts.

### A Linux x86-64 ELF ships inside the macOS bundle [OPEN]

- Attempted: nothing yet; noticed while inspecting the bundle for the signing problem.
- Symptom: `Hush.app/Contents/Resources/tor/tor` and its `libevent-2.1.so.7` are Linux ELF
  binaries, and `bundle.resources` in `tauri.conf.json` names them unconditionally, so every
  platform's bundle carries them. On macOS this is ~10 MB of dead weight that can never
  execute; RELEASING.md already documents the user-visible half ("the Mac reports no Tor").
  It is not known to break ad-hoc signing, but it is exactly the kind of payload Apple's notary
  service scrutinises, so it is a blocker for the notarization path rather than a cosmetic one.
- Resolution: needs a platform-conditional `resources` block (a `tauri.macos.conf.json`, or a
  per-platform resource list) so each bundle ships only its own Tor. The Windows plan at
  `docs/plans/2026-10-16-windows-release.md` Task 8 Step 3 already flags the same problem from
  the Windows side.
- Lesson: a `bundle.resources` map is not platform-scoped, and nothing in the build warns when
  it names a binary for the wrong OS.

## 2026-10-16 — Reach announcement outbox drain

### Reach toggle blocked the user on up to three 15-second relay attempts [FIXED]

- Attempted: toggling a trust's reach in the UI took 10–60 s. `setTrustReach` (app.ts) awaited
  `setContactReach` and then `contacts()` before repainting; the daemon's `set_contact_reach`
  saved locally and then **inline-awaited** the `MessagePayload::Reach` announcement, which is
  `send_payload_inner` = up to 3 delivery attempts × the 15 s `REQUEST_TIMEOUT` with 400/800 ms
  backoffs, over Tor where configured. Its own doc comment called the announcement best-effort,
  but the await was still paid before the HTTP reply — and the single sequential account worker
  was blocked the whole time, head-of-line behind heartbeats/outbox/recv besides.
- Symptom: UI badge froze for the full announce; every other account op queued behind it.
- Resolution: `set_contact_reach` now records the announcement in a persisted `pending_reach`
  queue (vault state, one entry per contact, latest scope wins) and returns after the save. The
  daemon's `outbox_loop` drains it (`Account::retry_pending_reach`, `Work::RetryPendingReach`)
  on the same 30 s tick as queued mail, and a new `POST /api/outbox/retry` route triggers a
  drain explicitly (tests now; an Outbox "send now" button later). The CLI, a one-shot process,
  drains inline before exiting and prints a note when the announcement stayed queued.
  `remove_contact`/`revoke_contact` drop pending entries for the contact, since a burned queue
  would otherwise refuse delivery forever. Verified: hush-core 210/210 (lib + all integration
  suites), hush-daemon 216/216, new test `a_reach_change_queues_and_delivers_when_the_relay_returns`
  pins the queue-then-deliver behavior.
- Lesson: "best-effort" must describe the *await*, not just the error handling — swallowing the
  error while still awaiting the network gives the caller all of the latency and none of the
  guarantee. Store-and-forward work belongs in the store-and-forward queue.

### Pointer-invite commit left four tests decoding hush1 codes as full invites [FIXED]

- Attempted: the first full `cargo test -p hush-core` run after the reach fix showed
  `internal_mail` 3/8 failing (`a_handle_round_trips_through_an_invite`,
  `setting_a_handle_invalidates_a_cached_invite`,
  `mail_queues_while_the_relay_is_down_and_goes_out_on_retry`); running the suite to completion
  surfaced `revocation` 1/2 (`a_revoked_contact_cannot_deliver_into_the_shared_inbox`) too.
- Symptom: `Err(Corrupt)` at `InvitePayload::decode(<hush1…>)` — commit 3d426b9 replaced inline
  v2 invites with short pointer codes, so `Account::invite()` now returns a `hush1…` string that
  only `ShortInvite::decode` reads. Two of the tests also paired against a dead relay
  (`127.0.0.1:1`, a `free_port()` helper), which pointer invites cannot do: the accept fetches
  the prekey record from the relay directory, so pairing itself now needs a live relay.
- Resolution: the two decode tests read `ShortInvite::decode` (the handle/vault fields they
  assert are still carried in the clear); the handle-round-trip test spawns a live relay for
  its add-contact step; the outbox test pairs live and simulates the outage with
  `set_relay_clearnet` to a dead port, then back — same queue/retry mechanics, reachable
  premises. All four pass.
- Lesson: two compounding ones. (1) A commit that changes a wire format must sweep tests that
  decode it, and "tests that never run" hide the sweep — cargo's fail-fast stopped the first
  full run at `internal_mail`, masking that `revocation` was broken too; use `--no-fail-fast`
  when auditing a whole suite tree. (2) Pairing is no longer offline-capable by design; any
  test (or doc) assuming offline pairing predates pointer invites.

### Bare `cargo fmt` reformatted 35 untouched files on a repo with no rustfmt.toml [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: `cargo fmt -p hush-core -p hush-daemon -p hush-cli` as a hygiene step after the
  reach fix.
- Symptom: `git status` jumped from 6 modified files to 42 — the committed code is not
  rustfmt-clean (no `rustfmt.toml` exists, and the 2026-10-16 pointer-invites commit shows no
  formatting pass), so fmt rewrote ~2,500 lines across files this task never touched, including
  a 439-line diff in `zine_store.rs`.
- Resolution: reverted every file without a functional edit (`git checkout --` on the 35), then
  reverted the 5 functionally-edited files too and re-applied those edits surgically, because
  fmt noise had mixed into their diffs (main.rs showed 1,555 changed lines for ~30 real ones).
  Final diff: 6 files, 206 insertions, 14 deletions.
- Lesson: check for `rustfmt.toml` before running any formatter; on a repo that isn't
  format-clean, a bare fmt run is a whole-tree rewrite that drowns the real change in review
  noise. If formatting is wanted, it is its own commit with its own justification.

## 2026-10-16 — Pointer invites (v3, address-shaped codes)

### Edit tool replaced a three-line block with two lines, silently deleting a field [FIXED]

- Attempted: while adding the `modalKeys` field to `App` (app.ts), the StrReplace `old_string`
  spanned `paletteOpen` through `filesContactNick` and the `new_string` ended at `filesOpen` —
  the replacement dropped `private filesContactNick: string | null = null;` outright.
- Symptom: none at edit time — the tool reported success; the class was missing a field that
  five later references still used. Caught only because the next verification step (build) was
  queued and a grep for the field was run alongside it; tsc would have flagged the unknown
  identifiers on five lines.
- Resolution: re-edit restored the field and added the intended `modalKeys` block in one
  replacement; `npm run build` (tsc + vite) then passed clean and all 78 tests green.
- Lesson: when the intent is "insert after X", the `old_string` should be the smallest anchor
  plus its `new_string` should *contain* that anchor unchanged. Splicing a replace that
  shrinks a known-good block is how silent deletions happen; a field deletion is invisible to
  review that trusts the edit summary.

### A kill-and-restart in one shell kills itself: the restart text matches the kill pattern [FIXED]

- Attempted: `pkill -f "hush-daemo[n].*reach-[b]" ; nohup ./target/debug/hush-daemon --dir
  …/instances/reach-b …` in one command — both patterns bracket-escaped per this log's rule.
- Symptom: the whole command died in 233 ms with no output. The pkill patterns no longer match
  their own *pattern text* (the class trick holds), but the same shell line also contains the
  restart invocation — `hush-daemon --dir …/reach-b` — which the pattern legitimately matches.
  The wrapper's cmdline is the sandbox eval of the WHOLE command, so pkill killed the shell
  running the restart.
- Resolution: split the kill and the start into two separate Shell calls.
- Lesson: the character-class trick protects the pattern text, but any *other* text in the same
  command line that legitimately matches the pattern (here, the restart command itself) is fair
  game. Kill patterns must be evaluated against the full command line, not just the pattern.

### A Full reach choice is unannounceable, so a peer's stale narrow reach can never widen [OPEN]

- Attempted: two fresh pointer-invite contacts, both added with `reach: full`; one side's
  `peer_reach` sat at `mail_only` from queued pre-pointer state, refusing the first chat with
  "this is a mail-only relationship".
- Symptom: `set_contact_reach(full)` on the full side is a no-op — `changed == false` returns
  before the `MessagePayload::Reach` announcement (account.rs ~1165) — and `Work::AddContact`
  skips the announcement for `Full` ("the default needs no announcement", account_worker.rs
  ~1010). `peer_reach` is only ever written from an inbound announcement, so nothing can widen
  a stale `mail_only` back to `full` short of the full side toggling narrow→widen by hand.
- Needed: either announce the reach on add unconditionally (Full included), or let an explicit
  set announce even when the local choice is unchanged (announce is about the *peer's* mirror,
  not the local choice, so a no-op local set should still send).
- Lesson: "X is the default so it needs no announcement" conflates *initial state* with
  *re-synchronization*. Defaults cover fresh state; a peer recovering from stale or reordered
  state needs the announcement regardless.

### convert_bits accumulator overflow corrupted every payload past four bytes [FIXED]

- Attempted: hand-rolled bech32 (BIP-173) encode/decode for the ~100-byte
  pointer-invite body, because the `bech32` crate rejects payloads past the
  standard's 90-character *address* limit (Lightning's bolt11 makes the same
  exception).
- Symptom: `ShortInvite::encode` produced a valid checksummed string, but
  `decode` returned `Err(Corrupt)` on round trip — for every pointer payload,
  while the empty-payload BIP-173 spec vectors and the tiny hand probes all
  passed. Cost five test round trips to localize: the failures were blamed
  first on the crate's length cap, then on closure index capture, before the
  trace showed the parse dying on the *second* length-prefixed field.
- Root cause: the bit converter never masked the accumulator
  (`acc = (acc << from) | v` with no `& (1 << (from+to)) - 1`). For short
  inputs the final `& maxv` on extraction hid the garbage; a 102-byte payload
  left-shifted the u32 accumulator past 32 bits and every extracted byte
  after the first four was noise.
- Resolution: added the standard mask (bounded accumulator), plus a
  regression test that round-trips a full 102-byte body — the empty spec
  vectors cannot see this bug class.
- Lesson: spec vectors with *empty* payloads validate the checksum but say
  nothing about a bit-packing accumulator. Any hand-rolled bit converter
  needs a full-length round-trip test, not just canonical vectors.

### Closing over a mutable index from two closures was too subtle to debug [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: in `ShortInvite::decode`, two `FnMut` closures (`take`, `next`)
  shared one captured `at` cursor.
- Symptom: worked for the happy path but made the failure above genuinely
  hard to trace — every instrumentation attempt inside the closures hit the
  borrow checker (`cannot borrow \`at\` as immutable because it is also
  borrowed as mutable`), because each closure holds the `&mut` capture from
  its definition to its last use.
- Resolution: rewrote the parse with an explicit `&mut usize` parameter on
  each helper — no captures, sequential and printable. The missing
  `*at += len` advance (see next entry) then surfaced immediately.
- Lesson: when two closures mutate shared parse state, pass the cursor
  explicitly. Captured-state closures compile even when the state flow is
  wrong, and they block the instrumentation that would expose it.

### A length-prefixed reader that never advanced past the content [FIXED]

- Attempted: `next()` read a length byte, advanced one byte, validated the
  bound, and returned the string — without advancing past the string's bytes.
- Symptom: any pointer payload with a second optional field after the first
  failed to decode (the cursor landed inside the first field's content, read
  its data as the next length byte, and the bound check rejected it). Every
  field-optional combination in the round-trip tests caught it, but only
  after the bech32 layer was cleared as the culprit.
- Resolution: `*at += len` before returning the parsed string.
- Lesson: a length-prefixed field has two advances (length byte, content);
  writing them adjacent to each other in one helper makes the missing one
  visible by symmetry with the sibling `take` helper.

## 2026-10-16 — Shorter invite codes (v2 encoding)

### pkill self-match recurred because only one of two patterns was escaped [FIXED]

- Attempted: restart two hush-daemon instances with `pkill -f "hush-daemon.*hush-firstrun" ;
  pkill -f "hush-daemon.*reach-[b]"` — the second pattern used the character-class trick
  recorded in this log, the first did not.
- Symptom: the whole command died in 133 ms with no output; the first pkill matched the
  sandbox wrapper's own cmdline (which contains the literal pattern text) and killed the
  shell running the command, so the second pattern never ran and no daemon restarted.
- Resolution: re-ran both pkills with the class trick on every pattern
  (`hush-firstru[n]`), verified with pgrep, then restarted.
- Lesson: the character-class escape is per-pattern, not per-command. Every `pkill -f`
  pattern must be written so its own wrapper cannot match it, even when other patterns in
  the same line already are.

### CDP `Animation.setPlaybackRate` rejected by the browser tool wrapper [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: to slow all page animations so a 650 ms transition could be screenshotted,
  called `browser_cdp` with `Animation.setPlaybackRate {"playbackSpeed": 0.12}` (after
  `Animation.enable`, which worked).
- Symptom: `Error invoking remote method 'vscode:webviewSendCDPCommand': Error: Invalid
  parameters` — twice, so the wrapper rejects this method/param shape, not a transient.
