  via `Runtime.evaluate` is the equivalent lever.

## 2026-10-16 — Logo SVG review (Downloads/log.svg)

Three tooling problems in one short session; none are repo problems.

### Read tool's line-number markers look exactly like file corruption [FIXED]

- Attempted: read `/home/sam/Downloads/log.svg` (the Hush logo source, user asked to look
  into it). The Read output showed `    10|` on its own line and `    20|` **inside** the
  right pillar's `d` attribute — which would be invalid path data and would truncate the
  pillar mid-render (SVG paths stop at the first parse error).
- Symptom: looked like someone pasted chat output with line numbers into the file.
- Resolution: false alarm. `rg '\d+\|'` on log.svg found no matches, and the same
  `    10|` / `    20|` markers appear mid-sentence when reading this log file — they are
  the Read tool's every-10-lines display markers, right-aligned to 6 chars. Confirmed the
  SVG is clean by rendering check instead (see below).
- Lesson: do not trust inline `N|` tokens as file content when reading; verify with
  `rg` before diagnosing "corrupted" files.

### Read tool returns empty content for image files [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: visually inspect `apps/hush-tauri/src-tauri/icons/icon.png`, the user's
  attached logo PNG, and an IDE-browser screenshot — all three Read calls returned
  "Read image file" with no image content.
- Symptom: no visual verification possible via Read this session, for both repo assets
  and tool screenshots.
- Workaround: analyzed pixels programmatically with PIL (content bounding box, per-column
  extents, mirrored-half symmetry diff, corner color samples). Sufficient for geometry
  and gradient checks; actual visual confirmation was not possible.
- Needed to resolve: image attachment path for Read (tooling), or accept numeric checks.

### No SVG rasterizer installed despite librsvg2-dev being a build dependency [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: render log.svg to PNG with `rsvg-convert`, ImageMagick `convert`, and
  `cairosvg` — all three absent. README's build deps list `librsvg2-dev` (the library,
  not the CLI). `sudo apt install librsvg2-bin` not run (needs sudo approval).
- Workaround: served `/tmp` via `python3 -m http.server` on localhost:8931 and screenshotted
  `file`-less via the IDE browser MCP (browser_navigate rejects `file://` URLs). Server
  killed after use; port verified free with curl (000). Later in the same session: `pip
  install --user` is refused by PEP 668 (externally managed env), but a throwaway venv
  works with no sudo: `python3 -m venv /tmp/svgenv && /tmp/svgenv/bin/pip install cairosvg`.
- Lesson: for repeat SVG work, the venv+cairosvg route removes the whole browser detour
  (used for the 1024px app-icon raster).

### My own `d="` regex matched `id="` — false "geometry mismatch" [FIXED]

- Attempted: verify the cleaned canonical SVGs kept the mark's geometry by hashing the
  `d="..."` attributes of original vs. rewritten files. Hashes differed, which looked
  like the rewrite had altered paths.
- Symptom: token comparison listed garbage "paths" like `['h','u','s','h','r','e','l','a','y']`
  — the pattern `d="[^"]*"` also matches inside `id="hush-relay-title"`.
- Resolution: use `\sd="` (whitespace-boundary) and compare token sequences; all three
  files then verified token-identical (3 paths each). Re-verified again after the color
  retheme.
- Lesson: when grepping for attribute-like patterns, anchor the attribute name or the
  comparison is guaranteed false positives on ids ending in the same letter.

### Browser screenshot background flipped to black between captures [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: render-verify `hush-relay-mono.svg` via the IDE browser + PIL as before.
- Symptom: screenshot came back entirely black; PIL found no content pixels. The same
  pipeline had produced a white-background capture 30 seconds earlier. A/B reload of the
  color SVG also came back black-backgrounded — but with `#8b7df0` pixels scattered
  exactly where the mark is, so content was rendering; the page background (standalone
  SVG document) had gone dark.
- Workaround: for the mono check, wrapped the SVG in a tiny HTML page with explicit
  white background and `<img>` (in `<img>` context `currentColor` resolves to black);
  shape then measured 265x257 at 512px with symmetric pillar columns. Never trust the
  standalone viewer's background; assert on the shape, not the page.
- Lesson/tooling: screenshot pipelines here can change page background between captures;
  pixel assertions must be background-agnostic or use an explicit-background wrapper.

### Actual SVG findings (the deliverable)

- `log.svg` is valid and correct: two slanted pillars + arch bridge, one diagonal
  gradient `#A5C5FF → #718CFF → #8060F5`, content symmetric (both pillars span identical
  rows in a 150px render; only 336/11k pixels differ from mirror symmetry, antialiasing
  noise). Matches the user's attached render exactly (bbox 36,37→113,112 at 150px ==
  viewBox 48,47→152,153 at 200).
- Minor quality notes, not bugs: no `width`/`height` (standalone open fills viewport);
  gradient id `relay` is collision-prone if inlined into the Tauri app HTML (prefix it,
  e.g. `hush-logo-relay`); no `<title>`/`role="img"` for accessibility. Repo has no SVG
  assets — the logo ships only as rasters (`icon.png/ico/icns`), so this file is the only

## 2026-10-16 — Hush instance web preview (reach-b)

### A forgotten passphrase is unrecoverable through any user-facing path [OPEN]

- Attempted: log into the live `reach-b` web view (`:5173/?api=`) for the user, who did not
  know the vault's passphrase. Searched shell history, terminal logs, and scripts (the vault
  was created by typing into the desktop window, so no record exists); checked for a
  lockout (none) and for a recovery path.
- Finding: `hush-core` has `unwrap_master_with_recovery` (`recovery.rs:71`) — the recovery
  code shown once at creation really does wrap/unwrap the master key — but **no daemon
  route and no `hush-cli` command exposes it**. The only recovery routes are
  `/api/recovery/pending` and `/api/recovery/acknowledge`, which record that the code was
  saved; they do not redeem it. A locked vault with a lost passphrase is dead weight.
- Workaround this time: the vault was effectively empty (0 contacts, no mail handle,
  511-byte `chat.enc`), so it was recreated: daemon stopped, dir moved to
  `/tmp/reach-b-backup-1855`, daemon restarted with the same flags, new vault created
  through the UI against `https://hushrelay.space`.
- Needed to resolve (product): wire recovery into a user-facing path — e.g.
  `POST /api/recovery/redeem {code, new_passphrase}` and/or `hush-cli recover`, or a
  "forgot passphrase" flow on the unlock screen. The library half already exists.
- Side effect to remember: the recreated `reach-b` has a NEW identity. Any trust entry
  other vaults hold for the old identity (e.g. `reach-a`'s contact row) is stale until
  re-invited.

### pkill -f self-match trap, hit again via a different door [FIXED]

- Attempted: restart the reach-b daemon — `pkill -f "hush-daemon.*instances/reach-b"`,
  then `mv` the vault dir and start a fresh daemon.
- Symptom: the whole `;`-chained command produced no output and did nothing after the
  pkill — the wrapper shell's own command line contained the pattern text, so pkill killed
  the shell running the command (same failure mode logged 2026-10-15: "`pgrep -f` matches
  the searcher").
- Resolution: anchored the pattern with a character class — `pkill -f
  "hush-daemon.*reach-[b]"` — then moved the dir and started the daemon; verified
  `vault_present: false` on `/api/status` and proceeded.
- Lesson: this keeps recurring whenever the kill and the work share one command line.
  Anchor patterns with `[x]` classes, or run the kill in a separate call from the work.

## 2026-10-16 — Update hosting on hushrelay.space

### Three wrong guesses about the minisign format, found by testing against a real release [FIXED]

- Attempted: verify that a published artifact matches the public key compiled into the app
  (`plugins.updater.pubkey`), as a check that the signing secret and the shipped pubkey are
  still the same pair. No `minisign`/`rsign`/`signify` on this machine, so it was written
  against `cryptography` from the format as remembered.
- Symptom: all four signed 0.1.0 artifacts failed with `InvalidSignature`, and every
  reconstruction of the global signature failed too. Three separate assumptions were wrong:
  1. The release `.sig` file is not a minisign file — it is the **base64 of** one. Reading it
     as text produced a one-line file and `IndexError: list index out of range` on line 1.
  2. The algorithm bytes `ED` mean **prehashed** (Ed25519 over the artifact's BLAKE2b-512
     digest), not legacy-raw. Tauri's tooling labels its output `ED`, so assuming the
     opposite failed every main signature.
  3. The trailing global signature covers `signature || trusted_comment` with the literal
     `trusted comment: ` prefix **stripped**. Keeping the prefix failed; eight variants were
     tried before the right one matched.
- Resolution: `scripts/verify-update-signature.py`, with the three format notes written into
  its docstring as findings rather than as spec. Verified 2026-10-16: all four artifacts of
  v0.1.0 verify against the app's pubkey, and both controls (a signature checked against the
  wrong artifact, and one artifact with a single flipped byte) are rejected.
- Lesson: for a wire format with no reference implementation on the box, the artifact itself
  is the specification. Decode it and print the structure before writing the parser, and keep
  a negative control in the test — a verifier that always fails and one that always passes
  look identical until something is supposed to fail.

### The rewritten manifest was uploaded as if it were a bundle [FIXED]

- Attempted: publish v0.1.0 to the relay with `scripts/publish-updates-to-relay.sh`, after a
  `--dry-run` against the same `--assets-dir`.
- Symptom: the upload list contained 10 files where the release has 9 bundles, including
  `latest.json.relay` — the script's own rewritten manifest. It had been left in the assets
  directory by the dry run, and the bundle scan was "everything except `latest.json`".
- Resolution: internal files now live in their own `mktemp` directory that is never scanned,
  and the scan also excludes `latest.json.*`. Re-run with the stale file still present: 10
  bundles, no manifest copy, and the stray name 404s on the origin.
- Lesson: a directory that is both input and scratch space will eventually publish its
  scratch. Give generated files their own directory, and make the exclusion pattern match the
  family of names rather than the one name known at the time.

### `ssh` to the relay box refused mid-test — ufw `limit 22/tcp` [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: a burst of five SSH/rsync connections within a few seconds to exercise the new
  deploy key (shell access, rsync upload, rsync into a forbidden directory, no-pty,
  no-port-forwarding).
- Symptom: the first connection succeeded; every connection after it failed with
  `ssh: connect to host 37.27.150.250 port 22: Connection refused`, while ICMP answered and
  80/443 stayed open with the relay still serving `/health` at 200. Looked like a fail2ban
  ban, a dead sshd, or a provider-side block.
- Cause: the box's firewall rule is `22/tcp LIMIT`. ufw rejects the source IP after six new
  connections to port 22 inside a 30-second window, with `REJECT --reject-with
  icmp-port-unreachable`, which surfaces client-side as "Connection refused" rather than a
  timeout. Nothing was actually broken.
- Resolution: space remote calls out and batch work into one SSH invocation. The limit is
  already written down in `docs/ops/relay-prod-vps.md` and
  `packaging/cloud-init/relay-vps.yaml`; I did not read either before looping connections at
  the box.
- Lesson: one refused port with every other port healthy and the service answering is a rate
  limit or a source ban, not a downed host. Read the repo's own ops notes for firewall rules
  before hammering a box with a test loop. The publish workflow is unaffected: it opens a
  single rsync connection per release.

### Re-exporting a cfg-gated constant broke debug builds with E0432 [FIXED]

- Attempted: added `DEFAULT_RELAY_ONION_URL` (exists only under
  `#[cfg(not(debug_assertions))]`) to the unconditional `pub use config::{…}` list in
  `crates/hush-core/src/lib.rs` while wiring the production relay defaults.
- Symptom: `cargo check --release` passed, but `cargo test -p hush-core` (a debug build)
  failed to compile — `error[E0432]`: unresolved import. The constant does not exist in
  debug builds, so the unconditional re-export names nothing.
- Resolution: split it out as its own re-export under the same
  `#[cfg(not(debug_assertions))]`. Debug tests then pass (137 unit tests + integration
  suites) and the release check still passes.
- Lesson: when touching cfg-split defaults, run the debug tests **and** a release check in
  the same round trip — either alone gives a false green, because each cfg sees only half
  the surface.

## 2026-10-16 — Production relay VPS setup (37.27.150.250, Hetzner)

### Deployed the workstation-built binary to an ARM VPS — systemd 203/EXEC crash loop [FIXED]

- Attempted: the lab doc's deploy path — `cargo build --release` on the workstation, scp the
  binary to the VPS. That path documents a glibc match and an x86_64 match as its safety
  condition; the glibc check passed (both 2.39) and nobody checked the arch.
- Symptom: unit enters `activating (auto-restart)`, journal shows
  `Failed to execute /usr/local/bin/hush-relay: Exec format error`, `status=203/EXEC`, restart
  counter climbing. Root cause: the Hetzner instance is **aarch64** (`CAX` line), the
  workstation-built binary is x86_64.
- Resolution: cross-compiled in a disposable `ubuntu:24.04` container
  (`gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu` + rustup target `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, source mounted ro,
  CARGO_TARGET_DIR inside the container so root-owned artifacts never touch the host target/),
  6m47s. Binary verified `ELF ... ARM aarch64`, deployed, service active, /health 200.
  `systemctl reset-failed` was needed before the restart — the unit had hit its start limit.
- Lesson: `uname -m` on the target belongs next to the glibc check in
  `docs/ops/relay-lab-vps.md` before any scp of a binary. The doc's "workstation and box are
  both x86_64" is an assumption to re-verify per box, not a property of the deploy path.
  Workstation sudo is password-protected, so the cross toolchain came from a container, not
  apt on the host.

### Tor config written after tor had already started, and `/etc/tor/torrc.d` did not exist [FIXED]

- Attempted: one `set -e` SSH script doing useradd, tor config, Caddyfile, ufw, service
  enables, on a freshly `apt-get install tor`-ed box.
- Symptom: script died at the first heredoc —
  `bash: line 5: /etc/tor/torrc.d/hush-relay.torrc: No such file or directory` (the directory
  ships as a comment in torrc, it is not created). Nothing after it ran. On the re-run tor
  came up `active`, `Bootstrapped 100%`, but no onion hostname appeared: tor had been started
  by its package's enable before the `%include /etc/tor/torrc.d` line existed, so the hidden
  service was never in its config. A 25 s post-restart `cat hostname` also raced publication
  and printed nothing.
- Resolution: `mkdir -p /etc/tor/torrc.d` before the heredoc; after the config re-run,
  `sudo systemctl restart tor@default` and read the hostname a beat later — the service keys
  and `hostname` then appear under `/var/lib/tor/hush-relay/`. Onion verified with
  `curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:9050 http://<onion>/health` → 200.
- Lesson: on a `set -e` provisioning script, everything after the first failed line silently
  does not happen — split config writing from service starts, and after changing tor config,
  restart the `tor@default` instance explicitly; `active` + `Bootstrapped 100%` says nothing
  about which config the running instance loaded.

## 2026-10-16 — Production relay VPS cloud-init (packaging/cloud-init/relay-vps.yaml)

### cloud-init's `swap` module rejects `state: active` shown in its own published examples [FIXED]

- Attempted: `swap: {filename: /swapfile, size: 2G, state: active}` in the cloud-init
  user-data, following the example that appears in cloud-init's public docs and most howtos.
- Symptom: `cloud-init schema --config-file` (cloud-init 26.1, the version Ubuntu 24.04
  ships) — `Error: Cloud config schema errors: swap: Additional properties are not allowed
  ('state' was unexpected)`. YAML parses fine; only the schema check catches it.
- Resolution: dropped `state`; the module creates and activates the swapfile from
  `filename` + `size` alone. Schema check now passes: `Valid schema`.
- Lesson: cloud-init's published examples lag its schema — run `cloud-init schema` locally
  (it is on this workstation) before pasting user-data into a provider, not after boot.

## 2026-10-16 — First tagged release: seven failures the workflow had never been in a position to find

The first tag (`v0.1.0`) was the workflow's first execution, and it took four attempts to get
macOS and Linux through. Every failure was pre-existing and none was reachable by the local
checks that had been done: the YAML parsed, `npm ci` worked, and the CLI accepted the bundle
args. Three of the seven (the apt list, the AppImage, the missing `libasound2-dev`) could have
been rehearsed locally before the tag by running the workflow's apt list in a container and
building the AppImage here. That is the cheap lesson of this slice: the workflow was treated as
untestable until it ran, and it was not.

One thing the release did not settle is the first entry below, left OPEN: the updater endpoint
cannot serve a private repository, which the tag made verifiable for the first time.

### The updater endpoint cannot serve a private repository [OPEN]

- Attempted: after publishing `v0.1.0`, verify the URL the app polls is reachable.
- Symptom: `https://github.com/sambitar/ProjectHush/releases/latest/download/latest.json`
  returns **404**, as do `/releases/download/v0.1.0/latest.json` and the release page itself —
  while `gh api repos/.../releases/latest` reports `v0.1.0`, `draft: false`, `prerelease: false`,
  and `gh release download` fetches the assets without complaint. The repository is private
  (`visibility: PRIVATE`), and GitHub answers 404 rather than 403 for every unauthenticated
  release URL in a private repository. The asset list, `latest.json` and the `.sig` files are all
  correct; nothing about the build is wrong.
- Consequence: no installed copy can fetch the manifest, so **auto-update cannot work while the
  repository is private**, however correct the signing pair is. The startup probe is silent by
  design (`STARTUP_UPDATE_DELAY_MS`), so this shows up only as a failed manual check in
  Settings → About rather than as an error at launch. Downloads carry the same constraint: the
  release page is visible to collaborators only.
- Resolution: none yet, and it needs a decision rather than a fix. Either the repository becomes
  public, or `latest.json` is hosted at a publicly reachable URL and
  `plugins.updater.endpoints` points there, or updates are shipped by hand for now.
- Lesson: "the release published successfully" and "an installed copy can see the release" are
  two different claims, and only the first one was ever checked before this tag.

### `bundle.icon` was never set, so macOS shipped iconless and the AppImage refused to build [FIXED]

- Attempted: build all four matrix legs on the first tag.
- Symptom: the Linux leg aborted in the AppImage bundler —
  `thread '<unnamed>' panicked at .../linuxdeploy.rs:101:6: couldn't find a square icon to use
  as AppImage icon / Aborted (core dumped)`. The icons were all present and square (32, 128, 256,
  512), because `bundle.icon` in `tauri.conf.json` was unset and Tauri bundles only the icons it
  is told about. The same absence meant the macOS legs had been "succeeding" while producing an
  `.app` with no `icon.icns` at all — a fact only visible by unpacking the published tarball.
- Resolution: `bundle.icon` lists the five existing icon files. Verified locally: the deb now
  installs `usr/share/icons/hicolor/{32x32,128x128,256x256@2}/apps/hush-tauri.png`.
- Lesson: a bundler that silently omits something will keep succeeding. The AppImage panicking is
  what made a latent packaging gap visible.

### linuxdeploy cannot resolve the libevent that Tor brings its own copy of [FIXED]

- Attempted: build the AppImage now that it had an icon.
- Symptom: `failed to bundle project: `failed to run linuxdeploy``. Reproducing the same command
  against the AppDir the bundler had already assembled gave the real error —
  `Deploying dependencies for ELF file Hush.AppDir/usr/lib/Hush/tor/tor / ERROR: Could not find
  dependency: libevent-2.1.so.7 / ERROR: Failed to deploy dependencies for existing files`.
  linuxdeploy resolves every ELF file in the AppDir, including the bundled Tor; Tor carries its
  own libevent beside it and finds it at runtime via `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (`tor.rs`), but linuxdeploy
  searches system paths and never looks in `usr/lib/Hush/tor`.
- Resolution: `libevent-2.1-7` in the workflow's apt list, so the library is visible to
  linuxdeploy at build time. Verified locally against the same AppDir: linuxdeploy completes,
  deploys `usr/lib/libevent-2.1.so.7`, and produces a 95 MB AppImage.
- Lesson: an AppImage bundler treats every ELF file as its own responsibility. A self-contained
  runtime layout (library beside its binary) is invisible to it.

### The Linux daemon links alsa, which the runner image did not have [FIXED]

- Attempted: stage the daemon sidecar on the Linux leg.
- Symptom: six minutes into the build,
  `pkg-config exited with status code 1 / Package alsa was not found in the pkg-config search
  path. / The system library `alsa` required by crate `alsa-sys` was not found.`
- Resolution: `libasound2-dev` (plus `libdbus-1-dev` for the app's `tao → dbus → libdbus-sys`
  path, which Tauri's documented list does not name). The chain is `hush-daemon → cpal → alsa →
  alsa-sys`, so the daemon — not the app — is what needs it; the app is the only thing that had
  ever been built on that image.
- Lesson: the dependency list a project inherits from a framework's docs covers the framework's
  app, not a sidecar the framework knows nothing about.

### The workflow's apt list named two conflicting appindicator packages [FIXED]

- Attempted: the same first run, in `install Linux dependencies`.
- Symptom: apt refused the entire list before installing anything —
  `libappindicator3-dev : Depends: libappindicator3-1 (= 12.10.1+20.10.20200706.1-0ubuntu1)` /
  `libayatana-appindicator3-dev : Conflicts: libappindicator3-dev` /
  `E: Unable to correct problems, you have held broken packages.`
- Resolution: the legacy `libappindicator3-dev` is gone; Ayatana is the maintained fork and the
  package Tauri v2 documents.
- Lesson: apt fails the whole list, not the offending package, so the error names packages that
  are individually fine.

### rust-cache rejected the Linux key, silently disabling that leg's cache [FIXED]

- Attempted: read the failure logs of the second run.
- Symptom: every run printed, while setting up the cache,
  `##[error]ValidationError: Key Validation Error: v0-rust-ubuntu-22.04---bundles
  appimage,deb-publish-Linux-x64-01b81e85 cannot contain commas.` and then built libsignal and the
  rest from scratch anyway. The key was `matrix.platform` + `matrix.args`, and the Linux args are
  `--bundles appimage,deb`. Cost: roughly ten minutes per run instead of one.
- Resolution: the key uses `matrix.target`, which identifies the build and cannot contain a comma.
- Lesson: a cache that fails to save looks exactly like a cache that is cold. The error was in the
  log from the very first run and read as noise.

### A tracked filename containing a colon stops Windows checkout [FIXED]

- Attempted: run the Windows leg.
- Symptom: `##[error]error: invalid path '# Project Handoff: Private, Local-First,.md'` at
  `actions/checkout`, before any step of ours. A colon is a drive separator on Windows, so the
  file cannot exist in a Windows working tree. It was the only tracked path with a character
  Windows refuses.
- Resolution: renamed to `Project-Handoff-Private-Local-First.md`; contents untouched.
- Lesson: a repository that has never been cloned on Windows can carry paths Windows cannot hold.

### MSVC has no variable-length arrays, so the vendored Opus would not compile [FIXED]

- Attempted: stage the daemon on Windows, after the filename was fixed.
- Symptom: every Opus C file failed —
  `vendor/opus/src\analysis.c(180): error C2057: expected constant expression`,
  `C2466: cannot allocate an array of constant size 0`, `C2133: 'tmp': unknown size`, from the
  `VAR_ARRAYS` define the build script set. That trio is MSVC's way of reporting a C99 VLA.
- Resolution: `hush-audio`'s build script defines `USE_ALLOCA` instead of `VAR_ARRAYS` when
  `CARGO_CFG_TARGET_ENV` is `msvc`, which is the mode Opus's own CMake build picks for Visual
  Studio and which resolves to `_alloca` on `_WIN32`. Only the `msvc` branch changed, so Linux and
  macOS keep the mode they already build with; the host build was recompiled afterwards to
  confirm it is unaffected.
- Not verified locally: this machine has no MSVC toolchain. The CI leg is what proved it — the
  build advanced past all of Opus and failed later, in Rust.

### The daemon cannot exist on Windows: tokio has no `UnixListener` there [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: the same Windows leg, with Opus fixed.
- Symptom: `error[E0433]: cannot find `UnixListener` in `net`` and
  `error[E0425]: cannot find type `UnixListener` in module `tokio::net``. The daemon's transport is
  a Unix domain socket and tokio does not provide one on Windows.
- Resolution: the Windows matrix leg is removed. A Windows bundle would carry no daemon, and the
  app would start and find nothing to talk to — worse than no Windows bundle. The transport port
  (named pipe, or loopback TCP) is a change to `crates/hush-daemon`, not to the workflow; the
  matrix comment carries the exact entry to restore.
- Lesson: this is the one problem here that is not fixed, and the release it blocks is a platform
  rather than a step.

### RELEASING.md predicted the Windows socket path "compiles" — the run disproved it [FIXED]

- Attempted: trust the document's own risk note when scoping the sidecar work.
- Symptom: the note said the socket path "compiles on Windows but has never been built or run
  there". It does not compile: `E0433`/`E0425`, above. A prediction written to be honest had been
  wrong for as long as it existed, and it was wrong in the direction that made the platform look
  cheaper than it is.
- Resolution: the note records what the tag actually found, the Windows platform note is marked as
  describing a leg that is not built, and the icon section says `bundle.icon` is load-bearing.
- Lesson: "not yet exercised" notes age into claims. Date them and replace them with results.

### tauri-bundler discards linuxdeploy's output, so its error message names nothing [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: diagnose `failed to bundle project: `failed to run linuxdeploy`` from the CI log.
- Symptom: the log contains nothing between `Bundling Hush_0.1.0_amd64.AppImage` and the failure.
  linuxdeploy's own `ERROR: Could not find dependency: libevent-2.1.so.7` was never printed.
- Resolution: the bundler leaves the assembled AppDir behind, so running linuxdeploy against
  `target/release/bundle/appimage/Hush.AppDir` by hand — the extracted binaries are under
  `/tmp/appimage_extracted_*` after a run — prints the real error. This is how the libevent cause
  was found, and it should be the first move for any future AppImage failure.
- Lesson: a bundler that swallows a subprocess's stderr turns a one-line cause into a guessing
  game. Its leftover artifacts are the way in.

### Tooling: a commit message containing backticks was executed by the shell [FIXED]

- Attempted: `git commit -m "<long message with `UnixListener` and `tokio::net` in it>"` through
  the Shell tool.
- Symptom: the backticks were command-substituted before git saw them —
  `error: pathspec 'on' did not match any file(s) known to git`, `Command 'run' not found` — and
  the commit silently did not happen. The `&&` chain stopped there, so the branch was created but
  left empty and the push never ran.
- Resolution: commit messages and PR bodies are written to files and passed with `-F` /
  `--body-file`. Backticks in commit messages are normal for this repository and will recur.
- Lesson: tooling-related. Shell metacharacters in prose are a trap, and the failure mode is a
  missing commit rather than an error about quoting.

### Tooling: in-progress run logs are not readable, and one grep rendered text wrongly [OPEN]

- Attempted: watch the Linux leg while it was still running, and read `tor.rs` through the Shell
  tool's `rg`.
- Symptom: two separate tooling problems. (1) `gh run view --log-failed` returned zero lines for a
  run that had failed jobs, and `gh api .../jobs/<id>/logs` returned
  `<Error><Code>BlobNotFound</Code>` until the run completed, so a long leg can only be watched
  by polling job status. (2) `rg -rn 'LD_LIBRARY_PATH|libevent'` printed `std::env::var_os("n")`
  for source that reads `std::env::var_os("LD_LIBRARY_PATH")` — the literal string was rendered as
  `n`. Reading the same file with the Grep tool showed it correctly.
- Resolution: none for either; both were worked around (poll status instead of reading logs; use
  the Grep tool for source). Recorded because the first one cost a diagnosis delay and the second
  briefly looked like a source corruption in `tor.rs`.
- Lesson: tooling-related, not repo problems. Treat a suspicious single-token reading from shell
  grep as suspect and re-read the file with the file tools before acting on it.

## 2026-10-16 — Bundling the daemon as a Tauri sidecar: one rejected flag, one build-time coupling

### `cargo build --profile debug` is rejected, and the stager's first version used it [FIXED]

- Attempted: a staging script that runs `cargo build --profile "$PROFILE"` with
  `PROFILE=debug`, so one flag shape covered both profiles.
- Symptom: `error: profile name 'debug' is reserved / To configure the default
  development profile, use the name 'dev' as in [profile.dev]`. The output directory
  is `target/debug` regardless, so the flag and the directory disagree by design.
- Resolution: the flag is built from the profile — empty for `debug`, `--profile
  release` for `release` — and the copy still reads `target/debug`. The script
  writes the decision down where the next reader will hit it.
- Lesson: cargo's profile *flag* and profile *directory* are not the same name.
  Tooling-related, not a repo problem.

### `bundle.externalBin` makes the daemon a build-time dependency of the app [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: add the daemon to the bundle by naming it in `bundle.externalBin` and
  spawn it from the app, expecting the file to be needed only when a bundle is
  packaged.
- Symptom: `cargo check -p hush-tauri` fails outright —
  `resource path 'binaries/hush-daemon-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu' doesn't exist` —
  because `tauri-build` resolves and validates the entry during compilation. That
  silently makes `cargo test --workspace`, a fresh clone, every run script and every
  CI leg depend on a built daemon first. The message names the file but not the fix.
- Resolution: `scripts/stage-daemon-sidecar.sh` builds the daemon and copies it
  under the triple-name Tauri looks for; the run scripts call it with the profile
  they already build, the release workflow calls it per matrix leg (and now installs
  `protoc` on all three platforms, because the daemon links `hush-core` and the app
  does not), and the README's test section says to run it once after cloning.
- Lesson: a Tauri sidecar is a compile-time dependency, not a packaging step. Check
  what `tauri-build` validates before assuming a config entry only affects bundling.

## 2026-10-16 — The sweep for the clinic's real hostname answered with 8075 license URLs

### A repo-wide URL grep was read as "no app hostnames here" [FIXED]

- Attempted: find out whether the clinic app on the box has a real public hostname
  configured, to judge whether nginx's catch-all is serving anything that matters.
  Grepped `/opt /home/alhakim /root /etc/systemd/system /etc/cloudflared` for
  `https?://<host>.<tld>` with a vendor blocklist.
- Symptom: the top 25 hits were `openpgpjs.org` (8075), `slsa.dev` (7686),
  `openssl.org` (4670), eleven variants of the ECMA-262 spec, and nextjs docs. The
  sweep walked `node_modules` and build output, so the output was noise at the top and
  the real answer was not in the visible list at all. It reads as "no app hostnames
  here", which is not what it demonstrated — anything further down was simply cut off
  by `head -25`. No `node_modules` exclusion, no `-prune`, no bound to config surfaces.
- Resolution: re-ran bounded — `find -maxdepth 4` pruning `node_modules`, `.next`,
  `dist`, `.git`, then grepping only `.env*`, `next.config.*` and `*.service`. That
  answered it: the clinic app configures no domain (it is reached by IP), and the only
  app URL on the box is cricket's `CRICKET_PUBLIC_BASE`, still pointing at the dead
  `sources-baghdad-sullivan-olive.trycloudflare.com`.
- Lesson: a repo-wide URL grep is not evidence about configuration. Name the files that
  can hold the answer and grep those; an unbounded grep plus `head` reports "none" for
  "not in the first 25".

## 2026-10-16 — Cloudflare quick-tunnel hostnames die, and a live connector hides it

### Three trycloudflare hostnames were NXDOMAIN while their connectors reported healthy [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: answer "can we use the Cloudflare HTTPS tunnel instead of the plain-HTTP lab
  relay, so teammates can run release builds?" by checking the box rather than the doc.
- Symptom: every `trycloudflare.com` hostname this repo names was gone — `ban-therapeutic-
  daughter-organic` (nginx/relay via path ingress), `sources-baghdad-sullivan-olive` (the
  cricket app's `CRICKET_PUBLIC_BASE`), `remedy-relief-patricia-main` (the relay-facing
  quick tunnel) — while `systemctl is-active cloudflared-*.service` said `active` for all of
  them and the journal still showed the old hostname. NXDOMAIN at 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, so it
  was not local resolver cache. Same failure as 2026-10-10, now for the third hostname on
  this box: Cloudflare reclaims account-less tunnel names and the connector does not notice.
- Resolution (workaround): restarting `cloudflared-hush-quick.service` mints a new hostname,
  and that one works — `/health` 200 with `ssl_verify_result=0`, `/drop` 200 at 53837 bytes,
  `smoke-relay-lab.sh` green end to end through it, and a **release** `hush-cli` accepts it
  where it refuses `http://137.184.129.205:8790` with `insecure relay URL`. Recorded in
  `docs/ops/relay-lab-vps.md` along with the three durable alternatives.
- Lesson: "the connector is active" is not evidence a hostname resolves. A quick tunnel needs
  the hostname fetched from the log and a live request against it, every time; anything that
  outlives a session needs a named tunnel with a real DNS record.

### The `hush` named tunnel has been up for days and can serve nothing [OPEN]

- Attempted: use the purpose-built named tunnel instead of a quick one.
- Symptom: account `75743fae14d6c875d63ca54494668df8`, tunnel
  `e8c187f1-e516-4371-ab7d-18053dcf5b11`, connector `cloudflared-hush.service` `active` with
  four QUIC connections — and no public hostname, so the connector logs `No ingress rules were
  defined … cloudflared will return 503 for all incoming HTTP requests`. The box has no
  `cert.pem` and no Cloudflare API token, so `cloudflared tunnel list` / `route dns` cannot
  even enumerate it from there.
- Needed: a Public Hostname added in the dashboard for that tunnel (service HTTP →
  `localhost:8790`, pointed at the relay rather than nginx), on a zone in that account. This
  is a dashboard action with no CLI path available from this machine, so it stays OPEN until
  someone with dashboard access adds it.

## 2026-10-15 — Test scratch directories: 1576 vaults' worth of private keys left in /tmp

### A test vault's private keys were left in the system temp dir, 2027 directories of them [FIXED]

- Attempted: tidy up after the onboarding slice and looked at `/tmp`.
- Symptom: 2027 `hush-*` directories, 1576 of them holding an `identity.secret`, spanning two
  days of runs, 215 MB, directories mode 0775 and files 0664 — readable by group and other.
  `fn scratch` in `vault.rs`, `account.rs`, and `device.rs` built a path from `temp_dir()` plus
  the process id and never removed it. The id changes every run, so the `remove_dir_all` at the
  *start* of the function never matched anything the previous run had made, and the count grew by
  one directory per test per run, without limit.
- Resolution: `crates/hush-core/src/testutil.rs` (test-only) with `ScratchDir`, a
  `tempfile::TempDir` that derefs to its path and deletes itself when the test ends, a panicking
  test included. Used by `vault.rs`, `account.rs`, `device.rs`, and the 13 sites in `chat_log.rs`;
  `tests/vault_identity.rs` holds a `TempDir` directly. Verified: `cargo test -p hush-core` leaves
  the `/tmp` count unchanged (2027 before, 2027 after) with all 202 tests passing. The existing
  2064 entries were deleted, 215 MB.
- Lesson: `temp_dir().join(pid)` is not a scratch directory, it is a directory that happens to
  have a unique name. Cleanup that only runs at the start of the next process never runs.

### A self-deleting scratch directory cannot be created inside a helper that returns the account [FIXED]

- Attempted: swap the three `scratch` helpers over to `ScratchDir` and move on.
- Symptom: `cargo test -p hush-core` went from 137 passing to 5 failing, all in `account::tests`,
  all panicking at `account.rs:4879` inside `create_conclave`. `intro_vault(name)` created the
  directory, built the account, and returned only the account — so the guard dropped at the end of
  the helper and deleted the vault out from under an account that still writes to it. The
  directory had survived before precisely because nothing owned it.
- Resolution: `intro_vault` returns `(ScratchDir, Account)` and the nine call sites bind it as
  `let (_dir, mut x) = ...`, so the test body owns the directory for as long as the account lives.
  All 202 tests pass.
- Lesson: turning a leak into an owned guard moves the question from "when does this get deleted"
  to "who holds it". A helper that returns something outliving the directory is the case that
  breaks.

### The same pattern is still in three other crates [OPEN]

- `crates/hush-daemon/src/reads.rs` (a reader cache), `apps/hush-tauri/src-tauri/src/tor.rs` (five
  Tor data dirs) and `daemon_client.rs` (a proxy test dir) still build `temp_dir()` paths from the
  process id and never remove them. None of them holds a vault or a key — the 2064 entries I
  deleted included 14 `hush-proxy-test` and a handful of `hush-tor-*`, all disposable state — so
  the harm is clutter rather than secrets.
- Not fixed here because `testutil` is `#[cfg(test)]` and private to `hush-core`, so each crate
  would need its own guard, and that is a change to three crates' test scaffolding rather than to
  the thing that was leaking keys. Recorded so the next run does not rediscover it as a surprise.

## 2026-10-15 — First run in the product: create the vault from the window

### The daemon could not tell "no vault" from "locked", and could not create one [FIXED]

- Attempted: make a teammate's first run create a brand new vault in the app, the way a packaged
  build would, instead of pre-creating one from a script before the UI starts.
- Symptom: `GET /api/status` reported only lock state. A window with no vault on disk was
  indistinguishable from one with a locked vault, and `app.ts` always rendered the unlock screen.
  There was no route that created a vault at all: `Account::create` was reachable only from the CLI
  and from the test helpers.
- Resolution: `hush_core::vault_exists(dir)` (the `vault.lock.json` marker that `Account::create`
  already writes) is surfaced as `vault_present` in `/api/status`, and `POST /api/vault/create`
  creates, names, and configures the vault in one call, returning 409 if one already exists. The
  window renders a Welcome screen while `!vault_present` and unlocks into the recovery-code modal
  after creating. Verified end to end in a headless browser against a fresh directory: filled the
  Welcome form, got `vault.lock.json` and `client-config.json` on disk, unlocked, and saw the
  recovery code.
- Lesson: "locked" and "absent" are different states and the UI needs both; a boolean that only
  covers one of them will silently render the wrong screen.

### A create route cannot be served straight from the axum handler [FIXED]

- Attempted: call `Account::create` inside the `vault_create` handler, next to the unlock handler.
- Symptom: `error[E0277]: the trait bound Account: Send is not satisfied` / "future cannot be sent
  between threads" / "required by a bound in `Handler`". `Account` holds state that is not `Send`, so
  holding it across an `await` in a handler is a compile error — the unlock path never hit this
  because it goes through `AccountWorker` and only sends a reply over a channel.
- Resolution: creation follows the existing worker pattern. `Work::Create` carries the directory,
  passphrase, name, and relay; the worker runs `Account::create` on its own thread and answers with
  `WorkResult::Created { recovery_code, vault_name, relay }`. The handler only awaits the reply.
- Lesson: in this daemon, nothing that owns an `Account` may be held across an `await` in a handler.
  The worker channel is the boundary, not an optimization.

### The recovery code is only obtainable at creation, and the UI must say so [FIXED]

- Attempted: rely on the existing post-unlock recovery-code prompt to show the code after creating.
- Symptom: reading `Account::create` and the unlock path showed the code is returned by `create` and
  is not re-derivable from a later unlock — `maybeShowRecoveryCode` shows a stored code only when the
  client already holds it. Without wiring the create response into the modal, a new user would have
  created a vault and never seen the one thing they must keep.
- Resolution: the create response's `recovery_code` is handed straight to the existing modal
  (`this.recoveryModalCode = created.recovery_code`), so the code is shown immediately after
  creation, once, and the client is never left without it.
- Lesson: a secret that exists only in one response has to be displayed by the screen that receives
  it; a later screen cannot recover it.

## 2026-10-15 — Handoff readiness: what a teammate gets from a clone

### `protoc` was a hard build requirement and named nowhere [FIXED]

- Attempted: answer "if I send this repo to my team, can they use it out of the box?" from the code
  rather than from the docs.
- Symptom: nothing in the repository provides `protoc`, and nothing named it. `crates/hush-core`'s
  build script only did `std::env::set_var("PROTOC", ...)` for the vendored copy under `.tools/`,
  which `.gitignore` excludes — and that assignment could not have worked anyway: cargo runs each
  build script in its own process, so `PROTOC` set there never reaches the crate that needs it.
  `libsignal-rust`'s build script is the one calling
  `prost_build::compile_protos(&["protos/WhisperTextProtocol.proto"], ..)`, so a machine without
  protoc fails with a prost error raised from a crate nobody typed, naming neither protoc nor where
  to get one.
- Resolution: `crates/hush-core/build.rs` resolves protoc (explicit `PROTOC` -> `.tools/protoc-dist`
  -> `PATH`) and panics with the install lines when there is none. Verified by hiding `.tools/` and
  dropping protoc from `PATH`: `cargo build -p hush-core` prints "protoc not found." with the
  apt/dnf/brew lines and exits 101 instead of the prost error, and a normal build still succeeds.
- Lesson: a prerequisite that exists only on the author's machine is invisible until someone else
  clones. `build.rs` is the earliest place a plain `cargo build` can name it.

### Every internal script overrode a working protoc with a machine-local path [FIXED]

- Symptom: `export PROTOC="${ROOT}/.tools/protoc-dist/bin/protoc"` in 11 scripts. On this machine that
  path exists; anywhere else it does not, and because the assignment is unconditional it *replaces* a
  protoc that is on `PATH` — turning a working build into the prost failure above.
- Resolution: one resolver, `hush_require_protoc` in `scripts/lib/prereqs.sh`, preferring an explicit
  `PROTOC`, then the vendored copy, then `PATH`, and printing install lines when it finds none. Both
  run scripts and all 11 internal scripts source it. Verified: with `PROTOC=/nope/protoc` it falls
  through to the vendored copy with a note; with no protoc anywhere it prints the message and returns
  1; `bash -n` is clean on every script in `scripts/`.
- Lesson: an environment variable exported "just in case" can override the correct value.

### The run scripts assumed `node_modules` already existed [FIXED]

- Symptom: `run-one-ui.sh` and `run-two-ui.sh` call `npm run build` and `npm run dev` directly, and
  `.gitignore` excludes `apps/hush-tauri/node_modules/`. On a fresh clone the first run dies at
  "vite: not found" before anything starts.
- Resolution: `hush_ensure_node_modules` runs `npm ci` against the committed lockfile when the
  directory is absent and does nothing when it is present. Verified on a materialized fresh tree (no
  `node_modules`, no `target`, no `.tools`): `npm ci` plus `npm run build` finished in 22s and wrote
  `ui/dist`. A stub `npm` confirmed the guard runs exactly once, only when the directory is missing.
- Method note: a real `git clone` cannot test uncommitted changes, so the fresh tree was materialized
  with `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard | tar -cf - -T -`, which is exactly the file set a commit
  would carry.
- Lesson: a build step that depends on an ignored directory needs the install step in front of it, or
  the first clone is the only one that ever fails.

### There was no entry point at the repository root [FIXED]

- Symptom: no `README.md`. The root held a design handoff document, `RELEASING.md`, and
  `docs/WORKSPACE.md`, which is stale in the direction that matters most: it opens with "do not
  scaffold until implementation is approved" while the workspace it describes is built. Nothing said
  which script to run, or that `protoc` and `npm ci` come first.
- Resolution: `README.md` with prerequisites and their install lines, the run scripts and their
  options, relay and Tor behaviour, the test commands, the crate layout, and pointers into `docs/`.
- Lesson: "the docs are in `docs/`" is not a substitute for telling a reader where to start.

### A display artifact in tool output nearly became a false bug report [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: read the `PROTOC` lines in the scripts before replacing them.
- Symptom: `Read` and `grep -n` both rendered the line as
  `export PROTOC="${ROOT}/.tools/protoc-dist/bin/protoc}"` — a stray `}` inside the quotes. That would
  be a real bug (a `PROTOC` path with a trailing brace), and it was reported to the user as one before
  being checked. `grep ... | cat -A` showed the actual bytes with no brace: the `}` was an artifact of
  the line rendering in the tool output.
- Resolution: read raw bytes (`cat -A`) before claiming a file contains something surprising. This is
  a tooling artifact, not a repository problem, and nothing in the repository changed because of it.
- Lesson: tool output that quotes file content is still a rendering. One `cat -A` beats a retraction.

### The two-peer run created its vaults before the relay they needed was up [FIXED]

- Attempted: run `run-two-ui.sh` on a tree with no `instances/` at all, the shape a teammate gets.
- Symptom: the script called `setup-two-peers.sh` before building and starting the local relay, and
  `setup-two-peers.sh` probes `${RELAY_URL}/health` while creating the vaults. Nothing answered, so the
  run died at vault creation — before the relay that was about to be started, and before anything the
  operator could see. The order was fine only for a tree whose relay was already running.
- Resolution: the relay is built and started before the vaults are created. Verified today in the
  materialized fresh tree, twice: with a local relay (`--relay http://127.0.0.1:8798`, relay built and
  started, vaults created against it) and with the cloud relay (`--relay
  http://137.184.129.205:8790`, no local relay started, vaults created against the remote one).
- Lesson: a setup script that probes the service it is about to need has to run after that service, and
  "the relay is already up on my machine" hides the ordering bug from the person most likely to run it.

### The relay a vault is on cannot be read back from the vault [FIXED]

- Attempted: pick the daemon profile in `run-one-ui.sh` (release normally, debug when the relay is
  plaintext HTTP off-loopback, because `hush-core`'s `HttpPolicy::LoopbackOnly` refuses the latter) by
  reading the relay the vault is on — the way `run-two-ui.sh` already reads
  `instances/<vault>/client-config.json`.
- Symptom: for vaults created with `hush-cli init --relay <url>`, `client-config.json` does not exist at
  all, and the running daemon reports the relay as coming from somewhere else:
  `{"locked":true,...,"relay":"http://127.0.0.1:8787","relay_source":"default"}` before unlock and
  `{"locked":false,...,"relay":"http://137.184.129.205:8790","relay_source":"vault"}` after. The
  authoritative relay is inside the encrypted vault, so a script cannot read it without the passphrase,
  and the plaintext file is only the override channel. Reading only that file would have chosen a
  **release** daemon for a plaintext remote relay — on the teammate's *second* run, after the first one
  worked, and the failure would have arrived as a relay error rather than as a profile choice.
- Resolution: `create_vault` also records the relay in `client-config.json` with
  `hush-cli --dir <vault> config set --relay <url>` (debug binary: a release build refuses to write a
  plaintext non-loopback relay, which is the point). Verified: the new vault's file reads
  `{"v": 1, "relay_url": "http://137.184.129.205:8790"}`, and `HUSH_PROFILE` still overrides the
  automatic choice in both run scripts.
- Lesson: `/api/status` is the only place the *effective* relay is visible, and only after unlock. A
  value the daemon resolves from encrypted state has to be written down somewhere plaintext if a script
  needs it before the daemon starts.

### The shared relay has no HTTPS origin, so a release daemon cannot use it [OPEN]

- Symptom: the shared relay is `http://137.184.129.205:8790` — plain HTTP on a public address, which a
  release daemon refuses by policy (the refusal itself is verified, and it is what
  `scripts/smoke-relay-lab.sh` documents and works around by using debug binaries). The HTTPS
  quick-tunnel origin recorded earlier is dead: the hostname no longer resolves, so it is not a way out.
- Resolution so far: both run scripts now detect the plaintext-remote case and build and run the daemon
  in **debug**, saying why in one line. The relay path itself works: today's run of the repository's own
  cross-machine smoke against the lab relay reported
  `ok: invite/contact exchange completed through the remote relay`,
  `ok: mail accepted from B and queued on the remote relay`,
  `ok: A received the mail that travelled through the remote relay`,
  `ok: reply travelled back through the remote relay`, `cross-machine relay smoke ok`.
- Still open: a **release** daemon — what a packaged app runs — needs TLS in front of the relay or the
  onion address with Tor. Neither is in place on the lab box, so "test together" currently means a
  debug daemon on both sides. `docs/ops/relay-lab-vps.md` has the deploy steps for both.
- Lesson: "plaintext off-loopback is refused" is a good default that turns the shared lab box into
  something the shipped binary cannot use. That trade needs to be made explicitly, in the open, not
  discovered by a teammate whose invite silently goes nowhere.

### `pkill -f` and `pgrep -f` matched the shell running them, three more times [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: (1) stop the previous fresh-tree run with
  `pkill -f "/tmp/hush-ootb/scripts/run-two-ui.sh"`; (2) stop a test daemon with
  `for p in $(pgrep -f "hush-daemon --dir /tmp/hush-handmade"); do kill "$p"; done`.
- Symptom: exit 0, no output, and the command returned in half a second — it had killed its own
  `/bin/bash -c` wrapper, so everything chained after it never ran (the tree refresh, the vault
  removal, the next run, the test itself). The next command's log was then empty or missing an expected
  line, which read as "the code did not do what it should" until the cause was clear. In (2) the pattern
  was unbracketed inside a `pgrep` substitution, so the bracket fix applied to the neighbouring `pkill`
  did not help. This is the same trap already logged three times in this file, once as `OPEN`/recurrence,
  and it landed three times in this one session: a pattern copied into a command that also runs the
  search is self-matching, bracketed or not, whenever the *unbracketed* text of it appears elsewhere in
  the same command line.
- Resolution: bracket every pattern (`[r]un-two-ui.sh`, `[h]ush-daemon --dir …`), never leave a bare
  pattern anywhere in the command being run, and prefer PIDs captured at launch over patterns.
- Lesson: the logged fix has not stuck, and the failure mode is silence rather than an error — which
  makes it expensive, because it looks like a result. One of the three occurrences caused a test to be
  reported as run when it had not run at all; it was caught only because the expected output was
  missing.

## 2026-10-15 — UI pass: the reach badge, the conclave picker, and the E2E marks

### The contact list inside a dialog was clipped by the dialog's own scroll box [FIXED]

- Reported: "in new conclave .. the popup to create a new conclave is kind of poorly designed .. the
  trustee menu opens the menu upwards .. should be maybe downwards?"
- Attempted: measure before changing. The list was an absolute overlay opened *above* the field
  (`dropUp`), and that had a stated reason: dropping downwards would cover the action buttons.
- Symptom (live bounding boxes from `.modal` and `.contact-picker-popup`): the field sat 253px below
  the dialog's top edge while the list could be 260px tall, and `.modal` is `overflow: auto`. So the
  one direction that avoided the buttons was the direction the dialog clipped — with a full list the
  top option was cut off at the dialog's edge and the dialog itself became scrollable. `dropUp` had
  traded a covered button for a clipped list without the measurement to know it.
- Resolution: an `expand` option replaces `dropUp`. Inside a dialog the list is `position: static`, so
  it takes layout space and the dialog grows to fit it. Verified in the live app by cloning options to
  the worst case: with 13 options the list caps at 260px and scrolls internally, the dialog grows
  388 -> 652px, `modalScrolls` is false, `clippedTop`/`clippedBottom` are false, and the action row
  moves to 687..727px — on screen and not covered.
- Lesson: an overlay inside a scrolling container is a bug waiting for enough rows to fill it. "Which
  direction should it open" was the wrong question; "what is allowed to grow" was the right one.

### The E2E mark on a member zine is the one claim worth re-reading [FIXED]

- Attempted: show "End-to-end encrypted" on every surface whose content the relay cannot read, as
  asked, and keep the claim honest per surface rather than pasting it everywhere.
- Symptom: none broke, but a zine is the one surface where "end to end" is not a pair. The body is
  encrypted to a per-post read key and the key is handed over inside a 1:1 session, so the relay holds
  only ciphertext — but any holder may re-share that key and the post is readable by every member, so
  the mark can read as "private to you and the author" when what it means is "not readable by the
  relay".
- Resolution: raised it as a product call rather than settling it alone; the user kept the wording, on
  the grounds that the relay genuinely cannot read the body. The mark is on the member-zine branch
  only — the ATProto document branch is a **public** post and stays unmarked, which is the exact
  confusion `renderAtprotoDocument` exists to prevent. The tooltip ("The relay only ever holds
  ciphertext it cannot read.") is the precise half of the claim, so the precise reading is one hover
  away.
- Lesson: one shared component makes the wording consistent, which is exactly why a surface where the
  claim means something slightly different has to be argued for explicitly instead of inherited — and
  why the argument belongs to the person who owns the promise, not to the code that renders it.

### Verifying a dialog header needed real state, and left a trace on the peer [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: confirm the new mark renders in the conclave header, not only in the mail one, rather
  than assuming it from the shared component.
- Symptom: the preview vault had no conclave, and `POST /api/conclaves` refuses an empty trustee list
  ("a conclave needs a name and at least one trustee"), so the header could not be rendered without
  inviting a real contact. The invite is store-and-forward, so it lands on the peer's queue.
- Resolution: created the conclave with the peer invited, read the header ("1 trustee · 1 invited ·
  End-to-end encrypted"), then ended it (which sends `ConclaveEnd`) and deleted the local record. The
  peer may still show a pending invite until it polls; the end payload follows it. Mail was verified
  the same way with one real message.
- Lesson: a header cannot be verified from an empty vault. When a surface needs two parties to render,
  either budget for a peer-visible side effect or say plainly that it was not verified.

### A wait loop that matched its own command line [FIXED — tooling, not the repo]

- Attempted: wait for a background `cargo build --release` to finish.
- Symptom: `while pgrep -f "cargo build --release" >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done` never exited, because
  the waiter shell's own argv contains the pattern, so `pgrep` found the waiter itself. The build had
  finished 2m43s in ("Finished `release` profile" in the log) while the loop kept reporting "still
  building" — several rounds of polling, and a second waiter doing the same. The same trap then bit
  `pkill -f 'while pgrep -f "cargo build'`, which killed its own shell before printing anything.
- Resolution: `[c]argo build --release`, or check the log and the binary's mtime, instead of the bare
  pattern.
- Lesson: `pgrep -f` matches the searcher. Anchor the pattern with a character class whenever the
  pattern text appears in the command that runs it.

## 2026-10-15 — Opening the desktop window on a vault another daemon holds

### `run-one-ui.sh` only stopped a stale daemon when its own socket answered [FIXED]

- Attempted: open the real desktop window on `instances/reach-a` with
  `VAULT_DIR=instances/reach-a ./scripts/run-one-ui.sh`, passing a separate
  `HUSH_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/1000/hush-reach-one` so the run would not disturb the `instances/peer-a`
  daemon already sitting on the script's default socket (`/run/user/1000/hush-one/hush.sock`).
- Symptom: the run built the dist and all three binaries — 2m45s of release build — and then died with
  `Error: "another hush-daemon is already running on /home/sam/ProjectHush/instances/reach-a
  (Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)); stop it before starting a new one"`. The script's
  stale-daemon cleanup is gated behind `if daemon_ready "$SOCK"`, and with a fresh runtime dir nothing
  answered on its socket, so the `pkill` never ran — while the daemon left over from the earlier
  browser preview still held the vault lock on `/run/user/1000/hush-reach/a.sock`. The guard could not
  see the conflict it exists to prevent, and the cost was the whole build.
- Resolution: the cleanup now matches on the vault directory rather than on the socket — `pgrep`/`pkill`
  on `hush-daemon.*--dir (<abs>|<rel>)` — and waits for that process to exit instead of waiting for the
  socket to stop answering. `bash -n` is clean, and `pgrep -af` against the three live daemons matched
  exactly the one for the requested vault and nothing else. Re-run then started the window cleanly.
- Lesson: a guard keyed to your own endpoint misses a conflict keyed to a shared resource. The vault
  lock is per directory, so the check has to be per directory — and the failure surfaced only after the
  expensive part of the run, which is the worst place for a cheap check to be missing.

### The desktop binary's embedded UI copy cannot be verified by grepping it [OPEN]

- Attempted: confirm that the freshly built `target/debug/hush-tauri` carries the new "Restrict to mail
  only" label. The script bakes `ui/dist` into the binary at compile time, so a binary that was not
  rebuilt would silently serve the old interface while the dist on disk looked correct.
- Symptom: `grep -c "Restrict to mail only" target/debug/hush-tauri` → `0`, which reads as a stale
  binary — but `grep -c "Change nickname"` → `0` as well, and that string has been in the UI all along.
  The embedded assets are compressed, so a byte grep cannot distinguish "not embedded" from "embedded
  and compressed". The check proves nothing in either direction, and without the control string I would
  have reported a false negative.
- Needed to resolve: not closed. The indirect evidence is that the dist was written at 16:46:12 and the
  binary linked at 16:46:25, and the window came up with a live `WebKitWebProcess` under the Tauri pid —
  but neither confirms the *content*. Driving the desktop window, or adding a way to read the embedded
  asset list, is what would close it.
- Lesson: before trusting a "the string is not in the file" result on a binary, run the negative control
  — search for a string that must be present. If that also comes back empty, the method is broken, not
  the artefact.

## 2026-10-15 — Reach toggle copy in the trust row menu

### The narrowing row of the reach toggle read as a state, not a command [FIXED]

- Attempted: ship the reach toggle as a single trust-row menu item whose label names the destination
  state — "Allow chat and conclaves" to widen, "Mail only" to narrow.
- Symptom: the user flagged it: "the allow chat looks fine .. but the mail only dont". Three things
  were wrong with the narrowing row, and they compounded. (1) "Mail only" was the *badge's* exact
  wording, three words above it in the same row, so the same phrase meant two things 30px apart and
  the menu entry read as a status report rather than a click target. (2) Its icon was `mail` — the same
  icon as the Email entry directly above it — so the toggle merged visually into Email. (3) The two
  labels did not name the same object: one named what turns *on*, the other named what is left over,
  which is why the widening label felt right and its counterpart did not.
- Resolution: the narrowing row is now "Restrict to mail only" with the `lock` icon (`trustRow` in
  `apps/hush-tauri/src/app.ts`); both directions are imperatives naming what the click does. The badge
  and the Add Trust radio keep "Mail only" — those are states, and a state label should read like one.
  Verified in the dev run against the live `reach-a` pair, whose `my_reach`/`reach` split
  (`my: full`, `reach: mail_only`) is exactly the case the changed branch renders: the menu read
  Email / Restrict to mail only / Change nickname / Delete with the lock glyph, and the round trip
  through "Allow chat and conclaves" returned the daemon to `my_reach: full`. State left as found.
- Lesson: a menu row is a command, so its label has to be an imperative. Reusing a state's wording for
  the action that produces that state makes one phrase mean two things in a single row, and sharing an
  icon with a neighbouring row merges two unrelated controls. Neither shows up in a type-checker or a
  unit test — the user's eye was the test.

### `browser_fill` wrote the literal string `undefined` into the passphrase field [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: fill alice's vault passphrase into the unlock field with `browser_fill`.
- Symptom: the call failed with `Error: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'substring')`,
  and a read-back of the field showed `undefinedpw-a` — the failing call had already written the
  string `undefined` before it threw. The `browser_type` that followed appended to that text rather
  than replacing it, so the unlock attempt failed with "That passphrase didn't work. Try again." A
  tooling artefact that presented as a wrong passphrase, which is a plausible-looking app failure.
  Tooling-related, not a repo problem.
- Workaround: set the field through `browser_cdp` `Runtime.evaluate` using the native value setter plus
  a dispatched `input` event, so the app's listener sees the change. `browser_type` does not replace a
  selection either — typing over a `select()`ed field appended instead.
- Lesson: a tool that fails can still have side effects. After any tool error that touched a form
  field, read the field back before concluding anything about the app — otherwise the tool's debris
  looks like an application defect.

## 2026-10-15 — Mail-only trusts leave the Chats rail

### `browser_press_key` silently ignores a `modifiers` argument [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: press Ctrl+K to open the command palette and read its contact entry, to verify the
  label change for a mail-only trust.
- Symptom: the call answered `Successfully pressed key: k (code: KeyK)` and the palette never opened.
  `browser_press_key`'s schema declares only `key` and `viewId` — there is no `modifiers` parameter —
  so the `modifiers: ["Control"]` I passed was dropped without an error, and the app's handler
  (`(e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey) && e.key === "k"`) never matched. Tooling-related, not a repo problem.
- Workaround: dispatched the event through `browser_cdp` `Runtime.evaluate`
  (`document.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent('keydown', {key:'k', ctrlKey:true, bubbles:true}))`),
  which the app's document-level listener accepts, and read the rendered palette items in the same
  call.
- Lesson: a tool that accepts an argument it does not declare fails silently and looks like a UI bug.
  Read the tool schema before trusting a "success" that changed nothing.

### Stale element refs after a render the click itself caused [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: after toggling a trust's reach, click the Chats rail button using the ref from the last
  snapshot.
- Symptom: `Error: Element not found: e1. Take a snapshot to get updated refs.` twice, once per reach
  toggle. The reach change re-renders the whole shell, so every ref taken before the toggle is dead
  even though the new snapshot reuses the same ref names.
- Workaround: re-snapshot immediately before clicking anything that follows a state change.
- Lesson: refs are bound to the snapshot that produced them, and this app re-renders on nearly every
  action. Budget one snapshot after each mutating click rather than reusing refs across it.

## 2026-10-15 — Contact readiness in the Chats list (found testing Task 24 by hand)

### `inbound_ready` was only set by a message, so a mutual add read as pending [FIXED]

- Reported: in the Chats list a contact that had been added in both directions still carried
  "Waiting for them to add you" underneath its name.
- Attempted: trace what drives that subtitle.
- Symptom: `apps/hush-tauri/src/app.ts` renders
  `c.inbound_ready ? "Ready to chat" : "Waiting for them to add you"`, and `inbound_ready` was set in
  exactly one place — the fall-through in `Account::recv` that files a `ReceivedMessage`
  (`crates/hush-core/src/account.rs`). `MessagePayload::QueueGrant` is matched earlier in the same
  loop and `continue`s before that line, and a grant is the *only* thing `add_contact` sends to the
  peer. So the one payload that always accompanies "they added my invite" was the one payload that
  did not count, and the flag stayed false until someone happened to send chat or mail. Seen on the
  live pair too: `inbound_ready: false` on both sides while both had added the other, both vaults
  online, and both relay inboxes drained empty.
- Resolution: a grant that verifies against the identity key the peer pinned in their invite is proof
  they added us, so `apply_queue_grant` now sets `inbound_ready` at the point the signature checks
  out, and reports "changed" when that flip still needs persisting. The field's doc comment already
  said "they added our invite"; the implementation had approximated it with "we received a message".
- Evidence: `a_verified_queue_grant_marks_the_contact_inbound_ready`
  (`crates/hush-core/tests/two_party_relay.rs`) failed before the change and passes after;
  `a_mutual_add_reads_ready_without_any_message` (`contacts_api_tests` in `crates/hush-daemon`) pins
  the same thing over `/api/contacts`, the DTO the UI actually reads.
- Lesson: the field's name and doc described the peer's action while its implementation described a
  different event that usually coincided with it. Because the only consumer is a UI label, nothing in
  the repo asserted the transition at all — the flag could be permanently wrong and every test passed.

### The `add_contact` comment promised a re-grant that does not exist [FIXED]

- Attempted: find the "next drain re-grants if the relay was down" path the comment on `add_contact`
  referred to, to work out whether a grant missed at add time ever recovers.
- Symptom: `grant_queues_to` has exactly one caller (`add_contact`), and `deliver_to` is a single
  `relay.put` with no outbox — a failed grant is logged and dropped, nothing re-sends it. The comment
  sent me looking for retry logic that was never there.
- Resolution: rewrote the comment to describe the code (one-shot and best effort; the peer keeps
  delivering to our inbox until it drains a message from us). No behaviour change.
- Lesson: an aspirational comment reads exactly like a description of the code. Cost: one wasted
  search of `hush-daemon` for a re-grant loop.

### `inbound_ready` was stored, so a vault whose grant predated the fix stayed wrong forever [FIXED]

- Reported: asked whether restricting a trust's reach to mail-only is what makes a contact read
  "Waiting for them to add you". Traced it: it is not. `MessagePayload::Reach` is a control payload,
  matched and `continue`d in `Account::recv` well before the fall-through that set
  `c.inbound_ready = true`, so the toggle could not move the flag in either direction. The two are
  unrelated code paths.
- Symptom: the flag was `false` on the live `reach-a`/`reach-b` pair while both had added the other, so
  both UIs said "Waiting for them to add you" for an established trust. The earlier fix covered only
  grants drained *after* it landed; these grants were drained by a daemon built before
  `apply_queue_grant` learned to set the flag, so `delivery_queue_id` was stored and `inbound_ready`
  was not. Nothing since could flip it — no chat, no mail, and no new grant, because `grant_queues_to`
  only runs at add time.
- Resolution (user's call: derive in code, not heal on load): the stored boolean is gone. The field is
  now `heard_from` — strictly "a filed chat, file or mail arrived from them", the fallback for a
  dropped grant — and readiness is a method, `Contact::inbound_ready()` =
  `delivery_queue_id.is_some() || heard_from`, with `#[serde(default, alias = "inbound_ready")]` so a
  vault written under the old name reads back. `ContactDto` maps through the method, so the UI reads
  the derivation and no vault is rewritten.
- Evidence: `cargo test -p hush-core` (137) and `cargo test -p hush-daemon` (216) pass. Live, over the
  daemon the UI actually talks to: `reach-a` — the vault this entry was opened for, whose stored flag
  was `false` — now answers `inbound_ready: true`, as does `reach-b`. `strings` on
  `target/release/hush-daemon` finds `heard_from`, so the running daemon is the rebuilt one.
- Lesson: fixing the write path does not repair data the old path already wrote. When a boolean
  duplicates a fact that is already stored elsewhere, the duplicate is what goes stale — and the only
  consumer here is a UI label, so nothing in the repo could notice.

### `cargo test -p hush-wallet` could not compile its own test target [FIXED]

- Attempted: run the wallet crate's tests on their own while checking the workspace after the
  `hush-core` change.
- Symptom: `error[E0432]: unresolved import hush_wallet::ethereum` in `tests/live_ethereum.rs`. The
  module is `#[cfg(feature = "ethereum")]` and the file's own doc comment says it needs
  `--features ethereum`, but the file had no `#![cfg]` gate — so the target was compiled and failed
  instead of being skipped. Pre-existing and unrelated to the change above. It does not show up under
  `cargo test --workspace`, because feature unification turns `ethereum` on for the whole build (the
  daemon enables it), which is why it went unnoticed.
- Resolution: added `#![cfg(feature = "ethereum")]` to the test file. Verified both ways:
  `cargo test -p hush-wallet` now builds and skips it (0 tests, no error), and
  `cargo test --workspace` still compiles the target and registers its six `#[ignore]`d live tests
  (`6 ignored`), so nothing was silently dropped.
- Lesson: a test that is only ever run through `cargo test --workspace` hides its own feature gating.

## 2026-10-15 — Trustee reach, Task 24 (mail-only or full)

### Adding a `MessagePayload` variant broke exhaustive matches in two other crates [FIXED]

- Attempted: add `MessagePayload::Reach { scope }` in `hush-core`, then build the workspace.
- Symptom: `cargo check -p hush-daemon` failed with
  `error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: MessagePayload::Reach { .. } not covered` at
  `crates/hush-daemon/src/main.rs:2187` (`to_dto`), and the later `--workspace` check found the same
  at `crates/hush-cli/src/main.rs:204` (the `recv` printer). Both are long `match msg.payload` blocks
  with an explicit arm per variant and no wildcard, so every new tag is a compile break in every
  consumer — by design, but it cost two build cycles because the consumers were not found up front.
- Resolution: added a `Reach { .. } => None` / `=> {}` ignore arm next to `ZineGrant` in both, with
  the same "control payload handled inside `recv`" comment. `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`
  is now clean.
- Lesson: before adding a payload variant, grep for the existing variants' names
  (`MessagePayload::ZineGrant`) rather than for the enum — that finds every exhaustive match, including
  the ones in `hush-cli` and the daemon's `to_dto`, which are not near the payload definition.

### An over-broad `old_string` consumed a doc-comment blank line [FIXED]

- Attempted: insert the `Reach` variant after `QueueGrant` in `payload.rs` with a `StrReplace` whose
  `old_string` ended at the `QueueGrant` closing brace.
- Symptom: the replacement text I supplied omitted the bare `///` separator line that had followed
  "A grant of the sender's per-contact receive queue.", so the doc comment merged its summary into the
  next paragraph ("...receive queue. Delivered into the recipient's inbox..."). Nothing failed to
  compile; it was a silent doc regression.
- Resolution: caught it on the immediate re-read of the region and restored the blank doc line in the
  next edit, which is also where the `Reach` variant went.
- Lesson: when editing next to a doc comment, anchor on the whole comment block or on a line that is
  not a bare `///`, and re-read the region after any edit whose `old_string` ended on a brace.

### Extracting the daemon test harness duplicated `holds` [FIXED]

- Attempted: move the shared two-vault harness (`relay_on_a_port`, `Member`, `connect`, `pair`) out of
  `zines_bulletin_tests` into a new `api_test_harness` module so the reach API tests could reuse it
  instead of copying ~70 lines.
- Symptom: the replacement text I wrote for the zines module included the `holds` helper, but `holds`
  already sat immediately after the block I was replacing — so the file briefly held two identical
  `fn holds` definitions (E0428).
- Resolution: deleted the duplicate before building.
- Lesson: when moving a block, write the replacement as the *remainder* of the region, not as the
  remainder plus the next helper; check the text on both sides of the `old_string` boundary.

### Grandfathered conclave membership had no test [FIXED]

- Attempted: decide what narrowing a relationship does to a conclave the trustee is already in.
- Symptom: the decision taken is "grandfather it" — `send_conclave_message` fans out to the joined set
  regardless of reach, and only *new* joins are refused, because silently dropping a member from a
  fan-out would be worse than the inconsistency. That decision was written into `docs/PROTOCOL.md` and

- Lesson: a deliberate behaviour with a documented rationale is still an unverified claim until a test
