    `reach: mail_only, my_reach: mail_only`.
  - Trusts view: carol's row carried the badge (`querySelectorAll('.trust-reach-badge')` →
    `["Mail only"]`).
  - Row menu: carol (mail only) → Email / Allow chat and conclaves / Change nickname / Delete, with
    **no** Chat entry; bob (full) → Chat / Email / Mail only / Change nickname / Delete.
  - Toggling bob from that menu recorded `{"nickname":"bob","reach":"mail_only"}`, showed the toast
    "bob is now mail only.", badged both rows, and the daemon agreed (`reach=mail_only`). Toggling
    back with "Allow chat and conclaves" returned the daemon to `reach=full` and the Chat entry.
  - Chats view with a mail-only trust: the composer is gone, replaced by "carol is mail only — chat
    and conclaves are off for this trust. Use Mail, or change this in their menu in Trusts."
  - Conclaves: the create picker offered bob (full) and not carol — typing "carol" gave "No contacts
    match that name." After creating a conclave with bob, the invite picker behaved the same way.
- Severity: was an honest gap, not a known defect. The core and daemon layers were already covered
  end-to-end (10 tests), so a failure here would have been presentation, not policy.
- Still not covered: only Alice's side was driven. The peer's UI was never unlocked, so nothing here
  exercises what bob's client renders when it receives the `Reach` control payload — only that the
  sending daemon and the core agree.
- Lesson: the type-checker plus unit tests do not cover a UI slice that has no DOM harness; for
  presentation work the dev run is the test. Patching `fetch` in the page is a cheap way to assert
  what the UI actually sends, which no amount of source reading proves.

### A truncated invitation paste surfaced as `signal session error` [WORKED AROUND, product half OPEN]

- Attempted: drive the Add Trust modal from the browser by typing carol's invite — a 9,199-character
  base64 bundle — into "Their invitation code", then click "Add contact".
- Symptom: the modal showed `signal session error` and no contact was added. The textarea held
  **9,198** characters: the paste was one short. The bug was the retyping, not the app.
- Resolution (worked around): copied the invite to `apps/hush-tauri/invite-c.txt`, fetched it from
  the page itself (`/invite-c.txt`, same origin as the Vite dev server), assigned it to the textarea,
  dispatched `input`, and deleted the file afterwards. The re-run added carol and the recorded body
  was `{"nickname":"carol","invite":"…","reach":"mail_only"}`.
- Still open, and this is a product observation rather than a tooling one: a code that is one
  character short is reported as `signal session error`, which says nothing about the paste being
  incomplete. Nothing validates the invite envelope before it reaches Signal, so an operator whose
  clipboard lost a character gets a crypto error. A pre-check (base64 decode, then the `v` / `relay` /
  `protocol_name` fields) with "that invitation code looks incomplete" would turn a dead end into a
  fixable message.
- Lesson: never retype a long opaque string across a tool boundary. Put it somewhere the browser can
  fetch it and compare the length before submitting — a 1-in-9,199 difference is invisible, and the
  error it produces points at the wrong layer entirely.

### The New conclave picker said "No contacts yet" when every trust was mail only [FIXED]

- Attempted: with two contacts, both narrowed to mail-only, open Conclaves → New conclave.
- Symptom: the member picker showed "No contacts yet. Add someone in Trusts first." — false, and it
  sends the user to do something they have already done. The list *is* filtered to
  `c.reach === "full"` (`apps/hush-tauri/src/app.ts:4712`); the empty message was just written for the
  unfiltered case. The sibling invite picker in the same file already had honest wording
  ("Everyone you know is already here, or is mail only."), so two dialogs doing the same job
  disagreed.
- Resolution: made the message depend on whether the account has any contacts at all —
  `this.contacts.length ? "Everyone you know is mail only. Chat and conclaves need a full trust." :
  "No contacts yet. Add someone in Trusts first."`. Re-ran the flow: with both trusts mail-only the
  dialog reads the new line; with bob restored to Full the picker offers bob again.
- Lesson: an empty state belongs to the *filtered* list, not the collection behind it. When a picker
  filters its items, re-read the empty copy against the filter, and keep it consistent with the
  wording of sibling pickers doing the same job.

## 2026-10-15 — The app work was sitting on the marketing-site branch [FIXED]

### "Merge it to master" would have dragged the marketing site onto the app trunk [FIXED]

- Attempted: commit the working tree and, per "if not on master merge it to master", merge the
  current branch into `master`.
- Symptom: the branch was **`website`**, which is not a feature branch for this work — it is
  `master` plus **8 marketing-site commits** (`Website: full feature grid…`, `…placeholder marketing
  site, separate from the app`). `master` is the **app** trunk (its tip is Conclave work), and it is
  a direct ancestor of `website`, so the merge would have been a clean fast-forward that carried all
  8 marketing commits onto master alongside the app changes. Nothing was *broken* — the two sets
  touch disjoint paths and would not have conflicted — but the history would have been wrong in a
  way that is annoying to unpick later, and `website/` would have become part of the app repo's
  trunk permanently. Worth noting the working tree was also carrying ~9,100 lines of deletions
  staged from an earlier session, so "commit changes" was never going to be a small commit.
- Resolution: stopped before touching trunk and asked, which is what the standing rule requires.
  The answer was to give the marketing site its own repository, which is also what its own README
  had said all along ("Deliberately separate from `apps/hush-tauri`… this repo directory is only its
  storefront") — the separation was intended, just never carried out in git.
  - `git subtree split -P website -b website-standalone` → the 8 website commits with the paths
    rewritten to the repo root, full history intact.
  - `git clone --no-hardlinks` that branch to `/home/sam/hush-website`, remote removed, branch
    renamed `master` → an independent repo.
  - Verified before deleting anything: the 4 unchanged files are **byte-identical** (`cmp`) and only
    `README.md` differs, by the intentional edit.
  - On the app repo, `git cherry-pick 459f0dd` onto `master` and deleted `website` /
    `website-standalone`. Checked with `git diff --name-only 459f0dd master` that the **only**
    difference is the 5 `website/` paths — the app work is intact.
- Lesson: `git log --oneline -1` and `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` cost nothing and should be
  the first thing run for *any* commit or merge request. The branch name (`website`) was the whole
  answer, and it was visible before a single file was staged. The deeper point is that a directory
  in the wrong repo is a **history** problem, not a file-layout one: `website/` looked fine as a
  subdirectory, and only the branch topology showed it had been quietly coupling two projects'
  commit histories.

## 2026-10-15 — Posts that opened as a title with nothing under them### The reported symptom had three causes, and the loudest one was not a bug in the parser [FIXED]

- Attempted: "im opening some posts and it shows no content just the title" reads like a parsing
  fault, so the first move was to go looking in `reads::rich_text_to_text` / `standard::body_text`
  for a block type the walker did not know.
- Symptom: measuring first said otherwise. Of **105** cached documents, **50** opened with an empty
  body. Of those 50:
  - **48** had `textContent=false content=false path=yes` — **no body in the record at all**. Keys
    were `$type, description, path, publishedAt, site, tags, title, updatedAt`. These are *pointer*
    documents: the words are on the author's own site.
  - **2** had `content=true` — a real parse gap, `{"$type": "co.idno.html", "html": "…"}`, where the
    words sit in an `html` field and only `plaintext` was collected.

  So the parser was responsible for **2** of 50. The other 48 were a **missing feature**: the record
  is a pointer, Hush stored the `path`, and nothing ever joined it to the publication's `url`. A
  third gap sat behind both: `description` was **written on publish and never read back**, so even
  the author's own summary was thrown away at ingest.
- Resolution: three changes, each measured against the live cache.
  - `description` is read at ingest and is the index row's `preview` fallback.
  - `fetch_follow` reads the account's `site.standard.publication` records in the same pass and
    resolves `url` + `path` into `Document.url`; the reader offers it instead of a blank page.
  - `hush_atproto::html` reduces `html` blocks, moved down from the daemon rather than copied.
  - Re-measured live: `with url: 104`, `with description: 102`, empty-bodied documents **48** (which
    is now *correct* — those records have no body), front-page rows with an empty preview **50 → 0**.
- Lesson: the symptom named the wrong layer. "No content" suggested the extractor; the numbers said
  **96% of it was a document shape nobody had modelled**, and only the remaining 4% was the extractor.
  Classifying the failures before opening the parser would have found the dominant cause first. The
  tell was in the data the whole time: those records had `path` and `description` and no
  `textContent`/`content` at all, which is not a parse failure, it is a different kind of record.

### `pkill -f` matched the shell that was running it, and the pattern was too broad [FIXED]

- Attempted: restart the dev daemon with
  `pkill -f "hush-daemon --dir instances/peer-a"` to stop the old process before starting a new one.
- Symptom: **no output at all** from the command, exit 0. `pkill -f` matches the *full command line*
  of every process, and the shell executing that very command contains the pattern in its own
  argument list — so it killed itself before it could print anything, and the build and restart never
  ran. A second attempt with a broader pattern (`pkill -f "[h]ush-daemon"`) worked, but **also killed
  three unrelated `hush-daemon` processes** (`/tmp/iv-a3`, `/tmp/iv-c3`, `/tmp/iv-d3`, all on
  release builds). Those looked like leftover test fixtures, but they were running before this
  session started and were not mine to stop.
- Resolution: use a bracket pattern (`"[h]ush-daemon"`) so the pattern cannot match the matching
  command itself, and scope the pattern to the exact vault (`--dir instances/peer-a`) so a restart
  cannot reach a process it was not aimed at.
- Lesson: `pkill -f` is a foot-gun in two directions at once — it can kill the caller, and it can
  reach processes outside the intended target. This was tooling damage, not a repo problem: no code
  in this workspace was wrong. The three killed daemons were collateral and were not restarted.

### A backgrounded build-and-run chain raced its own build, and the stale binary lied [FIXED]

- Attempted: start the dev daemon on the new code with
  `cargo build -p hush-daemon … && setsid nohup ./target/debug/hush-daemon … &` — the `&` binds to the
  **whole** `&&` chain, so the build went to the background too and `sleep 8` ran in the foreground
  alongside it.
- Symptom: the daemon answered, the refresh returned `200`, and the result was **wrong in a way that
  looked like a code bug**: `changed: 0`, and `x.get('url')` returned `None` for every document. The
  conclusion nearly drawn was that `absorb` refuses to update existing documents. It does not —
  `absorb` replaces on `*existing != document`. The real cause was that the **old binary** had won the
  race and was still serving; it had never heard of the `url` field, which is why the key was *absent*
  rather than empty. `changed: 0` was the old code correctly reporting that nothing had changed.
- Resolution: run the build to completion in the foreground, *then* start the process as a separate
  step. Confirmed by a positive signal rather than by absence of an error: the new binary answered
  `{"error":"locked"}` (a freshly started vault) and, after `POST /api/unlock`, returned
  `changed: 104` and `with url: 104`.
- Lesson: the distinguishing evidence was **absent key vs empty value** — a `#[serde(default)]` field
  is always serialised, so `"url"` missing entirely meant the serialiser predated the field, not that
  the value was empty. Checking which binary was actually running would have cost one `pgrep` and
  saved a wrong hypothesis about `absorb`. Chaining a build and a run behind one `&` is never safe.

### `<img src="x">` without a closing slash swallowed the rest of the paragraph [FIXED]

- Attempted: write a test for the newly-moved HTML reducer asserting that an image contributes
  nothing: `to_text(r#"<p>before <img src="x.png" alt="ignored"> after</p>"#)` should be
  `"before  after"`.
- Symptom: the assertion failed with `left: "before"`, `right: "before  after"` — the words ` after`
  were **gone**. `parse_tag` treats `img` as an ordinary opening tag, so the tree builder pushed a
  frame for it and every following word was collected *inside* an `img` node that renders nothing.
  The tag only avoided this when written self-closing (`<img … />`), which is what the zines
  sanitizer emits — so the zines lane never hit it, and pointing the same reducer at
  stranger-authored record HTML is what exposed it.
- Resolution: added `is_void` (the standard void-element list: `area, base, br, col, embed, hr, img,
  input, link, meta, param, source, track, wbr`) and the tree builder now closes those immediately
  instead of opening a frame. The test passes as first written. This is a **fix to the zines lane as
  well**, since both callers share the one implementation.
- Lesson: this was the good case — a test written from an assumption failed immediately and named the
  bug, rather than passing without exercising the path. It also shows why the reducer belongs in one
  place: the bug had been latent in the daemon for as long as it existed, and only surfaced when a
  second caller with different input reached the same code.

## 2026-10-15 — Explore (publication discovery)

### The frontend test file was written for `vitest`; the project uses `node --test` [FIXED]

- Attempted: add `apps/hush-tauri/src/lib/explorePage.test.ts` for the new follow-list rules, and
  copied the `import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest"` shape from habit.
- Symptom: two failures at once, which is what made it worth logging.
  `npx tsc --noEmit` reported `src/lib/explorePage.test.ts(1,38): error TS2307: Cannot find module
  'vitest' or its corresponding type declarations.` And `npx vitest run` reported
  `Test Files 5 failed | 1 passed (6)` — my new file passed, and **four existing test files failed
  with `Error: No test suite found in file ...`**, because vitest was collecting `*.test.ts` files
  that contain no vitest suites at all. The real runner is `"test": "node --test src/lib/*.test.ts"`,
  and the existing files use `node:test` with `node:assert/strict`.
- Resolution: rewrote the test with `node:test` / `node:assert/strict` and ran the project's own
  command. `npm test` → 71 pass, 0 fail. `npx tsc --noEmit` → clean.
- Lesson: a runner is a project decision, not a default. `vitest` was not a dependency and had no
  config; a two-second read of `package.json` scripts would have prevented writing the file twice.
  The misleading signal was that vitest *did* run and *did* find the file — it just could not find a
  suite in it, and blamed four innocent files rather than the one that was wrong.

### The first Explore dialog showed two publications per screen [FIXED]

- Attempted: lay out the discovery dialog as one block per publication — name, address, description,
  `via <seed>`, and a `Follow` button.
- Symptom: reported as "the explore section/pane is poorly designed ui", and the measurements agreed
  rather than leaving it a matter of taste. In the browser: **2 rows visible** of 66 (a 417px list
  against rows averaging 269px), scroll height **18,967px**, row heights swinging **105px to 386px**
  because descriptions ran 5 to 329 characters with no clamp, **62** of 66 rows carrying a
  `btn-primary` button, and `via leaflet.pub` / `via pckt.blog` printed **66 times** to convey **2**
  distinct values. The three-sentence intro sat above all of it.
- Resolution: a fixed **52px** two-line row (description clipped with `text-overflow: ellipsis`), the
  `Follow` control demoted to a quiet bordered button with no primary styling, the list **grouped by
  seed** under a sticky heading (`via pckt.blog · 39`) so provenance is stated once per group instead
  of once per row, a filter over name/handle/URL/description, and the intro cut to one line with the
  rest behind `title`. Re-measured: **9 rows visible**, scroll **3,503px** (5.4x shorter), row height
  flat at 52px, **0** primary buttons. Filter verified live: `book` → 4 rows, `zzzz` → the empty
  note, cleared → 66.
- Lesson: "it looks bad" was measurable. Two numbers — rows visible and row-height variance — named
  the cause (unclamped prose in a row that had no height contract) and would have caught it before
  the screenshot. A sticky heading also needs the *modal's* surface colour, not the page's: the first
  attempt used `var(--bg)` and rendered a `rgb(18,18,24)` band across a `rgb(27,27,36)` dialog.

### Testing the follow route against the live vault replaced the user's reading list [FIXED]

- Attempted: verify the no-account follow path by POSTing a single follow to
  `POST /api/atproto/follows` on the running dev vault.
- Symptom: the route replaces the **whole** list by design, so
  `{"follows":[{"did":"did:plc:btxr...","name":"Leaflet Lab Notes"}]}` silently dropped the vault's
  other follow. `follows` went from two entries to one, and nothing in the response said a follow had
  been removed.
- Resolution: re-POSTed the original two entries and confirmed them restored
  (`['leaflet.pub', 'pckt.blog']`). No data was lost permanently because the list is two DIDs and
  both were known.
- Lesson: this is the route behaving exactly as documented — "Replace the whole list" — and the
  mistake was testing a destructive whole-list write against real state with a partial payload. A
  replace-shaped route needs the current value read first and echoed back, or a throwaway vault.
  The frontend helper is written to do this correctly (`toggleFollow` takes the current list and
  returns the whole next one), which is the part the unit tests now pin.

### A daemon started with `&` from a one-shot shell did not survive the command [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: restart the dev daemon with the new binary —
  `env ... ./target/release/hush-daemon --dir instances/peer-a --socket "$SOCK" > log 2>&1 &` — then
  poll `/api/status` in the same command.
- Symptom: the log file contained the daemon's own startup lines
  (`hush-daemon vault=... socket=...`), so it had clearly started, but `pgrep` found no process, the
  socket did not exist, and `curl` got nothing. The parent shell exiting reaped the child.
- Resolution: `setsid env ... daemon ... > log 2>&1 < /dev/null &` — the daemon then stayed up
  (confirmed by `pgrep` and a live `/api/status`). Tooling-related, not a repo problem: this is a
  property of the sandboxed one-shot shell, not of `hush-daemon`.
- Lesson: a backgrounded process in a one-shot command needs `setsid` (and `< /dev/null`) or it dies
  with the shell that spawned it. The misleading part is the log file, which makes it look like the
  process started successfully — the same trap applies to `cargo build` in the background, where a
  killed build leaves an **older binary in place** that looks like a successful no-op.

### A doc-comment edit deleted the `///` separator from an unrelated method [FIXED]

- Attempted: insert a new `describe_repo` method above `parse` in `xrpc.rs` using a `StrReplace`
  anchored on the line `/// Turn a response into T...`, while separately having edited the
  `resolve_handle` doc comment.
- Symptom: the `resolve_handle` doc comment lost its blank `///` separator line, merging two
  paragraphs. Caught by reading the region back, not by a test.
- Resolution: restored the separator line, then inserted `describe_repo` against a unique anchor.
- Lesson: `StrReplace` on a short, generic line (`/// ...`) is how a one-line insertion becomes a
  one-line deletion somewhere else. Anchor on the surrounding code, and read the region back after
  editing a file that has several near-identical comment blocks.

## 2026-10-15 — Website placeholder build

### Reveal-on-scroll hid whole sections from any visitor without JavaScript [FIXED]

- Attempted: fade-up scroll animations on `website/` (`.reveal` opacity 0 in CSS, IntersectionObserver in `main.js` adds `.is-visible`).
- Symptom: the CSS hid `.reveal` unconditionally, so the class name promised JS would run. A browser with JS disabled (or a crawler with none) gets every feature card, screenshot frame, download card, and FAQ item rendered at `opacity: 0` — the page looks finished in a JS browser and is mostly blank otherwise. Found by reading the selector chain while fixing a related hack (`main.js` initially flashed `body` to `display:none` to force a paint, which is a blank page if JS throws before the restore line).
- Resolution: hidden state gated on `html.js .reveal`; the `js` class is the first thing `main.js` sets. Reduced-motion override matched to `html.js .reveal` for the same specificity. Verified in the browser with JS on; gating verified by reading, not by a no-JS run.
- Lesson: CSS that assumes "the script will run" is a single-file dependency the CSS cannot see. Any state introduced by JS must be introduced by JS in the DOM (a class on `<html>`), not assumed by the stylesheet.

### `git commit` committed 15 pre-staged deletions that were never mine to commit [FIXED]

- Attempted: commit the new `website/` directory on the `website` branch with `git add website/ && git commit -m ...`.
- Symptom: `git show --stat` reported **20 files changed, 1772 insertions(+), 4356 deletions(-)**. The commit included deletions of `crates/hush-articles/*`, `apps/hush-tauri/src/lib/markdown.*`, and two task docs. The first git-status snapshot showed them as if unstaged, but part of the user's in-flight work was already staged in the index before the session started — `git add website/` only added my files; the bare `git commit` committed everything staged.
- Resolution: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` (index preserved), then `git commit -- website/` so the pathspec restricts the commit. Verified after: commit touches exactly 5 website files, the 15 deletions are back to staged-but-uncommitted (`D ` in the first column), and `status --porcelain | wc -l` is 54 again.
- Lesson: `git add <dir>` does not make a commit of `<dir>`. In a dirty worktree, a bare `git commit` publishes whatever the index happens to hold. Use `git commit -- <pathspec>` whenever the commit must be a subset of the index.

### SMIL `<animate>` children of a `<g>` target the group, not the sibling circle beside them [FIXED]

- Attempted: dashed encryption rings around packets in the security simulation, with `<animate attributeName="opacity">` elements written as children of the packet `<g class="pkt">`, one beside each `<circle class="pkt-ring">`.
- Symptom: `.pkt-ring` has `opacity: 0` in CSS, and the animates the code "aimed" at the rings actually targeted the group's opacity (SMIL default target is the animate's parent). Result: three ring animates fought over one group opacity, and the rings themselves never appeared. Caught by reading the restructure, not by a screenshot — the small packet renders made the missing rings look like a style choice.
- Resolution: restructured so each animated circle contains its own `<animate>` child (a child targets its parent element), verified phase-by-phase in the browser: amber handshake dot visible, purple data dot with visible dashed ring visible, label swap visible.
- Lesson: with SMIL, placement *is* targeting. An `<animate>` affects its parent, so writing animations "next to" the element they should drive silently drives something else — in this case a wrapper, which hid the bug behind a plausible-looking render.




## 2026-10-15 — Reading real publications

### The docs recorded public comments as impossible, and the network disagreed [FIXED]

- Attempted: answer whether comments on public documents can be fetched, and whether they can be
  posted.
- Symptom: `docs/tasks/atproto.md` recorded Comments as **"None. Standard.site has no comment
  record"** (decisions row 13), and open question #5 said inventing one "would be wrong". Both are
  true about the *lexicon* and false about the ecosystem.
- What was actually there: there is no comment record, and nobody uses one. A document carries
  `bskyPostRef` pointing at an `app.bsky.feed.post`, and the comments are **replies to that post**.
  Measured live rather than assumed: 14 of 24 sampled documents carried a linked thread holding
  **45 real replies**, one post with 14. Both halves are reachable with the session the member
  already has — `app.bsky.feed.getPostThread` to read, `app.bsky.feed.post` with a reply ref to
  write. No new auth, and no record invented.
- Resolution: the decision table and the open question need rewriting, not the protocol. The
  comment lane is unblocked.
- Lesson: "the schema has no field for it" was read as "the ecosystem cannot do it". Absence in a
  lexicon is not absence in practice, and the only way to tell the two apart is to look at real
  records — which is the same lesson as the empty-body entry below, one layer up.

### The thread link and the publication link were both dropped at ingest [FIXED]

- Attempted: reach a post's comments, and tell one publication from another.
- Symptom: `Document::from_record` kept `title`, body, `tags`, `publishedAt` and `path`, and threw
  away everything else. Two of the discarded fields were load-bearing. `bskyPostRef` is the only
  pointer to a post's comments, and `site` is the only field naming which publication a document
  belongs to. Neither had a test, because nothing read them.
- Consequence, measured: following two accounts (`leaflet.pub`, `pckt.blog`) pulls in **5 distinct
  publications** — leaflet alone writes to 2 and pckt to 3. The lane could not tell them apart, so
  "follow this blog" was really "follow everything this account writes".
- Resolution: both preserved, `BskyPostRef` lenient about a missing `cid` (a shape that occurs
  live) and refusing only a ref with no `uri`. Verified end-to-end after a live refresh, not just
  in unit tests: **35 of 53** documents carry a thread link and **53 of 53** carry a publication
  link across **5** distinct publications. The 35 matches the count from the independent survey
  taken before the change, which is the evidence that nothing was lost in the mapping.

### The frontend type-check printed "TSC CLEAN" while it was failing [FIXED]

- Attempted: confirm `tsc --noEmit` passed after adding two fields to a DTO.
- Symptom: `npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | tail -15 && echo "TSC CLEAN"` printed a real `error TS2345`
  and then printed `TSC CLEAN` directly underneath it. A pipeline's exit status is the *last*
  command's, so `&&` was reading `tail`'s success, not `tsc`'s.
- Resolution: `set -o pipefail`. Re-run, which surfaced the error properly and then passed once the
  test fixture was given the new field.
- Lesson: this is tooling, not a repo problem, and it is the exact failure mode the log exists for —
  a verification step that reports success without exercising the thing it claims to check. Never
  gate a claim on the exit status of a pipeline ending in `tail` or `head`.

### A heredoc fed to `python3 -` silently ate the pipe it was supposed to read [WORKED AROUND]

- Attempted: parse a JSON API response inline, `curl ... | python3 - <<'PY' ... PY`.
- Symptom: `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)`. The heredoc
  becomes stdin, so it replaced the pipe and the script never saw the response body at all. Nothing
  was wrong with the response.
- Resolution: write the response to a file and have the script read the file. Tooling, not a repo
  problem.
- Lesson: `python3 -` takes its *program* from stdin, so it cannot also take its *data* from a
  pipe. Same shape as the entry above: the command looked like it ran and had not.

### The reader showed 40 of 53 real blog posts as a title with nothing under it [FIXED]

- Attempted: sign in to a real AT Protocol account and follow real publications, so a member can
  actually read other people's blog posts.
- Symptom: the lane filled correctly — `leaflet.pub` and `pckt.blog`, 53 documents, `failed: []`,
  every title and date right — but opening them showed **no words**. 40 of the 53 had an empty
  body, and all 38 from `leaflet.pub` did. `preview` was empty too, because it is derived from the
  body. The titles were the only part of the post that survived.
- Cause: `Document::from_record` read only `textContent`. That is the lexicon's own field and pckt
  and offprint write it, but it is **optional**, and Leaflet — the largest publisher in the
  ecosystem — writes a rich `content` tree instead (`pub.leaflet.content` → `pages[].blocks[].block`,
  with the words in a `plaintext` field per block). pckt writes **both**, which is what made the
  shape legible: `blog.pckt.content` → `items[]`.
- Resolution: `body_text` returns `textContent` when the author wrote it, and otherwise walks
  `content` for `plaintext` strings in document order. That single rule covers text, header,
  blockquote, code and list blocks in both shapes. Re-measured against the live network after the
  fix: **40 changed, 0 of 53 empty**, median body 3,070 characters. The walk reproduces
  `textContent` character-for-character (length ratio 1.00 on all 13 records that carry both
  encodings), which is the ground truth that made this safe to land without guessing.
- Note on ordering: `serde_json` here has no `preserve_order`, so object keys iterate alphabetically.
  That is harmless because every sequence that matters — pages, blocks, list items — is an array,
  and an object holds at most one `plaintext`. Said in the function's doc comment so it is not
  rediscovered as a bug.
- Lesson: "the wire format is standardised" is not the same as "everyone writes the same field".
  Both encodings are valid Standard.site, and the optional field is the one Hush happened to pick.
  The stub PDS in the test suite agreed with our code and could never have caught this — only a real
  peer could, which is exactly what the open entry below was warning about.

## 2026-10-14 — Nostr removal and the AT Protocol public lane

### Nostr survived the "removal" as dead code, dead deps, and dangling doc links [FIXED]

- Attempted: remove every Nostr surface (relays, BIP340, `npub`/`naddr`/`nevent`, NIP-23 export,
  NIP-22 comments, `public-identity.enc`, the neighborhoods read lane) and replace it with the
  AT Protocol / Standard.site lane. The code removal itself went cleanly — `crates/hush-articles/`
  deleted, the daemon routes and the frontend pane rebuilt, `cargo test --workspace` and the
  frontend suite green.
- Symptom: a repo-wide grep at the *end* of the slice still found live remnants the build never
  complained about, because none of them are referenced:
  - `apps/hush-tauri/src/lib/markdown.ts` — "a minimal Markdown renderer for NIP-23 bodies" — plus
    its test file, left with a now-unused `import { markdownToHtml }` in `app.ts` (no
    `noUnusedLocals`, so `tsc` passed).
  - `crates/hush-core/Cargo.toml` still declared `k256 = { version = "0.13", features = ["schnorr"] }`
    (BIP340) and `bech32` (npub/nsec). Neither is used anywhere in the workspace.
  - Doc comments in `crates/hush-atproto/src/standard.rs` and `crates/hush-daemon/src/zine_store.rs`
    still said "the retired Nostr export", and `docs/`, `PROTOCOL.md`, `THREAT_MODEL.md` and
    `apps/hush-tauri/API_GAPS.md` linked to `hush-articles.md` / `neighborhoods.md`, both deleted.
- Resolution: removed the import and deleted `markdown.ts` + `markdown.test.ts` (the ATProto body is
  plaintext by design, so the renderer had no consumer); dropped `k256` and `bech32` from
  `hush-core`; rewrote the comments; repointed or rewrote every doc link; added the public-lane
  sections to `PROTOCOL.md`, `THREAT_MODEL.md` and `DISTRO_READINESS.md`. Test count fell 77 → 64
  because the 13 Markdown-renderer tests went with the renderer.
- Lesson: deleting a feature is not the same as removing it. A clean build proves nothing about
  unreferenced files, unused Cargo dependencies, and documentation links — only a whole-repo grep
  for the feature's vocabulary does. Run that grep before declaring the removal done, not after.

### A new method reused the name `zinesPublish` and silently shadowed the draft editor's [FIXED]

- Attempted: add the public-lane publish modal method to the `App` class in
  `apps/hush-tauri/src/app.ts`.

### The byline-truncation test asserted the wrong truncation width [FIXED]

- Attempted: assert a long byline renders shortened.
- Symptom: expected `'a-very-…'`, actual `'a-very-l…'` — the helper truncates to 12 characters
  before appending the ellipsis, and the assertion had been written from memory.

  not from an eyeball.

### `atprotoRefresh` dereferenced a possibly-null daemon response [FIXED]

- Attempted: wire `api.atprotoRefresh()` into the pane.
- Symptom: TypeScript's type allowed the response to be absent, and the handler read fields off it
  without a check — a daemon that answered empty would have thrown a property-access error instead
  of a clear message.
- Resolution: an explicit `if (!out) throw new Error(...)` before the response is read.
- Lesson: an optional return from the daemon API is a real branch; treat it as one at the call site.

## 2026-10-14 — Conclave introductions

### Both sides consuming an invite leaves every message undecryptable; reverse card must not consume [FIXED]

- Attempted: the reverse-invite handshake was wired end to end
  (`accept_intro` sending the acceptor's invite back through the courier),
  both sides accepted their cards, both showed each other as contacts —
  and yet not one message decrypted in either direction. `POST /api/recv`
  on the target returned only "Could not decrypt a queued message —
  unknown sender or session not ready", on both the old mesh (iv-a2/d2)
  and a clean relay wipe.
- Symptom: the 1:1 probes and conclave messages landed on the peer's
  inbox as blobs that never decrypted. A cli-built mesh (a3/c3/d3, one
  invite consumed twice) decrypted fine, which eliminated the one-time
  prekey double-consumption theory: libsignal falls back to the signed
  prekey. The real difference was session direction. In the card flow
  BOTH sides ran `process_contact_bundle` (the seeker on the consent
  card, the target on the reverse card), so each vault held an outbound
  session for the other's address. libsignal refuses an incoming
  `PreKeySignalMessage` when a session already exists for that address,
  so neither side could ever establish the *other's* chain: every first
  message failed, and the ratchet never started.
- Resolution: the reverse card is now marked `reverse: true` in
  `MessagePayload::ConclaveIntro` and threaded through `receive_intro`
  into `PendingIntro.reverse`. `accept_intro` branches on it: forward
  cards consume the bundle (the acceptor is the session initiator,
  identical to a direct contact add); reverse cards go through the new
  `add_contact_from_intro`, which pins identity and queue routing without
  touching the session store and without granting a queue back (the
  acceptor's credentials already travelled with the invite the sender
  consumed). The target's session builds from the seeker's first prekey
  message. Card invites also mint via the new `Account::fresh_invite`
  instead of the shared cached invite. Verified live on the a3/c3/d3
  mesh: a3's conclave message decrypted at d3 with zero warnings, d3's
  reply decrypted at a3 with zero warnings.
- Lesson: in a Signal-style stack the bundle consumer and the first
  message sender must be the same party. Any flow where the *owner* of a
  mailbox also consumes the peer's bundle creates two disjoint session
  pairs, and the failure is silent until the first message.

### Queue rotation on device migration strands every contact holding a pre-rotation grant [OPEN]

- Attempted: after migrating the demo vaults to the introduction-capable
  binary, the second handshake round stalled: the courier relayed the
  request (`POST /api/conclaves/intros/relay` returned 204) but the target's
  `/api/conclaves/intros` stayed empty through repeated `POST /api/recv`
  polls.
- Symptom: the relay's sqlite db shows the relayed blob sitting in a queue
  the target never reads. Root cause: `device.enc` appeared today on both
  demo vaults — the legacy migration rotated the device queue token — and
  every contact still delivers to the pre-rotation queue id or with the
  pre-rotation delivery token from a stale invite/grant. The writer's PUT
  succeeds (the relay binds an unclaimed queue to the first credential), the
  owner reads a different derived queue id, so messages silently vanish.
  The intro request leg that worked earlier today rode a queue claimed
  before the rotation; after the relay db wipe the same delivery re-created
  the queue under the writer's stale credential.
- Resolution needed: the rotation path (legacy migration, restore, or any
  future rotation) must re-send a `QueueGrant` to every contact so stored
  delivery targets converge on the current derivation; alternatively the
  daemon should detect repeated undelivered sends. The bulletin queue
  already dodges this by never publishing its id — per-contact queues have
  no such escape.
- Lesson: rotating a capability invalidates every copy of it ever handed
  out; a rotation without a redistribution step is a partition, not an
  upgrade.

### The intro tests were written but never actually passed, and one hid a real protocol bug [FIXED]

- Attempted: after landing the intro slice, `cargo test -p hush-core
  --lib` was run to verify the state machine before calling the flow done.
- Symptom: 4 of 142 tests failed. Three test-harness causes stacked:
  `intro_vault` was a sync `fn` awaiting `Account::create` (E0728 plus six
  cascading E0277 "Account is not a future"), the test seed never set the
  account's own `protocol_name`, so no test vault matched its roster role,
  and every call hardcoded `"c1"` as the conclave id while
  `create_conclave` mints a UUID — so `chat_log.conclave("c1")` returned
  `None` and the receive paths short-circuited to "not dirty" before any
  assertion could exercise state. The fourth failure was real:
  `receive_intro` opened with `if target != from_account { return }`, which
  is unsatisfiable in the legitimate courier-forwarded case (the sender is
  the courier, never the target) — the add-as-trust path was unreachable
  end-to-end.
- Resolution: `intro_vault` is `async fn`; `seed_mesh_conclave` takes the
  local role, sets `protocol_name`, and returns the real id, which all
  calls now thread through. The authenticity guard was replaced with the
  correct backstop: the decoded invite's `protocol_name` must equal the
  roster target, so a courier cannot swap in their own identity and become
  the channel — verified by a new swap-attack test case. Suite green:
  142 passed, 0 failed.
- Lesson: a test suite that has never compiled and run is not a
  verification, and "should pass" claims must be backed by fresh output.
  Guards that mirror the happy path's origin assumptions should be checked
  against every forwarding topology the protocol allows, not just the
  direct one.

### Release build failed on committed code: AccountState initializer and serde derives [FIXED]

- Attempted: `cargo build --release -p hush-daemon -p hush-cli` after the
  master commit to deploy the intro flow to the running daemons.
- Symptom: `hush-core` failed first — `error[E0063]: missing fields
  `pending_intro_requests` and `pending_intros` in initializer of
  `AccountState`` at the vault-create path (old vaults deserialize with
  defaults, but the create initializer names every field). Then
  `hush-daemon` failed — `error: cannot find derive macro \`Serialize\`` on
  `PendingIntroView` and `IntroLists` in account_worker.rs, which also broke
  `intro_lists`' Handler impl (E0277) since the response type was not
  `IntoResponse`.
- Resolution: added the two fields to both initializers (init plus the test
  fixture), and matched the file's fully-qualified `serde::Serialize`
  convention. Release build green in 2m37s.
- Lesson: "the daemon compiles" must mean the exact commit being shipped,
  not the working tree of an earlier hour; type-deriving errors cascade
  into unrelated Handler trait errors, so the first error in an axum route
  is often not the root cause.

### New UI called new daemon-only endpoints unconditionally, so a successful conclave creation reported failure [FIXED]

- Attempted: the introductions UI slice added `api.introLists()` to
  `reloadConclaves` alongside the existing `pendingInvites()` call.
- Symptom: the user reported "why i cant create conclave". Reproduction in
  the live UI: `POST /api/conclaves` succeeded server-side (two duplicate
  "aasd" conclaves appeared in the list), but `reloadConclaves` ran after
  the POST inside the same try/catch, the daemon's `/api/conclaves/intros`
  route does not exist on the still-running pre-intro release binary, and
  `request` turns a 404 into a throw — so `createConclave` caught it and
  announced "Couldn't create the conclave." after the vault had already
  created it. The modal closed, the list never reloaded, and every other
  `reloadConclaves` caller inherited the same poisoned await.
- Resolution: `const intros = await api.introLists().catch(() => null);` —
  an introduction is an addition, not a dependency, so a daemon without the
  routes degrades to "nothing pending" until the freeze lifts and the
  daemon is rebuilt. Verified green with `npx tsc --noEmit`.
- Lesson: when in-flight UI gains calls to endpoints that only a newer
  daemon serves, every such call must degrade at the fetch boundary, and a
  work step that reports failure must never sit in the same try block as
  the step whose success it announces.

### "Can't create conclave" root cause outside the repo: the vaults' relay is a dead Cloudflare quick tunnel [FIXED]

- Attempted: full trace of the create path with a fetch instrument in the
  live page (`window.__reqLog`), then a direct `curl` of the daemon.
- Symptom: `POST /api/conclaves` returns 400 with body
  `relay error: error sending request for url (https://ban-therapeutic-daughter-organic.trycloudflare.com/q/...)`;
  every `/api/presence/heartbeat` 400s the same way, which is what the
  "Hush is disconnected." header reflects. `curl` to the tunnel host: 000.
  Conclave creation queues invites through the relay, so a dead relay
  blocks it.
- Cause: both `instances/peer-a` and `instances/peer-b` vaults store the
  quick-tunnel URL set on 2026-10-10; the manual `trycloudflare` process on
  the VPS died (quick-tunnel hostnames are assigned at process start and
  change on every restart — the failure mode this log already documented).
  The VPS itself is healthy: `hush-relay` is alive on
  `http://137.184.129.205:8790` (401 on `/q/health` = route answers), a
  token-based named tunnel "hush" runs, and the onion address on file
  answers in principle but no local Tor SOCKS exists on the workstation.
- Resolution so far: the durable fix is `hush-cli relay set --url <live
  relay>` for **every** vault that talks to the dead one (the CLI's own
  help: "contacts on the old relay must move too — the mailbox lives on
  the relay"). `set` opens the encrypted vault and needs the passphrase,
  and peer-a's daemon holds the vault lock, so the user is in the loop for
  the passphrase and the choice of target (direct IP HTTP vs the named
  tunnel's hostname from their Cloudflare dashboard). Left OPEN until the
  move is done and creation is verified end-to-end.
- Resolution: FIXED on 2026-10-14. Direct `http://137.184.129.205:8790`
  was refused by the daemon's own guardrail — `insecure relay URL: use
  HTTPS except for localhost` — which is why the tunnel setup existed.
  Stood up a quick tunnel to the relay under systemd
  (`cloudflared-hush-quick.service`, `Restart=always`,
  `--url http://127.0.0.1:8790`) on the VPS; new hostname
  `https://remedy-relief-patricia-main.trycloudflare.com` (verified 401 on
  `/q/health` through the edge). Moved both workstation vaults with
  `hush-cli relay set`, restarted peer-a's daemon, unlocked, heartbeat
  204, and created a conclave through the real UI — modal closed, announce
  fired, entry in the list. Caveats recorded below in the client-config
  entry. Permanent follow-up: add a Public Hostname route to the already
  running named tunnel in the user's Cloudflare dashboard, then one
  `relay set` per vault — quick-tunnel hostnames still change if the
  tunnel process is recreated.
- Lesson: the daemon's 400 "relay error: error sending request" text is
  the one string that separates "UI/logic bug" from "infrastructure down";
  check it before touching code when a whole feature class (anything that
  queues: invites, conclave creation, heartbeats) fails at once.

### `hush-cli relay set` and `client-config.json` are two separate stores that must be moved together [FIXED]

- Attempted: moved both vaults with `hush-cli relay set` and expected the
  plaintext `client-config.json` mirror to follow, the way the log note
  about the two agreeing "by construction" implied.
- Symptom: `relay set` reported "direct base updated", yet
  `client-config.json` still carried the dead trycloudflare URL for both
  peer-a and peer-b. A first `config set --relay-url …` invocation also
  failed silently-ish (clap usage error; the flag is `--relay`).
- Resolution: `hush-cli config set --relay <url>` per vault — the config
  command is the writer for that file, and it prints the caveat itself:
  "an existing vault keeps the relay it was created with" (the vault's
  encrypted state wins at runtime; the config file steers the demo
  scripts' relay-start decision and new-vault creation). Verified both
  files with grep afterwards.
- Lesson: any project with an encrypted source of truth plus a plaintext
  "mirror" needs one command that updates both; until then, the mirror
  will silently drift and the next reader (script or human) will trust the
  stale half.

### The agent suggested swapping invites "in the conclave chat" — there is no channel to carry them [FIXED]

- Attempted: asked how the user could add a conclave stranger as a contact,
  I proposed a cheap fix: "Copy my invite" in the member menu and paste the
  code into the conclave chat for the other side to click.
- Symptom: the user immediately asked "how can they send me the code if i
  cant see their messages". They were right — reading
  `Account::send_conclave_message` (account.rs, the `filter_map(contact_nick_for_protocol)`
  over the joined roster) shows fan-out silently skips trustees who are not
  the sender's contacts, and inbound conclave messages from unknown senders
  are dropped. Between two non-contact members there is no channel in either
  direction; the roster updates they both see travel via the mutual contact's
  session, which is why the stranger still appears in the list.
- Resolution: the whole suggestion was withdrawn. The real fix became the
  introduction flow: a request/invite pair of control payloads relayed
  through a member who holds both edges, with consent on the invite owner's
  side and a pending-record store mirroring `pending_invites`.
- Lesson: before proposing UX that rides a channel, verify the channel
  exists in the transport — roster visibility is not conversational reachability.

### Conclave fan-out drops non-contact trustees silently [FIXED]

- Context: discovered while answering the question above.
  `send_conclave_message` targets only `joined ∧ my contacts`
  (`filter_map`), and inbound conclave messages from non-contact senders are
  consumed and dropped. A conclave whose members are not a full mesh therefore
  half-works with no error anywhere: chips show joined, messages vanish.
- Resolution: accepted as the transport's design (per-pair sessions, no
  relay-side room) and made visible instead of changed — the conclave view
  now renders an unreachable-members warning banner computed from the local
  roster versus contacts, and the introduction flow gives every member a way
  to close their own gaps.
- Lesson: when delivery is pairwise, group state can look healthy while
  delivery is broken; surface the gap locally rather than trusting the roster.

## 2026-10-14 — Note attachments in internal mail

### The Chat history auto-delete fieldset rendered as a crushed flex row [FIXED]

- Attempted: reusing the label-left/control-right `.chat-history-section`
  row layout on the auto-delete `fieldset`, with a `:first-of-type` rule to
  drop the divider on the first section.
- Symptom: the user saw a broken dialog. Geometric audit via CDP confirmed
  two defects: the fieldset inherited `display: flex` as a ROW, so the three
  radio labels sat side by side wrapping into 100px-wide columns (heights
  117px/160px) and the "Save rules" button was crushed to 36px wide; and
  `:first-of-type` matched the fieldset anyway (it is the first of its own
  tag), silently stripping its divider.
- Resolution: `fieldset.chat-history-auto { display: block; min-inline-size: 0 }`
  with one full-width radio row per rule, and the divider moved from
  `:first-of-type`-complement to `.chat-history-section + .chat-history-section`.
- Lesson: a `fieldset` is never a drop-in for a `div` in a flex utility —
  the legend is special-cased out of flex flow and the tag is its own
  first-of-type, so both the layout and the sibling selectors silently
  misfire.

  CDP geometry showed the popup's second row below the container's clip edge;
  clipped content keeps its `getBoundingClientRect` but does not paint or
  hit-test.

### A node --test cannot import a module whose import chain is extensionless [FIXED]

- Attempted: put `noteToFileText`/`noteFileName` in `notesStore.ts` and unit
  test them via `notesShare.test.ts` importing `./notesStore.ts`.
- Symptom: `Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module
  '.../src/lib/api/daemon'` — node ESM resolves imports exactly, and
  `notesStore.ts` imports `"./api/daemon"` without an extension (fine for
  Vite, fatal for the `node --test src/lib/*.test.ts` runner).
- Resolution: the pure helpers moved to a leaf module `notesShare.ts` whose
  only import is `import type` (erased at runtime), re-exported from
  `notesStore.ts` so callers keep one store import. All 84 tests pass.
- Lesson: anything a node test imports must be a leaf with `import type`-only
  or extension-bearing imports — the existing test-covered modules
  (`paperText`, `markdown`, `voicePill`) all follow that shape for a reason.

### Pre-existing type errors in the paper-text slice surfaced by tsc [FIXED]

- Symptom: `npx tsc --noEmit` failed on `paperText.ts(103)` (implicit `any`
  on the Yjs delta `.map` callback) and `paperText.test.ts(46)`
  (`setAttribute("level", level)` — the Yjs typing says `string` while the
  editor writes a number at runtime). These had survived because only
  `npm test` was re-run after the paper-text slice, not tsc.
- Resolution: typed the delta callback (`(d: { insert?: unknown })`), and kept
  the runtime number with a cast in the test helper — a first instinct of
  `String(level)` silently broke `headingLevel`, which requires
  `typeof level === "number"`, and the heading test caught it.
- Lesson: `setAttribute` stores whatever you give it; a type-cast fix must
  preserve the runtime shape the consumer checks, not just satisfy the
  compiler.

## 2026-10-13 — Conclave voice Phase 2 two-peer test

### Conclave chat never auto-scrolled to a new message [FIXED]

- Context: flagged by the user during the two-peer voice test — messages
  arrived but the reader had to scroll down manually.
- Cause: `renderConclaveDetail` set `scroll.scrollTop = scroll.scrollHeight`
  while the pane was still detached, and a detached element has no layout, so
  the assignment silently clamped to zero on every render. The code comment
  on `pendingChatScroll` documents exactly this trap for the chats pane; the
  conclave pane never got the same treatment.
- Resolution: same contract as chats. The previous pane's position is
  captured at the top of `render()` (keyed by conclave via a new
  `renderedConclaveId` mirror), `renderConclaveDetail` decides the intent
  while detached — bottom when the reader was pinned (or opening fresh),
  restore otherwise — and the pending intent is applied after attachment in
  `render()`, next to the chats consume block. Verified live: pinned reader
  rides to the newest message (`scrollTop + clientHeight === scrollHeight`
  after a send), a reader parked in history stays put while a new message
  lands (`scrollHeight` grew, `scrollTop` held).
- Lesson: this is the third instance of the "author layout beats a UA default
  / detached measurement" class (`.trust-row[hidden]`, `.conclave-card[hidden]`
  precede it). Any pane that scrolls must decide intent detached and apply
  attached — copy the chats pattern, not the one-liner.

### Daemon playback was silent whenever the output device's default rate is not 48 kHz [FIXED]

- Attempted: the VM peer joined the voice room; its 440 Hz tone arrived and
  decoded at the host (`decoded_frames`/`played_frames` climbing), but the user
  heard nothing.
- Symptom: `wpctl status` showed the daemon holding only a capture stream —
  no playback stream existed, yet `played_frames` kept climbing. The daemon log
  said `hush-daemon: voice: no 48 kHz output device; playout is counted, not
  audible`.
- Cause: `voice_data.rs` only built the output stream when the device's
  *default* output config was exactly 48 kHz. HDA analog defaults to 44.1 kHz,
  so every run degraded to the counting playout ticker — counters lied while
  the speakers got nothing.
- Resolution: the plane now retries the output stream with 48 kHz requested
  explicitly (`SupportedStreamConfig::new` at the wire rate; the audio server
  resamples — the mix is already 48 kHz), logging the forced rate. Counting
  fallback remains only for devices that fail both opens.
  (`crates/hush-daemon/src/voice_data.rs`, voice tests green.)
- Lesson: `played_frames` was never an audibility signal in Device mode either
  (device callback) or in the fallback (ticker) — only PipeWire's stream table
  (`wpctl status` Streams section) proves a real playback link exists.

### Copy-my-invite served the old relay after the relay moved [FIXED]

- Attempted: added the user's pasted invite to the VM peer; the blob carried
  `"relay":"http://137.184.129.205:8790"` even though the vault had been moved to
  `https://ban-therapeutic-daughter-organic.trycloudflare.com` via `relay set` hours earlier.
- Symptom: `400: invite relay http://137.184.129.205:8790 does not match this vault relay
  https://ban-therapeutic-daughter-organic.trycloudflare.com`. The user's "Copy my invite"
  kept producing the stale blob across UI reopen and daemon restart.
- Cause: `Account::invite` caches the minted invite in `state.invite_cache`, and
  `set_mail_handle`/`set_vault_name` drop that cache on change, but `set_relay_clearnet`
  did not — the relay rides inside the invite payload, so the cache advertised the old
  address forever.
- Resolution: `set_relay_clearnet` now sets `self.state.invite_cache = None`
  (`crates/hush-core/src/account.rs`), with a regression test
  `moving_the_relay_invalidates_the_cached_invite` (asserts a fresh `invite()` differs and
  decodes with the new relay; green via `cargo test -p hush-core --lib`). Vault repaired in
  place with `hush-cli relay set` on the fixed build, then the daemon was restarted so its
  in-memory state could not clobber the cleared cache on its next `save()`.
- Lesson: anything embedded in the invite payload must invalidate `invite_cache`; the cache
  is a snapshot, not a view. Also: the daemon holds account state in memory — after editing
  a vault out-of-band with the CLI, restart the daemon before trusting the result.

Status tags: `FIXED` (resolved in-slice), `WORKED AROUND` (avoided, cause not fixed),
`OPEN` (unresolved, needs a different environment or a later task), `NO LONGER APPLICABLE`
(the configuration it described cannot occur any more).

## 2026-10-13 evening — trying the voice for real (same branch)

### A stray `run-one-ui.sh` daemon held the `peer-a` vault lock and `run-two-ui.sh` failed to start — `FIXED`

Attempted: the user ran `./scripts/run-two-ui.sh` to try the voice and it died at daemon start.

Symptom: `another hush-daemon is already running on /home/sam/ProjectHush/instances/peer-a
(Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11))`. Cause: a daemon from an earlier
`run-one-ui.sh` session (pid 699022, socket `/run/user/1000/hush-one/hush.sock`) was still
alive and held the vault lock. Both demo scripts share `instances/peer-a`/`peer-b`, so each
script's "is my daemon up" socket check can pass while *another* script's daemon holds the
vault.

Resolution: killed the stray; re-run works. Lesson: the vault lock is the only cross-script
mutual exclusion, and the error names it well — when it fires, `pgrep -af hush-daemon` and kill
the holder before re-running. The scripts cannot clean this up for each other safely.

### `run-two-ui.sh` started a local relay that nothing used, next to a remote relay the vaults already point at — `FIXED`

Attempted: the user runs the two-peer demo against the lab VPS relays (hakim: HTTPS quick
tunnel + Tor onion, same box) and does not want a local relay.

Symptom: with no `--relay` argument the script defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:8787` and starts a
local relay — while both peer vaults store
`https://ban-therapeutic-daughter-organic.trycloudflare.com` (set 2026-10-10) and the daemons
use the **vault's** stored relay at runtime, so the local relay carried zero traffic and was
pure confusion.

Resolution: the script now, when no `--relay`/`HUSH_RELAY_URL` was given and both vaults exist,
reads each vault's `client-config.json` `relay_url` (plaintext, no unlock) and adopts it when it
is remote and identical for both vaults — no local relay is started, and the printed URLs match
what the daemons will actually use. Explicit `--relay` still wins. Unverified end-to-end at
write time (see next entry) — verify with `./scripts/run-two-ui.sh --dev` and look for
"Vaults point at …".

### My own verification kept re-killing the daemon's release build and mistook it for a recompile loop — `WORKED AROUND`

Attempted: bounded (`timeout` 45–120 s) `--dev` runs of the script to verify the relay fix.

Symptom: every run showed `Compiling hush-daemon` and got killed before finishing — five runs
in a row looked like cargo refusing to cache. Root causes, all mine: (1) the script builds the
daemon in **release even in `--dev`** (`PROFILE` defaults to release, for vault AEAD speed), and
a release build of the ~1600-crate daemon tree under load average 3 takes longer than my
timeouts; (2) killing a compile mid-flight leaves no fingerprint, so the next run starts the
final crate over; (3) earlier direct `cargo build`s without the script's exported `PROTOC`
flipped fingerprints the other way. Also `… | head -18` SIGPIPE-killed one run silently.

Resolution: run the build to completion once, untimed, then test the script. Lesson: this
script's dev mode is not a debug-mode run; never bound-timeout a script whose first action is a
release build. Tooling-related, not a repo problem.

## 2026-10-13 — Conclave voice Phase 2 (real audio, branch `feature/conclave-voice-phase1`)

### The `pipewire-rs` capture probe cannot run on this machine — `OPEN`

Attempted: the spec (§2 #5) makes `pipewire-rs` the first capture backend, with the probe as
Phase 2's first step. The probe needs `libpipewire-0.3-dev`, which is not installed.

Symptom: `pkg-config --modversion libpipewire-0.3` → "Package libpipewire-0.3 was not found",
and `sudo -n apt-get install libpipewire-0.3-dev` → "sudo: a password is required". No
non-interactive way to install the dev headers here.

Resolution: built capture/playout on the spec's documented fallback — `cpal`/ALSA against the
host's PipeWire via the ALSA emulation, which the spike already probe-proved on this exact
hardware (default device records; the daemon now also plays back and mixes). What remains to
resolve it: a machine with the pipewire dev headers, a `pipewire-rs` input/output stream probe,
and — if it works — swapping the capture source behind the same 48 kHz mono contract and
restoring `PrivateDevices=true` in the shipped unit (socket access instead of `/dev/snd`).
Recorded in `docs/tasks/conclave-voice.md` §2 #5 and Phase 4.

Lesson: a "first choice, probe first" decision still needs a machine that can run the probe;
the honest fallback path (documented in the spec) is what kept the slice unblocked.

### The `VoiceAnswer` roster-join aborted the media handshake — `FIXED`

Attempted: keep Phase 1's inbound pattern — apply every `Voice*` payload's roster effect with
`.ok()?`, then do the media work.

Symptom: the dogfood's audio assertion saw nothing for 20 s; both daemons logged zero voice
lines. The handshake *looked* complete (rosters agreed on two speakers) because the roster side
did land — on Bob's own side, locally, at his join. But Bob's recv of Alice's `VoiceAnswer`
tried `mgr.join(...)` first, which refuses with `AlreadyConclaveTrustee` (he is already on his
own roster), and the `?` returned `None` — so `accept_answer` never ran and the DTLS connection
never got its remote description. The stats line proved it once added: `sent=957 decoded=956
played=954 live=1` on Alice (audio flows!) while the assertion still failed — the script's own
`sed -n 's/.../.../'` without the `p` flag printed nothing (second bug, fixed together).

Resolution: the roster effect of `VoiceAnswer` is evidence, not authority — `AlreadyConclaveTrustee`
proceeds to `accept_answer`; `VoiceOffer` keeps answering on a duplicate join but still refuses
on a real authority failure. Re-run: audio crosses both ways (`decoded=64` / `decoded=11` and
climbing) with mute and both leave paths still ending the room.

Lesson: Phase 1's stub made the answer payload's *entire* job cosmetic, so an early-return on a
benign refusal was invisible. When a stub is replaced by real behavior, every shortcut taken
because "nothing real rides here yet" needs re-reading.

### Dogfood stats assertion read `sed -n` output that was suppressed — `FIXED`

Attempted: extract the `decoded=` counter with `sed -n 's/.*decoded=\([0-9]*\).*/\1/'`.

Symptom: `decoded` was always empty (fell back to 0), so the assertion looped to its timeout
even though the stats line plainly showed `decoded=956`.

Resolution: `sed -n` suppresses the default print; the substitute needs the `p` flag:
`s/.*decoded=\([0-9]*\).*/\1/p`.

Lesson: `-n` + `s///` without `p` is the silent-output combo; test one iteration of the
extraction before wrapping it in a wait loop.

## 2026-10-13 — Conclave voice Phase 1 verification (branch `feature/conclave-voice-phase1`)

### The voice-dogfood script asserted a mute semantics that does not exist — `FIXED`

Attempted: the Phase 1 acceptance script (`scripts/voice-dogfood.sh`) asserted that a joiner's mic
reads `muted: true` on the receiver's roster "until the answer confirms it".

Symptom: the first run failed at exactly that assertion. Alice's roster showed Bob unmuted the
moment his offer landed:

```
FAIL: alice should see bob's mic unconfirmed until his answer: <id-a>:false <id-b>:false
```

The "muted until confirmed by answer" state was invented while writing the script. The code has one
consistent rule: an inbound `VoiceOffer` is applied as a `join` (the receiver's `voice_apply_inbound`
reuses `VoiceManager::join`), and `join` adds the sender unmuted; `VoiceMute` is documented as
advisory only ("silence is the truth and this is the label") and moves only by an explicit payload.
The answer's role is the handshake, not a mic label. The script was fixed to match the code, which
is the correct direction — the code's rule is simpler and matches the payload docs.

Lesson: when scripting acceptance checks, derive the expected DTO values from the implementation's
own semantics, not from a stricter design remembered mid-sentence. If the stricter design is wanted
(a "peer not yet handshake-confirmed" state), it is a Phase 2 decision to make deliberately, with
the UI for it, not a dogfood assertion smuggled in.

### Dogfood assertions matched nicknames against a roster of account ids — `FIXED`

Attempted: match roster strings containing `"bob:true"` / `"alice:false"`.

Symptom: the assertion never matched even though the JSON payload held exactly the right state
(`"muted": true` for Bob), because `joined[].account` carries account ids (hex), never nicknames.
Made this mistake twice in the same script; the first fix (the answer step) did not fix the class
(the mute step), which cost a third run.

Resolution: all roster assertions now compare against ids read from the view itself — the opener's
id from the `opener` field, joiner order from insertion — with the nickname placed only in comments.

Lesson: same class, twice in one file, is a prompt to grep the whole file for the pattern before
re-running, not to patch the one assertion that failed.

### Script bug: `if find …` tests find's exit status, not whether it matched — `FIXED`

Attempted: `if find "$VA" "$VB" -type f -name '*voice*'; then fail …` as a "no voice files on
disk" check.

Symptom: vacuous — `find` exits 0 whether or not it matched anything, so the branch could never
fire and the assertion proved nothing (a passed-without-exercising check, in the log's own
vocabulary).

Resolution: capture the output (`VOICE_FILES=$(find … || true)`) and test `-z` on it.

## 2026-10-13 — Voice engine spike (`crates/voice-spike`, Task 23 §2 #4)

### The facade's answer SDP is incomplete unless both peers register the codec registry — `FIXED`

Attempted: two `webrtc` 0.21 (the facade over `rtc`) peer connections on loopback; the receiver
built with no `with_media_engine`.

Symptom: `set_remote_description` refused the answer with `ErrSessionDescriptionMissingIceUfrag`,
and the dumped answer SDP showed the degenerate shape — `m=audio 0 … 0` (PCMU only, no Opus) and
**no `ice-ufrag`/`ice-pwd` lines at all**, though candidates were present.

Resolution: build the answerer with the same `MediaEngine::default()` + `register_default_codecs()`
as the offerer. The SDP then carries `m=audio … 111` with credentials, and the loopback proof goes
150/150 byte-exact. The other necessary piece was waiting for gathering complete before reading
`local_description()` — without it the offer goes out with no candidates and the same ufrag error
surfaces on the receiver's `set_remote_description`.

Lesson: the new `webrtc` facade keeps its media engine per connection and gives empty registries by
default; both halves of a handshake need the codec registry, and non-trickle signalling needs the
gather-complete wait on BOTH descriptions, not just the offer. The `paper_data.rs` pattern already
did the wait for its offers; the answer side needs it too.

### `pgrep -a a b` does not do what it reads like — `FIXED`

Attempted: `pgrep -a pipewire pulseaudio` to check for sound servers.

Symptom: reported nothing, and I concluded "no PipeWire session running". Later in the same
session, `pgrep -c pipewire` alone found **3 processes** — a full PipeWire session was up the whole
time. The two-argument form does not search two patterns; the second word was silently not a
pattern, and the first pattern's match was lost to whatever the combined invocation did.

Resolution: one pattern per call (`pgrep -a pipewire; pgrep -a pulseaudio`), or `pgrep -a 'pipewire|pulseaudio'`. The §2 #5 capture-backend probe was scoped on the wrong premise because of this.

Lesson: the cost of a bad negative here was under-probing (skipping the pipewire-rs capture probe
that was feasible all along), not a wrong product result — but a check that silently answers
"absent" is the classic shape this log exists for.

### Smaller build frictions in the same slice — `FIXED`

- Opus 1.4 fails to compile with only `OPUS_BUILD`/`HAVE_LRINT*`: `stack_alloc.h` demands one of
  `VAR_ARRAYS`/`USE_ALLOCA`/`NONTHREADSAFE_PSEUDOSTACK`. `VAR_ARRAYS` is the Linux norm.
- `cpal` 0.15's host methods (`default_input_device`, `build_input_stream`, `play`) live on the
  `traits::{HostTrait, DeviceTrait, StreamTrait}` traits — importing the crate is not enough.
  There is no `alsa` feature to enable (the Linux backend is a non-optional dependency); inventing
  one fails version selection.
- `hound::WavWriter::finalize` consumes `self` — an `Arc<Mutex<WavWriter>>` shared with the capture
  callback needs `Arc::try_unwrap` after the stream is dropped, not a `lock()`.
- The first loopback proof lost exactly one packet (149/150): the first `write_sample` raced the
  ICE pair opening. A 150 ms settle after `Connected` makes it 150/150 byte-exact.

## 2026-10-13 — `pgrep -f` and `pkill -f` matched the shell running them, again

### A self-matching `pgrep` reported a finished build as still running — `OPEN` (recurrence)

Attempted: wait for `cargo build --release -p hush-daemon` to finish by polling
`pgrep -f "cargo build --release -p hush-daemon"` in a loop.

Symptom: the loop never exited, and the final check printed `STILL BUILDING` while the build log
already said it was done:

```
Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 11m 50s
```

The poller's own command line contains the literal pattern it searches for, so `pgrep -f` matched
the polling shell and the answer was permanently "yes". This is a wrong *result*, not just missing
output — the loop would have run to its cap and the conclusion would have been "still building" about
a build that had been finished for minutes. The same command run with `pkill -f` instead of `pgrep -f`
killed the invoking shell outright and returned nothing at all, which is the shape already logged
twice in this file (the `pkill -f` entries below, marked `FIXED`).

Resolution: none applied — the build had already finished, so the poll was replaced by reading the
log. The fix that actually works is to stop pattern-matching on the command line: capture the PID
when launching (`echo $!`) and poll `kill -0 <pid>`, or poll the artifact
(`cargo build ... && echo done`), or anchor the pattern so it cannot match a shell wrapper
(`pgrep -f '^/home/sam/\.rustup/.*/cargo build'`). Where a process must be signalled, resolve the PID
with `pgrep -f` first and pass it to `kill`, never `pkill -f` with a pattern copied from the command
being typed.

Lesson: the earlier `FIXED` tag on this trap was too generous — the entry documented the anchoring
fix and the trap still landed twice in one session, once as silence and once as a confidently wrong
answer. Treat any `-f` pattern that appears in the command being run as self-matching until proven
otherwise, and prefer PIDs over patterns for both polling and signalling.
