## 2026-10-13 — The daemon's first TLS handshake panicked and wedged the socket

Trigger: `Public posts` → `Refresh` in a dev run answered "Can't reach the Hush daemon at
unix:///run/user/1000/hush-one/hush.sock. Start it with: `cargo run -p hush-daemon -- --dir <vault>`".

### Both rustls providers were enabled, so the daemon panicked on its first TLS connection — `FIXED`

Attempted: read the message as a connectivity problem — the daemon was not running, or the socket had
been cleaned up.

Symptom: the daemon *was* running, and the socket was not merely present but listening:

```
$ pgrep -af hush-daemon
328425 .../target/release/hush-daemon --dir .../instances/peer-a --socket /run/user/1000/hush-one/hush.sock
$ ss -xl | rg hush.sock
u_str LISTEN 0 4096 /run/user/1000/hush-one/hush.sock 1101577 * 0
```

Every request on it timed out with zero bytes, which is what the UI rendered as "Can't reach the
daemon":

```
$ curl -sS --max-time 5 --unix-socket .../hush.sock http://localhost/api/status
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 5002 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
```

The daemon log held the actual cause, one line above the silence:

```
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' (328428) panicked at .../rustls-0.23.45/src/crypto/mod.rs:249:14:
Could not automatically determine the process-level CryptoProvider from Rustls crate features.
Call CryptoProvider::install_default() before this point to select a provider manually, or make
sure exactly one of the 'aws-lc-rs' and 'ring' features is enabled.
```

Cause: rustls 0.23 will not choose a crypto provider when feature unification enables both, and this
binary enables both. `cargo tree -p hush-daemon -e features -i rustls` shows `ring` arriving from
`webrtc` → `rtc`/`rtc-dtls` `crypto-ring` and from `reqwest`'s `__rustls-ring`, and `aws-lc-rs`
arriving from `hush-wallet` → alloy's `reqwest-rustls-tls` and from `electrum-client`'s
`rustls`/`default`. Both native libraries are linked into the release binary, which is why the
release build spends time in `aws-lc-sys` and `ring` alike.

This is not a Phase 4 regression. `cargo tree -p hush-articles -e features -i rustls` shows the new
crate enabling only `rustls/std`, no provider — the collision predates it. What Phase 4 changed is
that it was the first daemon code path to *open a TLS connection*: the read lane dials `wss://`
through Tor, the first handshake reached `CryptoProvider::from_crate_features()`, and that returns
`None` here. The panic killed the runtime worker mid-request and left the listener open, so the
failure surfaced as an unreachable socket rather than a crash. Anything else in the daemon that
speaks TLS — electrum, the drop origins — was equally exposed and simply had not been reached.

Resolution: `main` now installs one provider before anything can dial out, the same choice the
desktop shell already makes for its own client (`apps/hush-tauri/src-tauri/src/irc/tls.rs` builds its
config from `rustls::crypto::ring`). `crates/hush-daemon/Cargo.toml` names `rustls` directly with the
`ring` feature rather than relying on a sibling crate's unification to keep the module compiled in.
The result of the install is deliberately discarded: `AlreadyInstalled` is the only error it can
return, and it means the job is done either way.

Verified by running the debug daemon against a copy of the dev vault — so the live window's daemon
and vault lock were left alone — unlocking it, pointing the relay switch at the running Tor's SOCKS
port, and calling the endpoint that had panicked:

```
$ curl --unix-socket /tmp/hush-tor-test/hush.sock -X POST http://localhost/api/relay/mode \
    -d '{"onion":true,"socks":"socks5h://127.0.0.1:44627"}'
http 204
$ curl --unix-socket /tmp/hush-tor-test/hush.sock -X POST http://localhost/api/neighborhoods/refresh
{"articles":[{"address":"30023:893633d3...:gallery-364420b0-...","title":"fake boobs for baby",...
http 200   real 0m20.540s
```

`rg -c "panicked|CryptoProvider" /tmp/hush-tor-test/daemon.log` → no matches, the log holds only its
two startup lines, `/api/status` still answers `200` afterwards, and 68 articles are cached.

The release binary was rebuilt from the same source (11m 50s) and the release artifact was then put
through the same run against the vault copy, so the verification is of the binary the launcher
actually starts, not only of the debug build:

```
$ .../target/release/hush-daemon --dir /tmp/peer-a-tor-test --socket /tmp/hush-tor-test/hush.sock
unlock http 204
relay mode http 204
refresh http 200   real 0m20.030s
```

`rg -c "panicked|CryptoProvider"` on that log → no matches, `/api/status` answers `200` afterwards,
and 71 articles are cached — three more than the debug run, so the second refresh reached a live
relay rather than replaying the cache.

The binary was rebuilt again after the regression test was added (12m 05s, `main.rs` changed), so the
final artifact was put through the same run once more rather than assumed equivalent to the previous
one:

```
unlock http 204
relay mode http 204
refresh http 200 in 20.035057s
```

No panics, `/api/status` answers `200`, and 91 articles are cached. The live daemon was then
restarted on that binary and answers `200` on the real vault.

A regression test now covers the mechanism, and it was checked against its own failure rather than
assumed to work. With the install in place:

```
test tls_provider_tests::the_process_default_tls_provider_is_installed ... ok
```

With `install_tls_provider` emptied out — the shape a careless refactor would leave behind:

```
thread 'tls_provider_tests::the_process_default_tls_provider_is_installed' panicked at
crates/hush-daemon/src/main.rs:10132:9:
no process-level rustls provider: the first TLS handshake would panic
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed
```

What the test does not cover, stated rather than implied: it runs the same function `main` runs, so
it catches a changed or emptied provider but not a deleted call site. That gap is what the doc
comment on the function is for. All 228 daemon tests pass, and `cargo clippy -p hush-daemon
--all-targets` reports nothing on the new lines.

One round trip while adding the test: the helper was first inserted between `#[tokio::main]` and
`async fn main`, which moved the attribute onto the helper and failed the build with "the `async`
keyword is missing from the function declaration" pointing at `fn install_tls_provider()`. The
attribute belongs to `main` and cannot have a doc comment or an item wedged between it and the
function it decorates.

Second round trip, and a trap for any future manual check of this path: the first run against the
final binary answered `502` in 5.6ms, which reads like the fix failing. It was a stale port. The
bundled Tor picks a **new random SOCKS port on every start**, and the instance the earlier run used
(`127.0.0.1:44627`) had been replaced by one on `43115`:

```
$ ps -eo pid,args | rg resources/tor/tor
406445 .../resources/tor/tor --defaults-torrc ...
$ ss -tlnp | rg tor
LISTEN 0 4096 127.0.0.1:43115 0.0.0.0:* users:(("tor",pid=406445,fd=6))
```

A `502` that returns in single-digit milliseconds means the SOCKS port refused the connection —
a dead proxy — not a relay problem. Read the live port off `ss` before pointing anything at Tor, and
treat a fast `502` as "no proxy there" rather than "the fix did not work".

Lesson: a panic inside a tokio worker leaves the socket listening, so "can't reach the daemon" can
mean the daemon is up and its runtime is broken. Read the daemon log before believing a connectivity
message — and when a workspace links two crypto providers, install one explicitly instead of letting
rustls infer it from crate features.

---


Trigger: opening Settings → Relay in a dev run and reading "Tor was not found. Install Tor, or point
`HUSH_TOR_BIN` at a Tor binary."

### The Relay panel reported Tor missing while the repo shipped one — `FIXED`

Attempted: check the onion path in a running `./scripts/run-one-ui.sh` window.

Symptom: the Relay panel said

```
Tor was not found. Install Tor, or point HUSH_TOR_BIN at a Tor binary.
```

Nothing in the repository had been removed — the sidecar is at
`apps/hush-tauri/src-tauri/resources/tor/tor` and is declared as a Tauri resource. Two independent
gaps meant the app never looked at it, and neither was visible from the panel's message.

Cause, part one: the resource directory resolves to a path that does not exist. Tauri's
`resource_dir_from` takes the cargo-output shortcut only when a path component is literally `target`
(`parts[len - 2] == "target" || parts[len - 3] == "target"`, plus a `.cargo-lock` check). Here
`target/` is a symlink to `/var/tmp/hush-target`, and `current_exe()` resolves it, so the executable's
directory is `/var/tmp/hush-target/debug` — `parts[len - 2]` is `debug` and `parts[len - 3]` is
`hush-target`, so the check fails. The Linux fallback is then
`/usr/lib/hush-tauri` (via `exe_dir/../lib/<name>`, which does not exist either), a directory this
machine has never had. Staging the sidecar in `target/debug/tor/` would not have helped on its own:
cargo does not put `src-tauri/resources/` there.

Cause, part two: the sidecar links `libevent-2.1.so.7`, which is not installed on this machine —
`ldd` reports `libevent-2.1.so.7 => not found`, and `ldconfig -p` has no entry for it. So even
pointed at directly, the bundled Tor cannot start without the loader being told about the copy
beside it. `TorManager::bundled_lib_dir` does exactly that, but only when the binary lives under the
resource directory, which — per part one — is the one place it was not.

Resolution: `run-one-ui.sh` and `run-two-ui.sh` now hand the window the sidecar and its directory
(`HUSH_TOR_BIN`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`), honouring an existing `HUSH_TOR_BIN` and falling back to a
system `tor` when there is no sidecar. They also print which of the three they found before the
window opens, because the panel is a bad place to learn it. Verified with the app's own live test,
which builds a `TorManager` with no resource directory — exactly the configuration the launcher now
creates:

```
HUSH_TOR_BIN=.../resources/tor/tor LD_LIBRARY_PATH=.../resources/tor \
  cargo test -p hush-tauri --lib -- --ignored
test tor::tests::bootstraps_with_a_real_tor ... ok   (11.53s)
```

That closes the "Tor was not found" path and proves the locator honours the override. It does **not**
yet prove a public relay answers over that circuit — see the entry below.

Lesson, and the reason this is worth an entry rather than a quiet fix: the Phase 2 and Phase 4
sections in this log recorded "no Tor in this environment" as a fact about the machine. It was also a
gap in our own launcher, and the binary was in the repository the whole time. A limitation written
down as environmental should be checked against what the repo already ships before it is used to
excuse an unverified claim. Two slices were marked "cannot be verified here" on a premise that was
one script line from being false.

### The read lane now reaches public relays over Tor; the write lane still has not — `OPEN`

Attempted: confirm the read lane and the export/comment path against a real relay now that the
bundled Tor runs.

Symptom: nothing had exercised `wss://relay.damus.io` and friends through a live circuit. The
bootstrap was proven; the WebSocket-over-SOCKS request through a real circuit to a real relay was
not, and the allowlist had never been contacted.

Resolution, reads: done. `POST /api/neighborhoods/refresh` over the bundled Tor's SOCKS port returned
`200` in 20.5s with articles from the allowlisted relays and cached 68 of them, so the allowlist has
now been contacted and the read lane is proven against real relays through a real circuit. This also
required the rustls provider install at the top of this file — the first handshake panicked before it
could succeed.

Resolution still needed, writes: export a zine and post a comment and confirm a relay returns `OK`.
Both publish permanently to public relays under the user's public identity, so neither was run
without the user asking for it.

## 2026-10-13 — Neighborhoods: export and commenting (Phase 4)

Trigger: "phase4". Scope: `Export to neighborhoods` (Task 11) and NIP-22 public commenting with
read-only inbound replies — `hush-articles` (`nip22`, `markdown`, `relay`, `store`, `refresh`),
`hush-daemon` (the export route, the comment route, the two-pass refresh), and `hush-tauri` (the
export confirm, the public thread, the gated composer). Verified by `cargo test --workspace`,
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm test` and `npm run build`, all
green from this turn's output. Not verified against a live relay or Tor, and the composer was not
driven in a browser — see the two `OPEN` entries.

### Multiple relay hints would have displaced the `pubkey` on an `e` tag — `WORKED AROUND`

Attempted: carry every relay hint a comment had for each `e` tag, the way a general-purpose Nostr
client does.

Symptom: none observed at runtime, which is the problem. In NIP-01 an `e` tag is positional —
`["e", <id>, <relay-url>, <pubkey>]` — so the *second* hint URL lands in slot 4 and is read back as
the author's pubkey. The tag would still parse, and the only visible damage would be a wrong or
absent `p` on a downstream client, i.e. a silently mis-threaded comment on someone else's relay.

Resolution: at most one relay hint per tag, and only if it is in the allowlist
(`crates/hush-articles/src/nip22.rs`). The comment is still signed and verified correctly; the cost
is that a reader who does not know our relays may not find the comment. Lesson: when a wire format
is positional, "carry everything we know" is not a safe default — the extra data does not fail, it
overwrites.

### A NIP-22 tag assertion checked the comment id where it meant the article id — `FIXED`

Attempted: assert `e` on a published comment against the id the test had built for the article.

Symptom: the assertion compared against `comment.id` (the event id of the comment itself), so it
was checking that the tag pointed at the thing it was attached to — which passes for the wrong
reason on any implementation, or fails while looking like an off-by-one. It failed; that is how it
was found.

Resolution: the helper now returns the article's *version* event id and the test asserts against
that. Lesson: a test that builds two ids of the same shape must name them apart, or the assertion
reads as correct while comparing the wrong pair.

### `&Arc<FakeSource>` did not coerce to `&Arc<dyn RelaySource>` — `FIXED`

Attempted: call `refresh(&fake, ...)` in a test where `fake: Arc<FakeSource>`.

Symptom:

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
expected `&Arc<dyn RelaySource>`
   found `&Arc<FakeSource>`
```

Cause: `Arc<T>` does not unsize-coerce behind a shared reference; only `Arc<T> -> Arc<dyn Trait>`
at the point of construction does. The production call site is fine because the daemon builds the
`Arc<dyn RelaySource>` once.

Resolution: bind it explicitly — `let source: Arc<dyn RelaySource> = fake.clone();` — then pass
`&source`. Lesson: the unsize coercion applies to the value, not to a reference to it.

### A test helper moved a value that the assertion then read — `FIXED`

Attempted: build a `CommentPlan`, move it into `event()` to get the signed event, then assert on
the plan's fields.

Symptom: `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value`. The plan owns the content it frames.

Resolution: `.clone()` at the call, since the test wants both. Lesson: an API that consumes its
input to produce the event is right (the plan is not reusable), but a test that wants to check both
sides has to pay for the copy rather than the API carrying an unnecessary `Clone` bound.

### Test helpers in `main.rs` were invisible to the comment test module — `FIXED`

Attempted: reuse `FakeRelay` and `long_form_event` from the neighborhoods test module in the new
comment test module, both inside the daemon's `main.rs`.

Symptom: `error[E0433]: failed to resolve` — the items were private to their sibling module. Making
the whole module `pub` to fix it would have leaked test scaffolding into the crate.

Resolution: `pub(super)` on the two items and a `FakeRelay::new(events, comments)` constructor so
the comment tests can seed replies without reaching into fields. Lesson: sibling test modules are
not friends in Rust; scope the export to the parent instead of widening the module.

### Clippy flagged an `impl Future` helper as an `async fn in trait` hazard — `FIXED`

Attempted: write the test-only `set_allowlist` helper as `fn set_allowlist(&self, ...) -> impl Future<Output = ...>`.

Symptom: `warning: use of `async fn` in public traits is discouraged` on the surrounding trait, plus
`async_fn_in_trait` noise that pointed at the helper rather than at a real problem.

Resolution: made it an `async fn`. Lesson: the workaround for the trait lint (returning `impl
Future` by hand) is itself flagged; when the trait is only ever used inside the crate, plain
`async fn` is the answer.

### The comment POST's response was dereferenced as non-null — `FIXED`

Attempted: `const out = await api.neighborhoodComment(...); if (out.published) { ... }`.

Symptom:

```
src/app.ts(6641,11): error TS18047: 'out' is possibly 'null'.
```

Cause: `request<T>` returns `Promise<T | null>` — it answers `null` for an empty or unreadable body
— and the export call had handled that but the comment call was written as if the daemon always
answered.

Resolution: `if (!out) throw new Error("The daemon sent no answer.")`, matching the export path.
Lesson: the shared `request` helper's nullable return is a property of the helper, not of the
endpoint; every new call site has to answer it.

### The comment path is verified against a local relay and a stand-in SOCKS proxy — `OPEN`

**See the 2026-10-13 entry "The dev launcher never provided the bundled Tor" above: the premise
below ("no network and no Tor daemon") was half wrong — there is network, and the sidecar was in the
repository all along. The bootstrap is now proven; a real relay over a real circuit is still the open
part.**

Attempted: prove that a comment leaves over Tor and comes back as a reply on the article page.

Symptom: this build environment has no network and no Tor daemon, so the only end-to-end run is
against a local WebSocket relay with a stand-in SOCKS proxy. That covers framing, the two-pass
refresh, the signature, the cache, and the refusal paths, but not Tor reachability, not a live
relay's `OK`, and not a relay that answers with hints or duplicates.

Resolution needed: run the daemon with Tor up and the allowlist pointed at a real relay, post one
comment from a second vault, and confirm it appears on the first vault's article page after a
refresh. Until then the Tor claim is inherited from Phase 2, which has the same gap.

### The public composer and thread were not driven in a browser — `OPEN`

Attempted: confirm the thread renders, the identity gate switches to the box after a mint, and a
posted comment appears without a reload.

Symptom: `tsc`, `npm test` (59 pass, including the six new thread/composer tests) and the production
build are green, but none of them paint the page. The DOM wiring — the re-parented textarea, the
`--post-depth` indent, the reply button flipping `postCommentParent` — is verified by reading the
code only.

Resolution needed: drive the article page in a running app (the `preview-protocol` route), post a
comment, and confirm the cache write shows up in the thread. This is the same gap recorded for
Phase 3's switch and article page and is still open for the same reason: the slice was written
offline.

## 2026-10-13 — Neighborhoods: the mixed page (Phase 3)

Trigger: "phase3" after the read lane landed. Scope: the `Public posts` switch, the `public post`
badge, the lead rule, and `lib/zinesPage.ts` composed over the mixed corpus. The composition is
covered by unit tests; the switch and the article page were verified by reading the wiring and by a
green `tsc`/build, **not** by driving the UI (see the last entry).

### `* * *` printed as a bullet instead of a rule — `FIXED`

Attempted: render a horizontal rule with a `/^\s*([-*_])\s*\1\s*\1/` style check placed among the
other block rules, after the list rule.

Symptom: `* * *` came out as a one-item list. The list regex (`^\s*([-*+]|\d+[.)])\s+`) matches it
first — `*` is a valid bullet and the next char is a space — so the block was consumed as a bullet
whose text is `* *`, which then reads as emphasis and prints as a blank bullet.

Resolution: an explicit `isRule()` (`/^\s*([-*_])(?:\s*\1){2,}\s*$/`) evaluated **before** the list
item, and added to `startsBlock` so a rule also interrupts a paragraph. Lesson: in a hand-rolled
block parser the order of the rules is the precedence, and `*` is the one marker that is both a rule
character and a bullet; the more specific rule has to be tested first.

### A link with parentheses in the URL swallowed its own closing paren — `FIXED`

Attempted: parse `[text](url)` with `\(([^()\s]*)\)`.

Symptom: a URL containing a balanced pair, e.g. `javascript:alert(1)`, matched up to the first `)`,
leaving a stray `)` behind and printing it as literal text after the link.

Resolution: `String.raw`\(((?:[^()\s]|\([^()]*\))+)\)`` — one level of balanced nesting. Lesson: a
"greedy up to the closing delimiter" pattern is wrong the moment the delimiter can appear inside;
this is the class of bug that also produces the classic `$1`-residue in link parsers.

### `node --test` could not resolve `./richText` without an extension — `FIXED`

Attempted: import the sanitizer in `markdown.test.ts` the way the app does, as `./richText`.

Symptom:

```
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '.../src/lib/richText'
imported from .../src/lib/markdown.test.ts
```

Cause: the tests run under plain Node ESM (`node --test`), whose resolver requires the extension; the
app's bundler is happy without it. The existing test files in the repo import with the extension
(`./zinesPage.ts`) — the convention was there and was not followed.

Resolution: import `./richText.ts`, matching the other test files. Lesson: tests execute in Node, not
through the bundler, so test imports need the same specifier form as the rest of the suite.

### A nullable settings payload was typed as non-null — `FIXED`

Attempted: `const settings = await api.neighborhoodSettings(); this.neighborhoodsShown = settings.default_show;`

Symptom: `tsc` rejected the dereference — `neighborhoodSettings()` is typed to return the DTO or
`null`, because the daemon can answer with an empty body.

Resolution: `settings?.default_show ?? false`, with a comment recording that a null answer means the
daemon had nothing to report, which is the same as the default (off). Lesson: a route that can answer
empty should be typed nullable at the client, and the "nothing to report" case should be folded into
the default rather than given its own error path.

### The frontend test count was carried forward from memory and was wrong — `FIXED`

Attempted: state the size of the new frontend coverage in the task doc from the working summary
rather than from the runner.

Symptom: `zinesPage.test.ts` was recorded as 27 tests; `node --test src/lib/zinesPage.test.ts`
reports **22** (13 for `markdown.test.ts`, both confirmed before the doc was written).

Resolution: re-ran each file and wrote the counts from the runner output. Lesson: a test count in a
doc is a claim like any other — read it off the command, do not recall it.

### The switch and the article page were not exercised in a running app — `OPEN`

Attempted: verify Phase 3's UI the way the acceptance criteria are phrased ("renders on cards and
story pages").

Symptom: what is proven is the composition (22 unit tests over the mixed corpus), the renderer (13),
and that `tsc --noEmit`, `vite build` and the full workspace `cargo test` are green. What is **not**
proven is any of it on screen: no build of the Tauri shell was launched, the switch was never
clicked, and a real `neighborhoods.enc` with posts in it was never rendered, because this environment
has no Tor and therefore no way to fill the cache through the real path.

Resolution needed: run the app, seed the cache (or point the read lane at a local relay), toggle
`Public posts`, and read a public article end to end. Until then the composition rules are tested and
the wiring is read, but no pixel of the mixed page has been seen.

## 2026-10-13 — Neighborhoods: the read lane (Phase 2)

Trigger: "go" after Phase 1 landed, then the transport choice. The lane — NIP-23 mapping, the quality
gate, the `(pubkey, d)` dedupe, the encrypted cache, the index, and a hand-rolled NIP-01 client over
the shell's Tor SOCKS proxy — is built and tested. The Tor path itself is not: see the `OPEN` entry
below.

### A locked vault answered 503 on `/api/neighborhoods/refresh` — `FIXED`

Attempted: write `neighborhoods_refresh` with the transport check first and the sidecar read after
it, assuming a lock guard sat in front of the router the way `axum` middleware would.

Symptom: `neighborhoods_read_routes_are_401_while_locked` failed with
`assertion left == right failed: POST /api/neighborhoods/refresh, left: 503, right: 401`.

Cause: there is no lock middleware. Every route's 401 comes from the worker answering
`WorkResult::Err("locked")`, which the handler maps through `worker_err`. A handler that answers
before it reaches the worker never sees the lock, so a locked vault learned whether a transport was
configured — daemon state leaked to a locked caller, and a break from the "all routes 401 when
locked" contract the spec states.

Resolution: read the sidecar (worker first) before the transport check, with a comment saying why
the order matters. Lesson: in `hush-daemon` the lock is a property of the worker call, not of the
router; any early return that precedes the first worker call bypasses it. New routes need a 401
test against the locked app, which is what caught this.

### The reading-time floor boundary was miscalculated in a test — `FIXED`

Attempted: assert that a 599-word body fails a 3-minute floor, assuming 599 words was under three
minutes.

Symptom: `the_floor_admits_a_real_article_and_refuses_a_stub` failed — at 200 wpm, 599 words rounds
up to 3 minutes and is admitted, so the assertion was wrong, not the gate.

Resolution: asserted the real boundary (401 words in, 400 words out), so the test pins the edge
rather than an arbitrary interior point. Lesson: a floor test belongs on the boundary; the rounding
direction (`div_ceil`) is the thing under test.

### The read lane's transport was unwired, then built — `FIXED`

Attempted: land Phase 2's lane logic before choosing a transport, so the pipeline could be verified
offline. That left `POST /api/neighborhoods/refresh` answering `503 no relay transport is
configured`, with no fetch exercised.

Resolution: the transport is `hush_articles::RelayClient`, a hand-rolled minimal NIP-01 client — a
WebSocket (`tokio-tungstenite`) dialled through the SOCKS proxy the shell reports for Tor
(`relay_socks`), `REQ` → `EVENT` until `EOSE` → `CLOSE`. `RelayClient::via_tor` is the only
constructor the daemon builds, so there is no clearnet path by construction, and a refresh with no
Tor is a `503` rather than a direct connection. The `rust-nostr` + `arti` route the docs named was
rejected: the repo already runs one Tor (an external SOCKS proxy) and `arti` would be a second Tor
stack beside it.

### The transport is verified against a local relay, not against Tor — `FIXED`

**Closed 2026-10-13 by the entry at the top of this file. The `wss://` branch now has a real
certificate chain behind it: a refresh through the bundled Tor reached the three allowlisted public
relays and cached 68 articles.** The text below is the state before that run, kept because the
distinction it draws — wire and handshake tested, Tor path not — is the one the fix removed.

**Superseded in part by the 2026-10-13 entry above: this environment does have network, and the repo
ships a Tor binary that the dev launcher was failing to hand to the app. Read that entry first — the
"no Tor" half of the premise below was our own launcher gap, not a fact about the machine.**

Attempted: prove the fetch end to end.

Symptom: this environment has no network and no Tor, so nothing here can exercise a real circuit or a
real public relay. What **is** proven: the NIP-01 wire (a `REQ`/`EVENT`/`EOSE`/`CLOSE` round trip
against a local `tokio-tungstenite` relay), the SOCKS5 handshake (against a stand-in proxy that
checks the target arrives as a domain name, i.e. `socks5h`), the dead-relay and refused-connect
paths, and the daemon's real transport construction (a reported-but-dead SOCKS port yields a `502`
naming the relays).

Resolution needed: run a refresh through a real Tor SOCKS proxy against a live allowlisted relay.
Until then the wire and the handshake are tested but the Tor path is not, and the TLS branch
(`wss://` via `client_async_tls_with_config`) has not been exercised against a real certificate
chain.

Resolved: `POST /api/neighborhoods/refresh` against `socks5h://127.0.0.1:44627` — the bundled Tor the
dev launcher now starts — returned `200` in 20.5s with articles from `wss://relay.damus.io` and
friends, and 68 articles are cached. The `wss://` branch is now exercised against real certificate
chains through a real circuit. Getting there required the provider install at the top of this file:
the first handshake panicked rather than failing, which is why this entry outlived the launcher fix.

### A SOCKS5 reply match had incompatible arm types — `FIXED`

Attempted: consume the CONNECT reply's bound address with
`0x01 => stream.read_exact(&mut [0u8; 4]).await?,`.

Symptom:

```
error[E0308]: `match` arms have incompatible types
   --> crates/hush-articles/src/socks.rs:64:13
    |
 57 | /     match head[3] {
 58 | |         0x01 => stream.read_exact(&mut [0u8; 4]).await?,
    | |                 --------------------------------------- this is found to be of type `usize`
```

`read_exact` returns the byte count, so that arm yields `usize` while the braced `0x03` arm yields
`()`. Resolution: braced every arm so all are `()`. Lesson: `read_exact(..)?` used as a match arm is
an expression of type `usize`; make it a statement.

## 2026-10-13 — Neighborhoods: public identity (Phase 1)

Trigger: "can we start implementing" after the spec in `docs/tasks/neighborhoods.md` (Task 22 /
Phase P). Phase 1 is the offline public identity: a fresh secp256k1 key in its own encrypted
sidecar, in the Task 6 backup, isolated from the account and the pen name.

### `cargo test ... | tail` masked cargo's exit code — `FIXED`

Attempted: run the full `hush-core` and `hush-daemon` suites in one command and view the tail of the
output.

Symptom: the command reported exit code 0, but that was `tail`'s exit code, not cargo's. A failing
`hush-core` suite would have been invisible above the truncation point while the run still looked
green.

Resolution: re-ran `cargo test -p hush-core` without a pipe and read the whole output; 115 passed,
0 failed, including the new vector test. Lesson: a piped cargo run proves nothing about cargo's
status; pipe only for display and confirm the real exit code separately.

### The worker's create path needed `as_mut`, not `as_ref` — `FIXED`

Attempted: add `PublicIdentityCreate` to the daemon work loop, mirroring `PenNameGet`, which reads
`account.as_ref()`.

Symptom:

```
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `*a` as mutable, as it is behind a `&` reference
    --> crates/hush-daemon/src/account_worker.rs:1265:51
     |
1265 | ...   None => match a.create_public_identity() {
     |                      ^ `a` is a `&` reference, so it cannot be borrowed as mutable
```

`Account`'s mutating methods take `&mut self` (as `create_pen_name` does), so the create arm must
hold `account.as_mut()`; the read arm's `as_ref()` is right for the getter.

Resolution: switched the create arm to `as_mut()`. Lesson: in `account_worker.rs` the read arms take
`as_ref()` and the mutating arms `as_mut()`, and they are not interchangeable even when the
underlying `Vault` method takes `&self`.

## 2026-10-13 — Zines: the bulletin lane, key epidemic and comments (Phases 2 and 3)

Trigger: "ok i thought you are done .. lets continute with all the phases". The design is in
`docs/tasks/zines.md` (sections 4 and 5). Entries below are the problems hit wiring the wire.

### The grant/comment UI was never driven in a live browser — `OPEN`

Attempted: verify Phases 3 and 4 in the running app the way the front page was verified on
2026-10-13 (Vite on 5173 against a real daemon, driven over CDP).

Symptom: not attempted. The flow needs **two daemons, two vaults, and a relay** running at once to
exercise a grant, and the browser harness in this session had no such pair standing. What was verified
instead is the daemon-level integration test (`zines_bulletin_tests`) over the same wire, plus the
composition rules as unit tests, plus `tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build`.

Resolution needed: start a relay, two daemons with separate data roots, grant A → B → C, then drive the
UI. Until then, treat the *paint* of the share dialog, the comment composer, the pending pile, the
byline filter chip, and the corpus note as unverified. The logic behind them is tested; the wiring
between the DOM and the routes is not. Lesson: an integration test proves the wire, not the button —
"the daemon does this" and "the user can do this" are two different claims and only the first is
evidenced here.

### The protocol doc described the bulletin's publish credential wrongly — `FIXED`

Attempted: bring `docs/PROTOCOL.md` up to the built wire, which had been marked "design not built".

Symptom: the design note said publish authorizes with the **delivery** credential and drain with the
**read** credential, reusing the queue split. `Store::put_bulletin` calls
`authorize_read_or_create(queue_id, read_token)`, and `crates/hush-relay/tests/bulletin.rs`
(`a_publish_needs_the_private_credential`) pins it: the read token publishes, and the delivery token —
the one that travels in invites — is refused with `401`. A second detail the note did not have: the
queue id in the path is **derived** (`hush_core::bulletin_queue_id`), not the inbox id, because the
relay self-binds an unclaimed queue to the first credential and an inbox id plus its delivery token
both travel in invites.

Resolution: `PROTOCOL.md` and `THREAT_MODEL.md` now state the built form, and
`docs/tasks/zines.md` lists both corrections at the end of Phase 5 so the older text is not trusted
over the code. Lesson: a design doc that says "not built" is a hypothesis about the wire; correcting it
is part of building, and a doc that disagrees with the code is worse than no doc at all.

### The retry sweep was a no-op: `zines_absorb` refused every blob it already held — `FIXED`

Attempted: verify the key epidemic end to end in `zines_bulletin_tests`. Test 2 drains the
bulletin as B (blob held, unreadable), then A sends a `ZineGrant` over the session, then B polls
again and is expected to open the blob it is already holding.

Symptom: after the grant, the post appeared in B's index with an empty title and empty sections:

```
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: String("")
 right: "On relays"
```

`unreadable_blobs` had gone from 1 to 0 and the blob was flagged readable, so the *key* had
landed; what had not landed was the *plaintext*. `zines_retry_unreadable` called `zines_absorb`
for each held-unreadable blob, and `zines_absorb` began with `if parsed.holds_blob(&hash) {
return false }` — the drain's dedup guard. The retry sweep exists precisely to revisit a blob that
is held and unopened, so that guard made every retry a no-op. The post stayed a placeholder:
`apply_grant` had created a `ZineFile` with an empty pen name and revision 0, and nothing ever
filled it in.

Resolution: split the placement from the guard. `zines_place` does the trial decryption and
filing; `zines_absorb` is now `if holds_blob { false } else { zines_place(...) }`, and the retry
sweep calls `zines_place` directly. Also made step 3 (`held unreadable, never discarded`) report
the real outcome from `hold_blob`'s `BlobHeld` instead of a hardcoded `true`, so a blob that is
already held and still opens to nothing answers "nothing changed" rather than making every poll
rewrite `zines.enc`. Lesson: a dedup guard belongs to the caller that needs dedup, not to the
function both callers share — putting it in the shared function silently disabled the one caller
whose job was to revisit what was already stored.

### Two integration tests dropped the relay's temp database while SQLite held it open — `FIXED`

Attempted: run the three-daemon bulletin tests, each of which starts a real relay on a port with
`relay_on_a_port()` returning `(url, NamedTempFile, Member, Member)`.

Symptom: every relay write in tests 2 and 3 answered `500 Internal Server Error`
(`bulletin put failed: 500`, `recv failed: delete failed: 500`), while test 1 passed. Patching
every `map_err(|_| RelayError::Internal)` in `hush-relay/src/store.rs` to print the underlying
error gave the actual cause:

```
DBG relay: attempt to write a readonly database
```

The tests destructured the tuple in the wrong order — `let (_relay_db, _, a, b) = pair().await;`
bound the *URL string* to `_relay_db` and the `NamedTempFile` to `_`, so the temp file was dropped
at the binding and deleted, and SQLite kept writing to an unlinked inode. The `500` was a
plausible-looking symptom pointing at the new bulletin SQL, which was not at fault.

Resolution: bind the file — `let (_relay, _relay_db, a, b) = pair().await;` — and the debug
`eprintln!`s were reverted (restored from a pre-patch copy of `store.rs`). Lesson: `_name` still
binds and `_` drops; when a handle's lifetime is load-bearing, the placeholder must be named. Also:
`RelayError::Internal` swallowing the SQLite message cost several build-test cycles — a log line
at the conversion point would have made this a one-run diagnosis.

### `hush-cli` did not know the new payload tag — `FIXED`

Attempted: build the workspace after adding `MessagePayload::ZineGrant`.

Symptom: `error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: ZineGrant { .. } not covered` in
`crates/hush-cli/src/main.rs`, in the `recv` printing match. The core crate compiled, so the break
was only visible from a workspace build.

Resolution: added the variant to the group of control payloads the CLI never prints, with a comment
saying why. Lesson: a new `MessagePayload` variant is a workspace-wide change; `cargo build
--workspace` is the check, not `-p hush-core`.

### A tie-break test asserted the wrong winner — `FIXED`

Attempted: test the rule that resolves two honest revisions under one revision number (a vault
cloned onto two devices): the greater content hash wins. The test picked its winner with
`content_hash(&a) > content_hash(&b)` on the descriptors it had built.

Symptom: `assertion left == right failed: the lesser hash does not displace the head — left:
Advanced, right: Superseded`. The store compares hashes of the *validated* descriptors, and
validation normalizes sections and clamps the clock, so it hashes different bytes than the test
did. Hashing is not order-preserving, so the two disagreed about which descriptor had the greater
hash.

Resolution: the test now asserts the property that actually matters — ingest both orders, assert
both vaults land on the same head and both keep the loser as history — instead of picking a winner
outside the code under test. Lesson: when the code normalizes its input before hashing it, a test
that hashes the raw input is testing its own copy of the rule.

## 2026-10-13 — Zines: the front page (two columns, corpus on the page)

Trigger: "i imagine zines home page to be like a newspaper first page and showing categories on
homepage instead of pane ... the pane is only control stuff". The reshape is described in
`docs/tasks/zines.md` (Phase 4 reshape note). The entries below are the problems hit doing it: two
are real defects in the new code, three are the verification harness reading a page that had not
finished loading, and one is an agreed design rule I had not implemented.

### The pending front-page scroll was consumed by the story page — `FIXED`

Attempted: carry the reader's place on the front page across a story, the same way the chat pane
carries its scroll position (`pendingChatScroll`).

Symptom: the browser check reported `{"left":149,"back":0}` — the position was captured and then
lost. Cause: the restore hook in `render()` looked for `.zines-page` and consumed the pending value
on the *next* render, which is the story's own render, because a story is rendered inside a
`.zines-page` too. The value was cleared before the reader ever came back.

Resolution: only the front page consumes it — the hook also requires `.zines-masthead` inside the
page. Re-verified: `{"left":149,"back":149}` at a 420px viewport, so the page really scrolled.
Lesson: a "pending" value applied by a generic render hook needs the hook to know *which* render
consumes it; matching on a container class shared by both states is not enough.

### The lead was the newest story, muted or not — `FIXED`

Attempted: build the front page from the agreed design, where Q4 settled "the lead is the newest
**unmuted** post".

Symptom: none in the code — `stories[0]` looks obviously right. It surfaced when the browser check
muted the story the page was leading with: the muted story stayed the lead, so muting ("stop this
zine competing for attention") did not move the page's loudest element. The rule had been agreed and
then not implemented, and no test or type could have caught it.

Resolution: `leadOf()` in `lib/zinesPage.ts` picks the newest unmuted story, falling back to the
newest when every story is muted, with unit tests for both. Verified end to end: muting the lead
hands it to the next unmuted story and unmuting gives it back.

### Group ordering contradicted its own comment — `FIXED`

Attempted: file a story carrying several sections under one heading, chosen by the section strip's
order so a double-tagged story cannot be printed twice and cannot move depending on the order the
author typed its tags.

Symptom: the test failed with `actual: [{ name: 'systems' }]` against `expected: [{ name: 'rust' }]`.
The code used `story.sections.find((s) => order.includes(s))` — the author's tag order — while the
comment above it promised the strip's order.

Resolution: `order.find((s) => story.sections.includes(s))`. Caught only because the rule was in the
pure module with a test; the same code inline in a render function would have shipped. Lesson: the
comment was the correct specification and the code disagreed with it — worth reading the comment as
a spec when writing the test.

### The harness clicked the rail before the app had painted it — `WORKED AROUND` (harness, not the app)

Attempted: drive the new front page over CDP, starting by pressing the `Zines` rail button.

Symptom: the whole run reported an empty pane — `paneText: ""`, no masthead, and every check failing
— with no exception anywhere. The app was still on Chats: `document.body.innerText.length > 50` was
satisfied by the unlock screen, the rail button did not exist yet, and the click helper returned
`false` into a script that never checked it.

Resolution: wait for the rail button itself before clicking, and assert the click returned `true`.
Lesson: a click helper that returns a boolean needs its caller to assert it; "the element was not
there yet" and "the feature is broken" look identical otherwise.

### The reader paints before the story arrives — `WORKED AROUND` (harness, not the app)

Attempted: assert the story's headline and body after clicking a headline on the front page.

Symptom: `{"back":"← Front page","title":null,"body":""}` — the reader and its way back were there,
the article was not, because `renderZinesReader` paints an "Opening…" placeholder while the detail is
in flight. Reading it at that moment is not a defect, but it is a false failure.

Resolution: wait for `.zine-article h1` rather than for `.zines-reader`. The same trap appeared twice
more: waiting for the masthead instead of the index (the masthead paints first), and clicking
"Unmute" on a story that was already muted, where the button read "Unmute" *before* the click and the
way back was therefore read from a view the daemon had not updated yet. Fixed by waiting for the
state the click should produce (the button flipping back to "Mute"), not for the button's label.

### The daemon's zines index takes seconds — `OPEN`

Observed: `GET /api/zines` answered in 3.4s on `peer-a` (a 1.7GB vault), and the UI shows an empty
pane until it lands — the masthead paints immediately, the pen name and the strip wait for the view.
Not a defect in this slice (the request is unchanged), and not something the front page made worse,
but it is the reason a cold open of the rail looks empty for a beat. Worth measuring against a large
corpus before Phase 4's browsing work leans on it further.

### The Write-a-post pill was 11px wider than its own pane — `FIXED`

Trigger: "fix button of write a post". Attempted: measure the button against the column it lives in
rather than eyeball the screenshot.

Symptom: `.zines-pane` reported `clientWidth 231` but `scrollWidth 255`, and the button's right edge
sat 11px past the pane's right edge, so the pill was clipped and the pane scrolled sideways. Cause:
`.btn-primary` sets `width: 100%`, and `.zines-pane` is a padding-less flex column, so 100% was the
*whole* pane width and the button's own `0 12px 12px` margins were added on top of it. Pre-existing,
not introduced by the front-page reshape — the button lived in the old `.zines-nav`, also a
padding-less flex column, so it had been clipped since Phase 1.

Resolution: `.zines-write { width: auto }`, which as a stretched flex item resolves to the pane's
content width *minus* the margins — the same fix `.trusts-add` and `.conclaves-new` already carry
for the same reason. Verified: `clientWidth 231 / scrollWidth 231`, no sideways scroll, button 207px
at a 12px inset, flush with the pen card and the view controls above it, and a real mouse click at
its centre still mounts the editor.

Lesson: the 33-assertion browser suite for the front page passed while the pane was visibly broken,
because every assertion looked at the page and none looked at whether the pane's own controls fit
the column. Measuring `scrollWidth` against `clientWidth` is a one-line check that catches the whole
class; the suite now carries it (40 checks) and it was confirmed sensitive by re-injecting
`width: 100%` at runtime, which reproduces `sideways: true` and `zines-write:11px`. Scanning the other
ten rails the same way found no second instance; `Reads` shows a phantom 8px sideways scroll from
the scrollbar gutter, with no descendant painting past the edge, and is left alone as cosmetic and
out of this slice's scope.

### The same button silently wiped a draft that was still being written — `FIXED`

Found while checking what else the button does. The pane is rendered in every Zines state, so
`Write a post` sat there while a draft was open and its handler (`zinesStartNewPost`) starts an
*empty* draft. Symptom, driven through the live UI: typed `"A draft I am still writing"` plus a
paragraph, pressed the pane button, and read back `{"title":"","body":"\n"}` — the text was gone with
no confirmation and nothing to undo.

Resolution: the button is rendered only when `!this.zinesEditing`, the way the Notes pane hides
`New note` while its editor is open (`if (!this.notesEditorOpen)`). The draft page already carries
`Publish` and `Discard`, so the pane has nothing to add mid-draft. Verified through the live UI with
a reload against the new source: front page offers the button and it fits, the draft holds what was
typed, the pane hides the button while drafting, `Publish` is still enabled, discarding brings the
button back with the front page, and pressing it again opens a genuinely clean draft.

Lesson: the first pass fixed what was reported (a clipped pill) and stopped there; the destructive
path was one click away and only showed up by asking what else the control does in each state it is
rendered in. A control that starts fresh work should be checked in every state where it is visible,
not just the state the report named.

## 2026-10-13 — Zines: many posts per pen name

Trigger: "Currently zine only allow one post?!" — a correct observation. Phase 1 had made the pen
name's seal public key the post id, so the id could not address two things and a pen name could only
ever hold one post. The reshape decouples them (`pen_id` is the identity, `zine_id` is a minted
address), and this section is the problems hit doing it. Two are the stale-binary and `pkill` traps
in a new guise; the third is the verification harness, not the app.

### `cargo test` left `target/debug/hush-daemon` on the previous build — `FIXED`

Attempted: verify the migration on the real `peer-a` vault, which held a genuine legacy record (a
post whose `zine_id` equalled the pen name id, at revision 3, with two superseded revisions and a
read key).

Symptom: after restarting the daemon on the new source, `GET /api/zines` still answered with the
**legacy id** (`73682e4a…`, identical to `pen_name.id`), so the migration looked like it had not
run — the opposite of what the store tests, all green, asserted. The tell was in the binary's
mtime: `target/debug/hush-daemon` was older than the source edits. `cargo test -p hush-daemon`
builds the `--test` artifact and does **not** refresh the bin target, so the running process was the
pre-reshape build; the same slot as before, a different mechanism from the entry above.

Resolution: `cargo build -p hush-daemon` explicitly, restart, re-check. The migration then ran on
real data and the result was verified twice: `zine_id` became a minted uuid
(`48b92ed5-62e7-429e-b303-78beb7a84e68`), `pen_id` recovered the old id
(`73682e4abccc262c0f5d4d786f24c70afaa59f941080f41b0eac144f040ca70f`), revision 3, both history
entries, the 64-char `prev_hash`, the body and the read key all intact; and the id was unchanged
after a restart, which a re-migration could not have produced because it mints a fresh uuid each
pass.

Lesson: "the tests pass" and "the process I am talking to contains the tests" are different claims.
Before verifying against a running daemon, check the binary's mtime, not just that it answers.

### `pkill -f` matched the shell that was running it — `FIXED`

Attempted: restart the `peer-a` daemon with `pkill -f 'hush-daemon.*--dir /home/sam/ProjectHush/instances/peer-a'`
followed by a `setsid nohup … &` in the same command.

Symptom: the daemon was killed, no replacement started, and the redirect target
(`/tmp/hush-daemon-zines.log`) did not exist — `tail` reported "No such file or directory". The
shell tool wraps every command in a `/bin/bash -c` whose own command line contains the pattern, so
`pkill -f` matched and killed that wrapper mid-command, before the `nohup` line ran. The earlier
`pgrep -af` output in the same session shows the wrapper text, which is what made the cause
identifiable.

Resolution: anchor the pattern to the process's own argv (`pkill -f '^\./target/debug/hush-daemon .*peer-a'`),
which the `/bin/bash -c …` wrapper cannot match, and `disown` the background start.

Lesson: any `pkill -f` run through a shell wrapper is a candidate to match itself. Anchor to the
start of the command line, or kill by pid.

### The CDP verification script hung with no output, and one assertion read `null` — `FIXED`

Attempted: drive the Zines pane in headless Chrome over CDP (publish a second post, then revise the
migrated one) and capture the result.

Symptom: the run was piped to `tail -70`, so nothing appeared until the process exited; the process
never exited because the open CDP WebSocket kept node's event loop alive, even after the script's
last `console.log`. A first pass had exited only because it threw a `TypeError` (an undefined row),
which is exactly why the hang looked like a new failure rather than a missing `process.exit(0)`. The
same pass also recorded `mainTitle: null` for a title that rendered fine: the sample was taken
immediately after publish, before the detail fetch resolved, and `.zine-article-head h1` did not
exist yet. Neither was an app defect; both cost a round trip to diagnose.

Resolution: `process.exit(0)` at the end of the script, output redirected to a file rather than
piped to `tail`, and the assertion re-read after the pane settled — which returned
`Field notes on a local zine`, `revision 4`, and the per-post history. The pane was then verified
end-to-end: "Write a post" → a "New post" draft → publish → two rows both marked "Yours", the
migrated post untouched at rev 3 → open it → "Write a new revision" seeded with **that** post's
title and body → publish → the original at rev 4 with three history entries and the second post
still at rev 1.

Lesson: a harness that never exits cannot report a failure, and a DOM assertion taken the same tick
as a click reads a pane that has not painted. Both belong to the harness, and neither is evidence
about the app.

### The dev vault's relay answers `429 Too Many Requests` on drop drains — `OPEN`

Not this slice, recorded because it is the last thing in the daemon log cited as evidence above:
`hush-daemon: drop drain failed: relay error: drop get failed: 429 Too Many Requests`, repeatedly,
against the cloudflared relay stored in `peer-a`'s config. It did not affect zines (nothing in this
slice publishes to the wire — Phase 2 is unstarted) and it is an environment/rate-limit condition
rather than a repo defect, but it means the daemon log is noisy and a drops claim made from this
vault would need the relay sorted first.

## 2026-10-12 — Conclave Paper, verification follow-up (ended-conclave read-only)

Trigger: an independent browser-verification pass over the finished Paper slice, run against the
two-peer dev stack. It found one real UI defect, one stale-build blocker, and one tooling limit. The
defect is the reason this section exists: the plan's read-only box had been ticked, and the tick was
wrong.

### An ended conclave hid the paper, so the read-only editor was unreachable — `FIXED`

Attempted: verify "the paper renders read-only after `ConclaveEnd`" in the live UI, in an ended
conclave (`9aeb64a4`, "Browser paper verify", which had a real converged document in it).

Symptom: the ended view was correct as far as it went — `Ended — read only` in the header, the
member row, and "This conclave has ended. Its history stays here, and no one can send in it." — but
`[role=tab]` was `[]` and `.ProseMirror` was `null`. There was no Chat | Paper pill, so there was no
way to reach the paper at all, and the read-only notice it was supposed to show
("This conclave has ended, so the paper is read-only.") never appeared on any path.

Root cause: `conclavePane` returned at its `ended` branch *before* the tab strip was built and
before `renderPaperSurface` — the only caller of `attachEditor` — so for an ended conclave neither
the pill nor the paper surface was ever constructed. `attachEditor`'s `readOnly` path was reachable
only for the other refusal case (a vault that is no longer a joined trustee), which is not the case
its copy names.

This was a UI bug contradicting a deliberate daemon design, not a missing feature: `GET
/api/paper/{id}` stays `200` on an ended conclave, and the daemon's own test says so in as many words
(`an_ended_conclave_paper_refuses_writes`: "The document is still readable — read-only, not gone").
The UI was hiding a document it was built to show, and the plan's Phase 5 box had been ticked against
the plan rather than against the running app.

Resolution: the ended branch now builds the pill first and keeps both surfaces — the paper renders
read-only (no toolbar, `contenteditable` off, the reason note), and only the composer is dropped, so
the chat surface is unchanged. Verified live on `peer-a`: `[role=tab]` = `["Chat", "Paper"]` with the
paper tab selected, `.paper-readonly-note` present, `.ProseMirror` `innerText` = the converged
document text, `contenteditable="false"`, 0 toolbar buttons; the chat tab still shows the ended note
with no composer; and a live (unended) conclave still renders its 11 toolbar buttons and an editable
surface. The plan and task docs now carry the correction.

Lesson: a read-only surface has two halves — refusing the write and still showing the document — and
a suite that asserts the refusal (daemon) plus a component test that asserts the flag (UI) can both
be green while the app renders neither. The check that would have caught it is a DOM assertion in an
*ended* conclave, which is what this pass added.

### The read-only notice named the wrong reason for a kicked trustee — `FIXED`

Attempted: same pass; read the copy on the read-only path.

Symptom: `attachEditor(..., readOnly: true)` hard-coded "This conclave has ended, so the paper is
read-only.", but `readOnly` was also true for a vault that is no longer a joined trustee — kicked, or
an invitation never accepted. A kicked trustee on a perfectly live conclave was told the conclave had
ended.

Resolution: `attachEditor` now takes the refusal's **reason string** (`null` = editable) instead of a
boolean, and the sentence is chosen by `paperReadOnlyReason()` from the roster the pane already reads.
Found and fixed in the same pass as the entry above; logged separately because it is a different bug
in a different layer, and it survived the earlier "verified" tick for the same reason.

### The live daemons were an older build than the source — again — `FIXED`

Attempted: verify fan-out and live cursors through the running two-peer dev stack.

Symptom: the same tell as the earlier entry of this name, which is why it is worth saying that the
tell was **not** learned: `GET /api/paper/{id}/presence` and `POST /api/paper/{id}/hub/rehome`
returned `404` with an **empty** body on both daemons, and `GET /api/paper/{id}` answered `200` but
serialised no `fast_path` field, which the current `PaperView` always writes. So the running
processes were a create/get/update-era build: no fan-out, no presence, no fast path. Two claims
(convergence, cursors) could not be tested at all, and a verification pass came back inconclusive for
reasons that had nothing to do with the code.

Resolution: rebuild, restart, and re-check rather than assume. The live `peer-a` daemon now
serialises `"fast_path": {"path": "relay", "live_peers": 0}` and answers `POST
/api/paper/{id}/hub/rehome` with `422` and a real deserialisation message (`missing field 'hub'`)
instead of an empty `404`; `peer-b` answers `401 {"error":"locked"}` on the presence route while a
bogus route on the same daemon is `404`, which shows routing resolves before the lock check, so the
route exists there too. `peer-b`'s `fast_path` field could not be read while it is locked, and is
recorded as unchecked rather than assumed.

Both unverified claims were then closed against the current build: `./scripts/paper-dogfood.sh` on a
fresh three-daemon run, 24 checks, 0 failures — descriptor and delta fan-out in both directions,
byte-identical convergence, the late joiner's catch-up snapshot, the DataChannel proven with the
relay left undrained, lock degradation and recovery, cursors with name and colour in both directions,
re-home, succession on a kicked hub, and an ended paper that is read-only and still readable. The
UI-level half was confirmed separately: in the live "UI paper verify" conclave, Alice's editor
renders `ALICE-BROWSER-7Q4BOB-BROWSER-3Z9`, i.e. both authors' text in one document.

Lesson: this is a recurrence, and the earlier entry already had the diagnosis and the tell. What was
missing was the habit, not the knowledge — so the fix that matters is procedural: treat "restart the
daemons" as the first step of a verification pass against a running stack, not as the step after a
claim comes back unverified. A stale binary in the same slot as the last one will look like the last
one's bug.

### Multi-tab interaction is pinned to one tab — `WORKED AROUND`

Attempted: drive Alice's window and Bob's window in the same browser session to watch cursors cross.

Symptom: `browser_navigate`, `browser_click` and `browser_type` all acted on a single controlled tab
regardless of `viewId` or a `browser_tabs select` first, so the second peer's UI could not be driven
directly. Bob's window was instead driven by injecting a same-origin
`<iframe src="http://127.0.0.1:5173/?api=http://127.0.0.1:9877">` into the controlled tab and using
CDP `Runtime.evaluate` for clicks and reads. A dev-server hot reload mid-pass wipes that iframe and
resets the view, so the workaround is only stable while no file is being edited.

Tooling-related, not a repo problem: it costs time and it is why the earlier pass leaned on daemon
API evidence for the two-sided claims. Not fixed here — the fix belongs in the browser tooling.

### Two dead-code warnings in a build that was otherwise clean — `FIXED`

Attempted: read the dogfood run's build output rather than only its check results.

Symptom: `cargo build -p hush-daemon` warned that `paper_conclave_ended` (main.rs) is never used, and
that `COMMENTS_CAP`, `normalize_comment_body` and `merge_comment` (zine_store.rs) are never used.
Both are real signals, and they are not the same signal.

Root cause, paper: `paper_conclave_ended` was superseded by the inline `conclave.ended` check inside
`paper_write_refusal` and left behind. Genuinely dead, so deleted.

Root cause, zines: the comment plumbing is Phase 3 work — the task doc has "Comments: seal to the
pen-name public key, publish, pull, trial-decrypt, merge, republish" as an unchecked Phase 3 box —
but Phase 1b delivered the sidecar shape it needs, and the unit tests are the only caller today. A
`#[cfg(test)]` caller does not count as a use for dead-code analysis, which is why a tested function
reads as unused in a normal build.

Resolution: the paper helper is gone; the three comment items carry `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a
comment saying Phase 3 is what reaches them from a route. Verified: `cargo build -p hush-daemon` is
clean for `main.rs`, `zine_store.rs` and the paper modules, and `cargo test -p hush-daemon` is 157
passed / 0 failed. The remaining warnings in that build are pre-existing and in `torbox.rs`.

Lesson: a "never used" warning is a question about intent, and the answer differs per item — delete
what was superseded, annotate what is staged. Leaving it unread makes the next real one invisible.

## 2026-10-12 — Zines Phase 1 (implementation and live verification)

Trigger: "implement Zines as a new button in Rail". Scope: the pen-name keypair in the vault, the
`zines.enc` sidecar, the `/api/zines/*` routes, and the Rail pane with a ProseMirror editor. The
four entries below were all found by driving the finished slice in the real UI, not by the suite.

### An authored zine was stored with no read key, so its own body never rendered — `FIXED`

Attempted: publish a zine from the Rail pane and open it.

Symptom: the list row, the byline, the tags, and the facet counts all updated, and the article head
rendered — but the body was missing. `GET /api/zines/{id}` returned `"read_key": null` for a zine
this vault had just authored, and the UI showed "This vault has no read key for this zine."

Root cause: `ZineFile::read_key` documents that "Phase 1 mints it for our own zine so the field is
populated before anything publishes", but `ZinesState::write` set `read_key: None` on create. The
doc described the intent; the code did not implement it. Every other symptom of a successful publish
was present, which is what kept it invisible — the store tests never asserted on the field.

Resolution: `mint_read_key()` (32 random bytes, base64) is called on create; `backfill_read_keys()`
mints one for any authored zine that predates the change and `zines_sidecar` persists the result, so
the upgrade runs once on the first read rather than waiting for the next edit. A held zine is left
alone — only the author holds the plaintext. Verified live: the existing zine on `peer-a` gained a
32-byte key on the first read after the rebuild, the key is stable across reads, and the article body
now renders with its `<strong>` mark intact.

Lesson: a doc comment that states a behavior is not evidence the behavior exists. The check that
would have caught this is an assertion on the field, not on the endpoint's status code.

### The article guard refused a zine the vault had written itself — `FIXED`

Attempted: same run, before the daemon fix was in.

Symptom: even with a body present in the descriptor, `renderZineArticle` returned early.

Root cause: the guard was `if (!read_key)`, which is true for a held zine that has not been given its
key yet **and** for an authored zine whose key was never minted. Only the first is a real "cannot
read" state; an authored zine's plaintext is in the vault's own descriptor.

Resolution: the guard is now `if (!read_key && !authored)`. Held separately from the daemon fix on
purpose: the two are independent, and either one alone would have hidden the other's bug.

### `richText.ts` was clobbered when the ProseMirror schema was extracted — `FIXED`

Attempted: create a shared ProseMirror schema for Paper and Zines by writing a new module.

Symptom: the write landed on `apps/hush-tauri/src/lib/richText.ts`, overwriting the existing
mail-body sanitizer (`escapeHtml`, `sanitizeHtml`, `bodyToDisplayHtml`, `htmlToText`, `isBlankHtml`).
Mail bodies would have rendered through the editor's schema instead of the sanitizer.

Root cause: the new module was named after the concept rather than after what it holds, and the name
collided with a file that already owned a different concern.

Resolution: the original `richText.ts` was restored from git and the new code went to
`proseSchema.ts`. The sanitizer and the editor schema are separate files with separate jobs.

Lesson: check for an existing file at the target path before writing a new one, especially when the
name is the obvious one.

### An `EditorView` mounted into a detached element, so the editor rendered unstyled — `FIXED`

Attempted: mount ProseMirror into a host container that a re-render could re-parent.

Symptom: the editor host was in the DOM, but the ProseMirror surface was not — no toolbar styling,
no cursor. The same bug appeared in both Paper and Zines, because both were written the same way.

Root cause: `new EditorView(surface)` mounts **into** `surface`, and the code then called
`wrap.appendChild(view.dom)`, which moved `view.dom` out of `surface` into `wrap` and left `surface`
detached. The ordering looked right in the source and was only visible in the rendered DOM.

Resolution: `surface` is appended to `wrap` first, then `new EditorView(surface)` is constructed, and
the redundant `wrap.appendChild(view.dom)` is gone. Both call sites were fixed.

### The publish button stayed disabled after typing — `FIXED`

Attempted: type into the draft editor and publish.

Symptom: the button was enabled for a seeded draft and stayed disabled for an in-place edit, so a
user who typed a new article could not publish it.

Root cause: `publish.disabled = !zineEditorIsDirty()` was evaluated at render time, and ProseMirror
edits mutate the document in place without triggering an app re-render.

Resolution: `renderZinesDraft` keeps a reference to the publish button and `zinesDraftChanged()` is
called from `dispatchTransaction` on `tr.docChanged`, so the button updates in place.

Lesson: an in-place editor inside a render-on-demand UI needs an explicit change channel back to the
UI. Re-rendering on every keystroke would have been the other option, and it would have thrown away
the cursor.

### The rail's write button opened a blank editor over an existing article — `FIXED`

Attempted: press "Write a new revision" in the rail, then publish.

Symptom: the title and sections were pre-filled from the existing zine, the editor was empty, and
Publish was enabled the moment a character was typed. Publishing would have replaced the head
revision with a blank article. The old body survives in `history`, but the head is what a reader
opens.

Root cause: the rail button seeded `""` for the body, because the rail holds the index and a
`ZineSummary` carries a `preview`, not the article. The title and sections *were* seeded, so the
editor read as "the body is gone" rather than "write a new one". The article's own revise button
seeded correctly from the detail, so the two paths disagreed — which is why clicking the one in the
reading pane looked fine.

Resolution: `zinesStartOwnDraft()` seeds from the open detail when it is the caller's own zine, and
fetches it otherwise. A failed fetch announces and opens no draft at all: an editor that looks ready
and would destroy the article is worse than a refusal. Verified live both ways — the rail button and
the article button now seed the same body, bold run included.

Lesson: two entry points to one destructive action must be tested as two paths. Only one of them was
wrong, and the one that worked is the one that got exercised first.

### The reading pane kept rendering a stale detail after mute and rename — `FIXED`

Attempted: mute the open zine, then rename the pen name, watching the article.

Symptom: the daemon recorded both changes, but the article's Mute button kept its old label after
the toggle, so a second click repeated the same request instead of reversing it.

Root cause: `renderZineArticle` renders from `zinesDetail`, which is fetched by `zinesOpen` and never
refreshed. `zinesMute` and `zinesSetPenName` store the returned **index**, which the list and the
facets read, but the detail was left as it was.

Resolution: both handlers patch the open detail from the daemon's answer — the mute flag from the
returned index, the byline only when the detail is authored, since a rename does not move a held
zine's byline. Verified live: Mute toggles to Unmute and back with the row gaining and losing
`muted-row`, and a rename round trip moves the byline in both the article and the rail without a
refetch.

### A probe read the mute label before the re-render and looked like a second bug — `OPEN` (tooling)

Attempted: drive the mute toggle from one CDP script with fixed 800 ms waits.

Symptom: the label appeared to lag one click behind. A second, longer-waited probe showed the
sequence was correct, and the earlier reading was a race: the daemon was slow under a failing drop
drain loop (`429 Too Many Requests` in its log), so the response had not arrived inside the wait.

Resolution: not a repo problem. Re-probed with a poll-until-condition loop instead of a fixed sleep,
which is what the first probe should have done.

Lesson: a fixed sleep in a probe is an assumption about latency. Poll for the condition being
asserted, or the probe reports the harness's timing as a product defect.

### The forget path cannot be exercised in Phase 1 — `OPEN` (by design, not a defect)

Attempted: open the forget confirmation on the demo zine.

Symptom: no Forget button. `renderZineArticle` only offers it when `!authored`, so the modal is
unreachable for a zine this vault wrote — and in Phase 1 every zine is authored, because held zines
need Phase 2's bulletin.

Resolution: none needed. The route is covered by `zines_round_trip_a_create_an_edit_a_mute_and_a_forget`
and a live check that a zine this vault does not hold is 404 with a reason, but the **modal** has no
end-to-end evidence. Recorded rather than claimed.

## 2026-10-12 — Zines spec (design, docs-only)

Trigger: the user proposed member blogs with comments, broadcast to all members, and asked to grill
the idea into a locked spec. Scope: docs only — `docs/tasks/zines.md` (new), the milestone index,
`PROTOCOL.md`, `THREAT_MODEL.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `docs/tasks/hush-articles.md`, and the roadmap. No
code.

### "A blog is a single-author Paper" was too broad — the CRDT does not carry over — `FIXED`

Attempted: framing the blog idea as a direct generalization of Task 19's Paper ("a blog is almost
exactly a single-author Paper"), then writing the spec on that basis.

Symptom: the framing implied zines would reuse Paper's `yrs` CRDT and the ProseMirror/Yjs bridge.
Writing the spec made the mismatch explicit — a zine article has exactly **one** writer (its pen
name), and each comment is a separate signed blob merged by the author, so there is no concurrent
edit to merge. A CRDT would be dead weight and `y-prosemirror` a dependency with no purpose.

Resolution: the spec states the correction up front — zines reuse Paper's **spine** (sidecar-store
pattern, per-trustee fan-out, payload codec, tolerant `Unknown` decode) but **not** its CRDT; the
editor reuses the ProseMirror rendering and toolbar without Yjs. Recorded in `zines.md` Section 2.

Lesson: "reuses task X's spine" and "reuses task X's mechanism" are different claims. Name the
spine's parts explicitly before leaning on the analogy — the CRDT was the one part that did not
transfer, and it was the part most likely to be assumed.

## 2026-10-12 — Conclave Paper, verification and the create collision

Trigger: driving the finished slice end-to-end in two real app windows instead of trusting the
suite. That turned up one real correctness bug and two process problems.

### Two trustees starting the paper at once produced two papers for one conclave — `FIXED`

Attempted: open the Paper tab in two app windows and click "Start paper" in both, to check
convergence in the real UI.

Symptom: the text converged **both ways**, so nothing looked wrong — but
`GET /api/paper/{conclave_id}` on the two daemons returned **different** `paper_id`s, each with
`hub` set to its own vault. `fast_path` was `{"path":"relay","live_peers":0}` on both sides, for the
life of the paper, and no cursors ever appeared.

Root cause: `PapersState::adopt` looked a paper up by `paper_id` while `create` and `get` key on the
conclave. A second descriptor for the same conclave therefore did not match the entry already
there — it was pushed as a **second** paper. Each side kept its own as "first", so `get(conclave)`
returned each side's own descriptor, `paper.hub == me` was true on both, and `paper_dial` returned
early on both. Neither side ever dialled. The content still converged because the relay fan-out is
by **conclave** and `conclave_of` resolved both ids once each side had adopted the other's
descriptor, so the only visible symptom was a permanently dead fast path.

Resolution: `adopt` keys on the conclave, and a collision is settled deterministically — the
earlier `created_ms` wins, ties go to the smaller id, and the loser takes the winner's identity
while keeping its own document. That is the rule the UI already promised ("the first create wins
and everyone else adopts it") and it is total, so both sides pick the same winner from the same two
descriptors with no extra round trip. Because the loser's earlier deltas went out under the old id
and the winner dropped them as unknown, the daemon re-announces the folded document as a
`PaperSnapshot` when it notices its paper has been re-identified. Verified end-to-end: after the
fix both daemons report the same `paper_id`, `hub` = the earlier creator, and
`fast_path: {"path":"live","live_peers":1}`; cursors then render in both editors. Three unit tests
cover the rule (`a_create_collision_settles_on_the_earlier_paper`,
`the_later_create_loses_on_the_side_that_started_first`,
`a_create_collision_on_the_same_millisecond_still_picks_one_winner`).

Lesson: `create` refusing a second paper it has never seen cannot prevent a distributed collision,
and keying a sidecar on one identity while a sibling method keys on another is the kind of
inconsistency that produces no error at all. The fan-out being keyed on the conclave is what hid
it — a bug whose only symptom is a performance feature quietly not working is invisible to a test
suite that only checks convergence.

### The dev stack was running a daemon binary older than the source — `WORKED AROUND`

Attempted: `./scripts/run-two-ui.sh --dev` after changing `paperStore.ts`, then driving the UI.

Symptom: the UI behaved as if the feature did not exist. Probing the running daemon directly:
`GET /api/paper/{id}/presence` → **404 with an empty body**, `POST /api/paper/{id}/hub/rehome` → 404
empty, and `GET /api/paper/{id}` had no `fast_path` key. An empty 404 is axum's fallback, so those
routes did not exist in the running binary; a real handler answers with JSON
(`{"error":"no paper in this conclave"}`), which is what a bogus path did not do. The daemons had
been left running from an earlier session.

Resolution: killed the daemons and re-ran the script. This is a **process** problem, not a repo
problem — the script says it reuses a daemon that is already up, which is right for editing the UI
and wrong after touching `crates/`. Worth knowing the tell: **an empty-bodied 404 from the daemon
means the route is not in the running binary**, so the binary is stale, not the request wrong.

Lesson: "the code is right but the behaviour is old" is a stale binary until proven otherwise.
Probe for a route the change added before debugging anything else.

### The remote cursor's label was a 64-character account id — `FIXED`

Attempted: read the rendered cursor markup in the live editor.

Symptom: `<div style="background-color: #b7791f">05cde85f415c09d24220b5bda8dc1ce04364e9678c4509
60d7272376de9f0cbd37</div>` — the caret was drawn with the right colour and the wrong label.

Root cause: a peer publishes its account id as `user.name`, which is deliberate (it is the identity
the relay authenticated, so a peer cannot label its caret with someone else's name), but nothing
resolved it to a name for display.

Resolution: the receiver relabels the frame before applying it (`relabelAwareness` in
`paperWire.ts`), looking the id up in the conclave roster — the same source the member list and the
chat use. An account the roster cannot place is passed through untouched, so an unknown peer keeps
its id rather than losing its cursor. Verified in the live UI: Alice's editor renders
`<div style="background-color: #b7791f">bob</div>` and Bob's renders `alice`. Five unit tests cover
the codec, including two-peer frames and unreadable bytes.
